title: SNB sight deposits hit highest on record last week
text:
ZURICH, April 27 (Reuters) - The amount of cash commercial banks hold with the Swiss National Bank hit the highest on record last week - when the franc marked its biggest fall in two months - suggesting the central bank may have intervened to weaken the currency.

Switzerland's currency soared against the euro following the SNB's shock decision in January to scrap a 1.20-per-euro cap on the franc.

The safe-haven currency has since pared some gains, and sight deposits data is closely followed for signs of possible SNB intervention in the market to weaken the franc, which would support Switzerland's export-driven economy.

Sight deposits stood at 385.899 billion francs ($403.4 billion) in the week ending April 24, SNB data showed on Monday, up from 383.984 billion francs the previous week and the highest since public records began in 2004.

"The fact the sight deposits rose implies that the SNB has probably been active buying foreign assets, particularly euro-denominated assets," said IG Bank market analyst Andreas Ruhlmann.

Sight deposits - which can be freely transferred or converted into cash - measure the amount of money commercial banks hold with the SNB.

The SNB can expand such deposits through foreign exchange swaps and repurchases of its own debt.

A spokesman for the SNB declined to comment when asked about possible market intervention by the central bank.

Switzerland's currency weakened 0.8 percent against the euro last week, the biggest weekly slide since the middle of February.

The SNB's move last week to reduce the number of institutions exempt from negative rates on their cash deposits held at the central bank also put downward pressure on the franc.

SNB Chairman Thomas Jordan stressed again last week that the central bank remains willing to intervene in foreign exchange markets to weaken what it sees as too strong a currency.

However, Zuercher Kantonalbank economist David Marmet said any intervention by the SNB at the moment would probably be on a small scale.

"They can intervene but ... not with a bazooka," Marmet said. "If they intervene it's a small intervention." ($1 = 0.9566 Swiss francs) (Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: Europe's Central Bankers Hit Calmer Waters
text:
The Wall Street Journal's Daily Report on Global Central Banks for Wednesday, April 8, 2015:

Sign up for the newsletter: http://on.wsj.com/grandcentralsignup ("http://on.wsj.com/grandcentralsignup")

Highlights

-- Blackstone's Take: Europe's Central Bankers Hit Calmer Waters

-- Kocherlakota Says Fed Should Be "Extraordinarily Patient" On Rates

-- 5 Things to Watch in the Fed's March Minutes

-- Bank of Japan Votes Down Call to Slash Easing

-- Ukraine in Talks to Boost Emergency Cash Reserves

BLACKSTONE'S TAKE: EUROPE'S CENTRAL BANKERS HIT CALMER WATERS

After a topsy-turvy start to 2015, Europe's central banks appear to have found their footing.

The European Central Bank said Tuesday that it hit its monthly target of 60 billion euros ($65.1 billion) in bond purchases in March, the first month of its new quantitative easing program.

This occurred despite the fact that government bond purchases only began on March 9, and helped to alleviate concerns that the ECB won't be able to find sufficient assets to buy to meet its ambitious goal of EUR1.1 trillion in asset purchases by September 2016.

And things have stabilized in smaller European countries whose currencies had been rocked by the ECB's QE program. Denmark's central bank--which intervened massively in currency markets in January and February to keep the krone from strengthening too much against the euro--didn't intervene last month, the bank said Tuesday.

In Switzerland, where a soaring franc early this year fueled concerns of deflation, consumer prices fell less than expected in March on an annual basis, by 0.9% versus market expectations of a 1.1% drop. That will likely reduce pressure on the Swiss National Bank to take additional unconventional easing steps, such as deeper cuts to its already negative deposit rate.

This week's reports support the prevailing view that the focus of financial markets will shift away from Europe in coming months and toward the Federal Reserve, which will decide as soon as June whether to raise interest rates for the first time in nearly a decade.

Still, if the past few years in Europe are any indication, the calm could prove fleeting. A rising share of the eurozone government debt market trades at negative yields-- Spain joined the club Tuesday with a negative rate on six-month T-bills--which could make it harder down for the road for the ECB to buy large amounts of government bonds unless it pays a high premium for them.

And any hiccups from Greece or elsewhere in the eurozone could put renewed upward pressure on currencies in Denmark, Sweden and Switzerland, forcing those central banks to respond.

But for now, central bankers in Europe should welcome the reprieve, however long it lasts.

-By Brian Blackstone

MORNING MINUTES: KEY DEVELOPMENTS AROUND THE WORLD

Kocherlakota Says Fed Should Be "Extraordinarily Patient" On Rates. The Federal Reserve should hold off on raising interest rates until the second half of 2016, Minneapolis Fed President Narayana Kocherlakota said Tuesday. "Under my current outlook, I continue to believe that it would be a mistake to raise the target range for the fed funds rate in 2015," he said.

5 Things to Watch in the Fed's March Minutes. The Fed last month gave itself the option of raising interest rates in June, but also signaled it will remain cautious about actually pulling the trigger. More clues about the debate inside the U.S. central bank could be revealed when the Fed releases minutes of its March 17-18 policy meeting. Here's what to watch when they come out Wednesday at 2 p.m. EDT.

Fed's Bear Stearns, JPMorgan, AIG Bailout Records Remain Secret -- Courthouse News Service. Federal Reserve memos and spreadsheets regarding emergency loans to three big financial firms during the 2008 crisis are not subject to release under the Freedom of Information Act, a federal judge ruled Tuesday.

Dollar Coin Loses Currency on Savings. At one time, the U.S. could have saved billions by ditching the flimsy dollar bill in favor of a durable coin. But for a dollar coin to succeed, the dollar bill needed to be eliminated. Now, the lifespan of paper money has increased, the bulk of the potential savings has been forfeited and the U.S. Federal Reserve, which once supported the change, is against it.

ECB Hits Its March Bond-Purchase Target. The European Central Bank reached its target of EUR60 billion in monthly bond purchases under a new stimulus program launched in March, a sign of resolve that the bank will eventually pump more than EUR1 trillion in freshly created money to stoke the European economy and boost inflation.

ECB's Mersch Shoots Down Speculation of Deposit Rate Cut--Boersen-Zeitung. ECB executive board member Yves Mersch rejects speculation the bank could cut its deposit rate below the current rate of -0.2%. He said in an interview with German newspaper Boersen-Zeitung, "From my point of view, a cost-benefit analysis rules out another cut in the deposit rate." --Dow Jones Newswires.

Bank of Japan Votes Down Call to Slash Easing. The Bank of Japan's internal split widened Wednesday, as Gov. Haruhiko Kuroda's toughest critic on the policy board officially called for a steep reduction of its aggressive monetary stimulus.

Denmark Stays Out of Currency Market. Denmark's central bank refrained from intervening in the foreign-exchange market in March, in a sign that the national currency has stabilized against the euro following weeks of volatility brought on by the European Central Bank's stimulus efforts.

Bank of Russia Sees No Ruble-Related Risks to Financial Stability. The Bank of Russia sees no risks to financial stability from volatility in the ruble, which has firmed to levels last seen in late December, the head of the monetary policy department at the bank said on Wednesday --Dow Jones Newswires.

Ukraine in Talks to Boost Emergency Cash Reserves. Ukraine is in talks with several countries to provide currency swap lines to boost the country's emergency cash reserves, the International Monetary Fund's No. 2 official, David Lipton, said Tuesday.

Hungary's Central Bank to Build Portfolio of Chinese Yuan Bonds. The Hungarian central bank said Tuesday it had decided to build a bond portfolio denominated in Chinese yuan in a bid to diversify its foreign-currency assets. The move, which will take place in several steps, won't materially influence the adequacy of the central bank's foreign-exchange reserves since the portfolio will be relatively small in size, the National Bank of Hungary said in a statement --Dow Jones Newswires.

Hungary Central Bank Wants Big Rise in Investment Guarantee Limit. Hungary's central bank wants a four-fold increase in the amount of compensation investors would receive for unlawful losses or bankruptcies, the bank said Tuesday, after thousands of retail investors saw big losses following the recent bankruptcies of various locally owned brokerages. The bank has proposed increasing the maximum indemnity payment to 100,000 euros ($109,861) from the current limit of 6 million Hungarian forints ($22,030). --Dow Jones Newswires.

Spain Joins Negative Yield Club. Spain's government on Tuesday issued short-term debt yielding a shade under 0%. The EUR725 million ($796 million) in six-month Spanish debt delivers an average yield to investors of -0.002%. Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland and Austria already have all their short-term debt trading with yields under 0% in the post-issuance market.

India's Central Bank Still Struggling With New GDP Figures. While it's the job of every central bank to find the fine balance between growth and inflation, India's top central banker says he's feeling a bit wobbly, as he's uncertain how to read the country's recently revised gross domestic product numbers.

GRAPHIC CONTENT

How Rich and Poor Spend (and Earn) Their Money. For many Americans, the rise in food and housing prices is a tough squeeze. That's because--even in an era with low overall inflation--low-income Americans spend a disproportionate share of their money on food and housing. New data from the Labor Department show the extent of the discrepancy.

FORWARD GUIDANCE

-8 a.m. EDT: Fed's Powell speaks on "Challenges for Monetary Policy" in New York

-10 a.m. EDT: New York Fed's Dudley speaks in New York

-2 p.m. EDT: Federal Reserve releases minutes from its March 17-18 policy meeting

RESEARCH

Nominal GDP: Target or Benchmark? Robert L. Hetzel wrote in an Economic Brief from the Richmond Fed: "Implemented as an activist rule, nominal GDP targeting could be destabilizing. Even if it were feasible, keeping nominal GDP on a preset path in the face of an inflation shock could initiate a recession, while keeping nominal GDP on a target path left unrevised periodically would force changes in inflation if persistent changes in productivity occurred," Still, he wrote, "articulation of a benchmark path for the level of nominal GDP would be a useful start in formulating and communicating policy as a rule. An explicit rule would in turn highlight the importance of shaping the expectations of markets about the way in which the central bank will behave in the future."

COMMENTARY

On Secular Stagnation, Ben Bernanke's Theory Meets Larry Summers's Evidence. "Two of the biggest names in macroeconomics met on the battlefield of the blogosphere last week," Greg Ip writes for the Journal. "Former Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke and former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers were debating why interest rates are so low. .. They both make persuasive (and entertaining) cases. My read is that Mr. Bernanke has theory on his side, while Mr. Summers has the evidence."

Should Monetary Policy Take Into Account Risks to Financial Stability? "Let there be no mistake: In light of our recent experience, threats to financial stability must be taken extremely seriously," former Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke writes on his blog. "However, as a means of addressing those threats, monetary policy is far from ideal. .. In their efforts to promote financial stability, central banks should focus their efforts on improving their supervisory, regulatory, and macroprudential policy tools."

America's Endless War Over Money. "The "Audit the Fed" debate is the latest manifestation of a conflict as old as the nation, between those who argue that a strong central bank improves economic stability, and those who see an overbearing government engaged in harmful meddling," K evin Granville and Binyamin Appelbaum write in a New York Times illustrated timeline of U.S. central-banking controversies.

BASIS POINTS

- The number of job openings in the U.S. climbed to the highest level in 14 years, surpassing five million for the first time since January 2001. But the number of Americans actually getting hired for jobs fell for the second consecutive month, as did the number of people who voluntarily quit.

- Americans pared their credit-card debt in February, the Fed reported Tuesday. Outstanding consumer credit--reflecting Americans' total debt outside of mortgages--grew in February, but the gain was entirely driven by car loans and education debt rather than credit cards.

- Aging populations and sluggish advances in worker productivity are binding the global economy to a bleaker, low-growth fate, the International Monetary Fund said in a new report Tuesday.

- The Czech central bank, which recently has stepped up its rhetoric warning of possible foreign exchange interventions, on Wednesday said its foreign-exchange reserves at the end of March edged up slightly on the month in euro terms, but fell when measured in U.S. dollars--Dow Jones Newswires.

- Inflationary expectations in Russia have started to stabilize, the central bank monetary policy chief said Wednesday, underpinning expectations that more rate cuts are in the pipeline --Dow Jones Newswires.

- The Reserve Bank of Australia and the People's Bank of China extended a local-currency-swap agreement worth A$40 billion (CNY 200 billion) --Dow Jones Newswires.

- Retail sales in the eurozone fell in February after four successive monthly increases, an indication that the boost to the spending power of households from lower oil prices may be waning.

- The Bank of Portugal has a new smartphone app, available in both Portuguese and English.

title: Will Denmark Throw in the Towel on the Peg?
text:
The Swiss National Bank shocked markets last month by abandoning its cap on the value of the Swiss franc against a plunging euro. Since then, speculation has been rife in markets that Denmark's central bank could be the next to throw in the towel.

With almost alarming regularity, the Nationalbanken, Denmark's central bank, has lowered interest rates four times already this year to limit the krone's appeal and defend its peg--which is intended to provide a stable backdrop for Danish companies.

The peg seeks to stop the euro falling more than 2.25% below (or rising 2.25% above--although that's not the issue right now) 7.46038 krone, by buying (or selling) foreign currency. The bank's also stepped up its intervention in currency markets and even suspended issuance of government bonds in a bid to lower the krone.

But all the rate cutting has fueled talk that the Danish central bank is starting to think twice about the huge quantities of foreign assets it needs to buy to defend the peg.

Jens Nordvig, head of fixed income research at Nomura, notes that so far this year the Nationalbanken has increased its reserves by more than $30 billion as it buys foreign currency to hold down the krone. That means in terms of the size of its economy, Denmark is intervening at a similar pace to that of Switzerland right before the Swiss bank decided to remove the limit on the exchange rate between the franc and the euro.

"There is no doubt that the pressure on the krone is very significant, and that the fight for the peg will be a tough one," Nordvig said.

But investors shouldn't get carried away with the Swiss-Danish parallels. That's because the background to Denmark's peg is very different, according to Mr. Nordvig.

Unlike the Swiss currency cap, a recent innovation introduced in 2011 to deal with the franc's strength during the euro crisis, the Danish peg has been around since 1982 (when the currency was pegged to the Deutschmark). And the Danish peg has widespread political support and the backing of all major political parties. There's no sign of the popular opposition to monetary policy that led to a Swiss referendum late last year aiming to force the central bank to hold more gold.

As long as the political will remains, analysts reckon the Nationalbanken has the tools at its disposal to defend the peg. A central bank trying to prop up its currency by selling reserves (like Russia recently) can run out of assets to sell. But buying assets to weaken your currency is, at least theoretically, a limitless exercise.

"Even if a central bank turns insolvent for a while, IT IS A CENTRAL BANK. They don't care about liquidity, and can survive technical insolvency [in the] worst case," said Aurelija Augulyte, a senior currency strategist at Nordea.

title: SNB Ready to Curb Any Franc Strengthening -- Bank President
text:
ZURICH--Switzerland's central bank remains ready to intervene in foreign currency markets to curb any strengthening of the franc, Swiss National Bank President Thomas Jordan said Tuesday, adding the currency remains "significantly overvalued."

Mr. Jordan said the currency will pose "major challenges" for the Swiss economy and the SNB has introduced negative interest rates to blunt its strength. But he offered no new insight as to why the central bank scrapped a three-and-a-half-year-old cap on the currency last month, a move that sent it shooting higher and roiled the foreign exchange market.

The SNB has "lowered rates to unprecedented levels to cushion the effects of the franc's currency appreciation and this should have a corrective effect on the franc's valuation," Mr. Jordan said in prepared remarks to be delivered in Brussels on Tuesday.

Mr. Jordan's comments come a month after the SNB abandoned a policy of preventing the franc from strengthening above 1.20 francs per euro as investors sought the currency as a safe haven. The policy was designed to protect Switzerland's export-dependent economy, which is reliant on the eurozone as a market for more than half of its exports.

The franc had surged to above parity with the euro when the SNB dropped the cap on Jan. 15. It has since eased to around 1.0600 per euro, but remains high by historic measures.

"The Swiss economy is now dealing with very difficult exchange-rate conditions," Mr. Jordan said. "In an interdependent world with highly integrated and liberalized capital markets, the strengths of an economy like Switzerland can, paradoxically, turn into a major challenge."

Mr. Jordan said the cap was an "exceptional and temporary measure," repeating comments he has made since the cap was lifted. He added that the European Central Bank's quantitative-easing program would have made the SNB's defense of the cap unsustainable.

"The SNB had no choice but to discontinue its policy," Mr. Jordan said. "By maintaining the minimum exchange rate for longer, the SNB would have run the risk of losing control over its balance sheet."

Mr. Jordan acknowledged the decision to abandon the cap came as a surprise but said this was unavoidable.

"No pre-emptive guidance is possible for this kind of decision, as any guidance would have invited speculative attacks."

title: UPDATE 1-Swiss sight deposits rise, add to signs of possible SNB  intervention
text:
(Updates with strategist comment)

ZURICH, Feb 9 (Reuters) - The amount of cash commercial banks hold with the Swiss National Bank crept up slightly last week, adding to signs that the central bank may have intervened to weaken the franc since removing the currency's cap last month.

The SNB on Jan. 15 scrapped the 1.20-per-euro cap it imposed on the Swiss franc in September 2011, surprising financial markets. Maintaining the policy would have cost the bank 100 billion francs ($108 billion) in January alone, the SNB later said.

The move sent the safe-haven franc soaring against the euro, though the single currency has regained some ground amid speculation that the SNB is intervening in the market.

In the week ending Feb. 6, sight deposits rose to 384.889 billion francs, SNB data showed on Monday, from 383.325 billion the previous week.

An SNB spokeswoman declined to comment on Monday when asked whether the central bank had intervened.

Sight deposits - which can be freely transferred or converted into cash - measure the amount of money commercial banks hold with the SNB. The SNB can expand such deposits through foreign exchange swaps and repurchases of its own debt.

"I think they (the SNB) are intervening, and they haven't tried to pretend that they're not," said Jane Foley, a senior FX strategist at Rabobank in London.

"But what we saw last week was euro/dollar off its lows, and I think that relieved some of the pressure for the Swiss and the other European central bankers too."

SNB Chairman Thomas Jordan said in an interview broadcast on Saturday that the bank is prepared to intervene in foreign exchange markets and has room to push interest rates further into negative territory, if necessary, to weaken the franc.

Jordan declined to say whether the SNB had intervened recently, though data last week showing Switzerland's foreign exchange reserves hit a record high in January also pointed to interventions.

The SNB has attempted to discourage new flows into francs - viewed as an ultra-safe investment - by imposing an interest rate of -0.75 percent on some cash deposits.

($1 = 0.9235 Swiss francs) (Reporting by Alice Baghdjian and Joshua Franklin in Zurich and Jemima Kelly in London; Editing by John Stonestreet and Susan Fenton)

title: Swiss  central bank 's  forex  reserves rise sharply in December
text:
ZURICH, Jan 7 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank's foreign exchange reserves rose sharply in December, data showed on Wednesday, after the central bank said it intervened last month to keep a lid on the red-hot franc.

The figures are the first indication of Switzerland's intervention last month, when a rapidly weakening Russian rouble pushed the franc up further and prompted the SNB to defend a three-year old cap on the franc against the euro by intervening in currency markets.

The central bank said last month it would start charging banks for deposits in francs for the first time since the 1970s, hoping to stem a flight to the safe-haven currency driven by concern over the euro zone and Russia's deepening crisis.

The SNB held 495.104 billion Swiss francs ($490.15 billion) in foreign currency at the end of December, compared with 462.669 billion francs in November, revised from an originally reported 462.395 billion, preliminary data calculated according to the standards of the International Monetary Fund showed.

The SNB capped the soaring franc in September 2011 to help stave off recession and the threat of deflation and was forced to intervene heavily in 2012 as the euro zone crisis flared, swelling its already large foreign currency reserves. title: RPT-Euro zone's troubles, gold vote test Swiss  central bank
text:
(Repeats, without changes, story first published on Sunday)

* Euro crisis prompted 1.20 euro cap on Swiss franc

* Intervention risk rising again

* Gold referendum feeds upward pressure on franc

By Alice Baghdjian and Silke Koltrowitz

ZURICH, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank faces the biggest test of its cap on the franc in two years but may find it easier to defend now than when euro zone breakup fears were rampant and the strategy unproven.

The franc rose to its strongest level since September 2012 on Friday, brushing up against the 1.20 euro limit the Swiss National Bank introduced in 2011 when the currency's strength was squeezing exporters and threatening deflation.

Renewed weakness in the euro zone, and the European Central Bank's readiness to use radical measures to kick-start the economy, have fired up demand for the franc.

A referendum this month on Swiss gold reserves is also playing a role. While approval seems unlikely, a Yes vote would force the SNB to buy gold alongside any currency interventions.

Still, capital flows into Switzerland have declined sharply from the height of the euro crisis, as have fears that the interventions would spark inflation.

More importantly, the SNB's success in defending the cap back in 2011 and 2012 means it may not have to intervene on the same scale to fend off any new market challenges.

"The difference between now and 2011 is that the wider markets and most economists believe these interventions can break the neck of speculation," said Rudolf Strahm, an economist and former Swiss lawmaker.

"Some market players tried once to attack the franc but all they got was a bloodied nose and lost vast sums of money. Since then no one has dared to try again."

INTERVENTION POINT

The franc was trading at 1.2015 per euro by 1200 GMT on Friday, close to the 1.2010 francs per euro level where economists say the SNB has intervened in the past.

The SNB shocked markets when it imposed the limit in September 2011 after the currency shot to record highs against the euro. The following year, as fears of a Greek exit from the euro zone grew, traders unsuccessfully challenged the cap. It has since become the backbone of SNB policy.

The latest bout of franc strength is unlikely to prompt such intense purchases, economists say.

The SNB poured billions of francs into the market until September 2012 to establish the limit, swelling its currency reserves, now around 460 billion Swiss francs ($475 billion) or about 70 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

The cap was breached only once in April 2012, adding credibility to the central bank's pledge to defend the policy with the utmost determination and purchase foreign currency in unlimited amounts to do so.

"It is possible that the SNB intervenes in coming days or weeks, but we would not expect the same level of interventions as in 2012," said Maxime Botteron, a Credit Suisse economist.

Back then, Swiss investors were repatriating foreign funds out of fear for the euro zone. Anxiety has since subsided.

Stagnating prices and faltering economic growth in Switzerland have silenced critics who warned of inflationary risks from the interventions and has underscored the need for the cap to ward off deflation.

The policy has garnered support from exporters and tacit approval from other central banks. The risks from the vast purchases are limited because losses on forex reserves are pure accounting losses, economists say, though the bank will need to unwind the reserves at some point.

"We really don't see any inflationary pressure yet, even for the next one or two years, so there is no real limit to balance sheet expansion," said Botteron. "From our point of view, the exchange rate floor brings more benefits than costs."

This could change quickly if the nation votes on Nov. 30 to oblige the central bank to hold at least 20 percent of its reserves in gold, up from 7 percent currently. However, polls show limited support.

SNB Chairman Thomas Jordan has gone out of his way to warn of the risks attached to the proposal.

The alternative to interventions would be negative interest rates. But that could add fuel to Switzerland's real estate boom and prove expensive for its large financial sector. (1 US dollar = 0.9656 Swiss franc) (Editing by Noah Barkin/Ruth Pitchford)

title: Rates to Zero. What Does Sweden's Riksbank Do Now?
text:
Will Sweden's central bank be forced to put a lid on its currency?

That may seem like an odd question to ask when the krona has just plunged to a four-year low against the euro and the dollar. But a growing chorus of analysts is tipping the Riksbank to follow central banks in Switzerland and the Czech Republic by intervening in markets to stop its currency growing too strong.

The reason is a familiar one for central bankers around the world: chronically-low inflation. Swedish inflation has been stuck close to zero for most of this year, way below the Riksbank's target of 2%. That's why it cut interest rates to zero on Tuesday.

The krona duly tumbled. That should help: a stronger currency dampens inflation by making exports more expensive and squashing import costs. But with no room left to cut interest rates further, the Riksbank may have to cook up some new measures if the krona begins to rise again or inflation doesn't pick up.

Crucially, the central bank is hostage to developments outside of Sweden. Inflation is tumbling pretty much everywhere--but particularly in Sweden's closest neighbor, the eurozone. And the European Central Bank has already slashed its own rates to negative territory and is widening the scope of its asset purchase program. That puts downward pressure on the euro, effectively lifting the krona.

"The Riksbank isn't the only central bank with this problem-- a large number of global central banks are undershooting their inflation targets. [But] Sweden is a small, open economy so it's very dependent on global trade and vulnerable to the spillover effects of low inflation," said Thomas Kressin, a currencies portfolio manager at Pacific Investment Management Co., which has $1.87 trillion under management.

If the ECB ramps up its stimulus efforts, Mr Kressin thinks the Riksbank will have to respond, probably by selling krona on the open market. To do so, it could purchase foreign bonds, but would probably stop short of publishing an exchange rate target that could be challenged by speculators, he said.

Many think the central bank will go further.

"The cut to zero may not have the desired effect; and we expect inflation to remain low over the next few years. If the currency does appreciate against the euro, we may see a currency floor," said James Pomeroy, an economist at HSBC.

It wouldn't be the first. Since 2011, the Swiss National Bank has pledged to intervene in the foreign-exchange market to prevent the euro from trading under 1.20 against the Swiss franc. In doing so, the SNB has accumulated huge stacks of foreign assets. The Czech Central bank also has a commitment to keep the euro above CZK27 against the Czech koruna.

Some think Sweden will avoid monetary policy experiments.

"We do not see a repo rate below zero or the launch of unconventional measures. The Swedish economy and the credit-channels are working well," wrote analysts at Nordea after the rate decision. But if the Riksbank is forced to do more, a lower limit for the exchange rate is the most likely course of action, they added.

Expect months of guesswork over what exchange rate might be picked as the limit, if any.

title: Swiss c.bank should use any franc weakness to unwind  intervention  -IMF
text:
* SNB could unwind forex positions amid franc weakness

* IMF report compiled earlier in May, before franc slide

ZURICH, May 21 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank should use any weakness in the franc to unwind the large foreign currency reserves it has built up to keep a lid on its currency, the International Monetary Fund said in a report released on Tuesday.

The SNB set a cap of 1.20 Swiss francs to the euro in September 2011 to help stave off recession and the threat of deflation.

It then intervened heavily last year as the euro zone crisis flared, selling francs and swelling its own foreign reserves to prevent its currency from strengthening as investors sought safety in the franc.

The SNB should maintain its cap on the franc, given low inflation and growth and the risk of further capital inflows, the IMF said in the report, compiled early in May before the franc hit multi-month lows against the dollar and euro.

"The authorities should also take full advantage of any capital outflows to unwind past currency interventions," the IMF's executive board said in its Switzerland consultation report, concluded on May 8.

The franc hit a nine-month low against the dollar and a four-month low against the euro this month and could fall more in coming months as concerns about a euro zone break-up wane and risks of deflation in Switzerland mount.

The SNB should also consider introducing negative interest rates on excess bank reserves if the franc comes under fresh appreciation pressures, the IMF said, reiterating views expressed in a March statement.

The central bank still sees the franc as overvalued and will continue to defend its cap as long as necessary, SNB board member Fritz Zurbruegg was quoted as saying last week.

(Reporting by Alice Baghdjian; Editing by Hugh Lawson)

title: UPDATE 1-SNB denies it is driving down euro zone core yields
text:
* SNB rejects S&P findings on bond-buying

* Bought 80 bln euros of "core" bonds Jan-Jul-S&P

* SNB buying exacerbates euro zone bond divergence-S&P

(Adding SNB reaction)

ZURICH, Sept 25 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank (SNB) has denied claims by ratings agency Standard & Poor's that its bond buying was driving down yields for the "core" euro zone states as fundamentally flawed and unfounded.

S&P said in a report on Tuesday that the SNB had bought about 80 billion euros ($103.7 billion) of bonds issued by Germany, France, the Netherlands, Finland and Austria over the first seven months of 2012, effectively funding half of their budget shortfall for the full year.

However, the Swiss central bank said that S&P's report ignored key data and that the assumption that it had bought 80 billion euros of government bonds of the states in question was unfounded.

"It (the S&P report) ignores the sizeable increase of SNB deposits with other central banks and international institutions, which are published monthly by the Swiss National Bank," SNB said in a statement. 

The S&P report had said that the bond purchases, the result of SNB's intervention to cap the Swiss franc by buying euros, are part of the reason for yields for "core" euro zone bonds sinking close to record lows while borrowing costs for other euro zone states remain high.

"Largely unnoticed, Switzerland's decision to stem the appreciation of the Swiss franc has led to a de facto recycling of funds from the eurozone periphery to its core, via the Swiss National Bank," the S&P report said.

SNB imposed a cap on the soaring franc a year ago at 1.20 per euro to fight off a flood of money fleeing the euro zone and lessen the risk of the strong currency causing deflation and recession in Switzerland.

Heavy interventions to defend that level pushed SNB's holdings of foreign currency to 418 billion Swiss francs ($446.4 billion) at the end of August, 71 percent of annual output, though the pace of the rise has slowed as market tensions have eased.

The most recent quarterly data to the end of June showed that SNB held 60 percent of its reserves in euros and 22 percent in dollars, with the bulk invested in highly rated government bonds, though SNB gives no detailed breakdown.

S&P said that SNB was unlikely to reverse the inflow into core euro zone bonds because central banks are typically hold-to-maturity investors.

"However, we also think that this inflow may diminish at some point in the future, potentially leading to upward movement of borrowing costs for some sovereigns that are currently benefiting from peripheral capital flight," it said.

SNB Chairman Thomas Jordan said on Tuesday that falling sovereign bond yields supported the view that a gradual recovery in Europe was under way, but added that it was too early to sound the "all clear" and the SNB was still committed to holding down the franc. title: UPDATE 1-Swiss exports slip in May on weakening EU demand
text:
* Watches only sector to see growth in exports

* Machine exports see sharp declines

* UBS SME barometer shows deterioration in May

(Adds details, background, economist quotes)

By Catherine Bosley

ZURICH, June 21 (Reuters) - Switzerland's exports fell for the third month in a row in May, hit by the strong Swiss franc and weakening demand in the euro zone, raising the likelihood that the country's economic growth will slow in coming months.

Exports fell by a real 3.7 percent in May to 17.5 billion francs ($18.5 billion) compared with the same month last year, the Federal Customs Office said on Thursday. Exports to the European Union dropped 10 percent, or by about a billion Swiss francs, while exports to Asia eased 4 percent, the data showed.

More than half of Switzerland's exports go to the euro zone, and Swiss companies have been battling a soaring safe-haven franc since the financial crisis erupted in 2008.

To prevent Switzerland slipping into recession and deflation, the Swiss National Bank (SNB) in September set a cap of 1.20 francs per euro. But slack demand in euro zone is now giving Swiss firms more of a headache than the exchange rate.

"Of course the franc does not help, but we've had this level of exchange rate for nearly a year now and the effect at one point is fading," Sarasin economist Alessandro Bee said.

"At the moment it's really the global environment rather than the franc."

Fears of Greece leaving the euro zone rose sharply in May. This has increased new safe-haven flows into Switzerland and prompted the SNB to intervene more heavily to maintain the franc cap than earlier this year.

Last month also proved gloomy for small and medium sized business - the backbone of the Swiss economy, whose situation declined, a barometer published by UBS on Thursday showed.

TOUGH FOR MACHINES

Among the sectors suffering particularly are the machinery sector and the chemicals sector, which includes drugs made by Roche and specialty chemicals by Lonza.

According to the trade data for May, exports from the machine and electronics industry sank by a real 15.3 percent from a year earlier, while exports from the metals industry fell 15.9 percent.

Earlier this year, exporters and the tourism sector called on the SNB to shift its cap on the franc and weaken it further. Those calls have died down of late, however, and the SNB has said it cannot just move the cap at will to any desired level to insulate the economy.

"For us, the cap on the franc is justified by the economic situation," said Credit Suisse economist Maxime Botteron. "But we don't think the SNB will raise the cap to 1.40. We've seen the central bank is under considerable pressure of late, I think it would be quite difficult to raise it."

Although better-than-expected first-quarter growth prompted the SNB to revise up its growth forecast to 1.5 percent for 2012, Chairman Thomas Jordan said at a policy review last week that growth would slow significantly later this year.

Jordan's assessment was mirrored by the ZEW investor sentiment index, which plunged in June and indicates that weak foreign demand will drag on growth in Switzerland in the second half of the year.

However exports of watches continued to buck the trend, withstanding the strong currency mainly because shoppers in Asia value Swiss timepieces for their quality and prestige.

Watches, including those made by Swiss-listed firms Richemont and Swatch, were the only sector to see export gains in May. They climbed by 10.2 percent in real terms to 1.911 billion Swiss francs, a faster rate of growth than in April. ($1 = 0.9454 Swiss francs)

(Reporting by Catherine Bosley; Editing by Catherine Evans)

title: Sov. wealth fund wouldn't help cap franc-Jordan
text:
ZURICH, June 14 (Reuters) - The chairman of the Swiss National Bank on Thursday rejected the idea of using foreign currency reserves to create a sovereign wealth fund, saying it would not help defend the central bank's cap of 1.20 per euro on the safe-haven Swiss franc.

"The creation of such a fund would not help to enforce the minimum exchange rate," Chairman Thomas Jordan said in the text of a speech for the bank's quarterly policy review. "It does little to assist Switzerland or Swiss monetary policy."

The SNB's foreign exchange holdings have risen sharply in recent years as the bank has intervened to stem the franc's rise during the euro zone's debt crisis. The SNB capped the franc at 1.20 per euro last Sept. 6, threatening unlimited interventions if needed.

Some politicians and commentators in Switzerland have suggested the SNB create a sovereign wealth fund to help boost the return on its forex holdings, which are now chiefly invested in highly rated government debt.

title: WSJ(4/6) Europe's Markets Are Tested Anew
text:
(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL) 
   By Tom Lauricella and Charles Forelle 

New strains surfaced in European markets as a slide in the euro forced Switzerland's central bank to intervene in currency markets and Spanish bond yields climbed to their highest level this year.

While trading was thin ahead of the Easter break, traders said the moves reflected further erosion of the positive tone that had supported European bonds, stocks and the euro since the start of the year. On Wednesday, a poor auction of Spanish debt reminded investors that the euro zone's sovereign-debt crisis remains far from resolved despite an enormous injection of cash into the banking system by the European Central Bank.

"The medicine is wearing off," said Richard McGuire, a senior interest-rate strategist at Rabobank International.

The euro sank against the dollar, sliding to $1.3066 late in New York, its weakest level since mid-March, from $1.3142 late Wednesday.

At the end of 2011 and again in February, the ECB provided cheap loans to European banks through long-term refinancing operations, known as an LTRO, totaling some $1.2 trillion. For market sentiment, said Mr. McGuire, "LTROs were a sizable boost but only a temporary one."

On Thursday, much of the attention was on the currency markets, where the Swiss franc lurched higher against the euro and briefly broke through 1.20 Swiss francs per euro, hitting 1.1990 before bouncing back. Traders said the Swiss National Bankintervened to stem the franc's rise.

The Swiss central bank has vowed to keep 1.20 as a line in the sand that it will defend, seeking to halt damage to the Swiss economy from a higher currency, which hurts exporters by making their products more expensive overseas. Last summer the Swiss currency saw heavy demand as a haven amid worries about the euro zone's debt crisis. The aggressive stance by the Swiss central bank generally has been considered a success.

But investors recently have been pushing the Swiss franc higher amid concern that Europe's economy may be worsening and governments will have a tougher time meeting fiscal targets. Some of the selling of euros Thursday also may have been traders lightening up positions ahead of a four-day Easter break in Europe.

Elsa Lignos, currency strategist at RBC Capital Markets in London, said the pressure is on the central bank. "The Swiss National Bank has to step up . . . and make sure it doesn't let its credibility slip," Ms. Lignos said.

Stresses also mounted in the European government-bond market Thursday, with Spanish borrowing costs hitting levels last seen before the ECB refinancing operations. Ten-year yields on Spanish bonds climbed 0.15 percentage point to 5.81%, their highest level since Dec. 1, according to Tradeweb.

The LTRO money had been vital to supporting asset prices across Europe in the first quarter, and Italian and Spanish yields fell sharply. But bondholding data show that much, if not nearly all, of the ECB-fueled buying came from domestic banks.

Wednesday's auction, at which Spain sold 2.6 billion euros ($3.42 billion) in bonds, near the bottom of what it hoped to sell, suggests that even that demand may be waning. In addition, the ECB's cash injection came in the form of three-year loans, and Spain had to pay much steeper yields to attract buyers for debt that is longer than three years.

That could present a problem for Spain. Foreigners have been selling Spanish debt all year, and if domestic banks aren't able to fill the gap, the country could struggle to issue what it needs to in order to cover a budget deficit.

"We're seeing some doubts creeping back in about whether or not Spain is going to be able to stick to all its promises," said David Mann, head of research in the Americas for Standard Chartered Bank. There also is worry about "how much Germany is going to pressure them and how much stress that's going to create in the markets," he said.

As with the currency market, some traders in the bond market felt moves were being magnified by thin trading in the run-up to the Easter break. Spain also has some room for maneuver. The country already has raised nearly half of its 2012 borrowing needs.

---

Neil MacLucas, Tommy Stubbington and Neelabh Chaturvedi contributed to this article.

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: 2nd UPDATE: Global  Forex  Turnover Likely Fell Sharply Into 2012 - BIS Paper
text:
-- Average daily foreign exchange trading volume hit $4.7 trillion in October before dropping

-- Trading volumes declined as the euro zone's sovereign debt crisis intensified

-- Higher emerging market bond issuance in the fourth quarter helped offset tight credit conditions

(Adds February data from EBS in 6th paragraph, quote from hedge fund manager in 7th-8th paragraphs.)


 
   By Martin Vaughan and Enda Curran 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

Foreign exchange trading volumes fell sharply toward the end of 2011 as the euro zone's sovereign debt crisis flared up and European banks cut back lending worldwide, the Bank for International Settlements said in its quarterly report.

Non-European banks and emerging market bond issues helped to fill funding gaps as European lenders retrenched from global markets in the final part of last year, the BIS said in its report, released Sunday.

Daily turnover in global foreign-exchange markets likely reached $4.7 trillion on average in October 2011, but volumes likely fell sharply toward the end of the year and into the start of 2012, BIS researcher Morton Bech wrote.

Foreign exchange volumes were hit hard through 2011 by the euro zone's debt crisis, as rolling volatility kept investors on the sidelines. Figures from a range of trading centers show volumes during October fell for the first time since 2009, when markets were recovering from the collapse of U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers.

The last time the BIS measured daily foreign exchange trading volumes was in April 2010, in its triennial report. At that time it estimated daily turnover at $4 trillion. The Basel, Switzerland-based BIS describes itself as a banker to central banks, serving as a counterparty for central bank transactions and conducting research.

A number of brokers and trading platforms have reported declining foreign exchange volumes over the past several months. ICAP, which operates the EBS platform, said last week average daily spot foreign exchange volumes for February were $126.7 billion, up 9% from January but still 9% below where volumes were in February 2011.

Beyond the dampening effects of the European crisis, central bank intervention has also played a role in why volumes have decreased since October last year. Bernard Lock, Asia Pacific head at hedge fund FX Concepts, said that intervention by Japan and Switzerland in markets to weaken their respective currencies initially caused volumes to spike as traders scrambled to unwind positions.

"At first, people tried to go against it, then they rushed to cover their positions and then ultimately they had to surrender," he said. "That $4.7 trillion is quite a special number. We cannot count on seeing that again soon," said Lock.

BIS researchers also found that a roughly 50% increase in emerging market bond issuance in the fourth quarter of 2011, compared with the previous quarter, helped compensate for shrinking available bank credit as a result of European deleveraging.

That helped support asset prices and kept trade finance flowing even as European banks sold assets and reduced lending, the BIS said. "An open question is whether other financial institutions will be able to substitute for European banks as the latter continue to deleverage," the BIS wrote in its quarterly review.

-By Martin Vaughan and Enda Curran, Dow Jones Newswires; +65 6415 4033; martin.vaughan@dowjones.com [ 12-03-12 1150GMT ]

title: Swiss Franc's Bulls Get Ready For SNB's  Intervention
text:
By William L. Watts 
 

FRANKFURT (Dow Jones)--Switzerland is renowned for watches, knives and chocolates. How about bazookas?

A showdown between Switzerland's central bank and investors bullish toward the Swiss franc appears inevitable as the euro sinks ever closer toward a 1.20 franc trading floor officials set last September. That means the deflation-fearing Swiss National Bank will likely find itself with no choice but to deploy maximum firepower by intervening heavily to sell its own currency, known commonly as the Swissie, versus the euro.

The euro on Tuesday traded at CHF1.2038, down 0.1% from Monday.

Swissie bulls, who had pressed the currency to record highs against the euro and the U.S. dollar last summer, stampeded for the exits when the central bank established the floor, marking one of the most dramatic trading days of 2011.

That was a testament to the credibility of the Swiss National Bank, which vowed to halt a rising franc it feared would otherwise sink the alpine country's export-oriented economy into a deep recession and deflationary spiral.

Traders remembered the central bank's earlier interventions to weaken the franc. While they ultimately failed to reverse the tide, the interventions did serious damage to traders caught on the wrong side.

The well-timed interventions appeared aimed at creating pain for speculators and touching off chaotic market conditions. And in 2011, the Swiss National Bank appeared poised to be even more aggressive.

But things have changed.

Earlier this month, Philipp Hildebrand resigned as chairman of the central bank in the wake of a controversy over his wife's foreign-exchange trading activity. Vice Chairman Thomas Jordan took the helm on an interim basis as the central bank decides on a new permanent chief.

The Swiss National Bank vowed that its commitment to the 1.20 franc trading floor remained unchanged in the wake of Hildebrand's resignation, stating that it would pursue its policy "with the utmost determination."

It was also widely assumed that Swiss National Bank veteran Jordan would soon be formally named to succeed Hildebrand.

That initially kept the Swissie in check. But since then, the Swiss government has indicated that it may take weeks or months to name a permanent successor to Hildebrand.

Moreover, critics of the Swiss National Bank have been emboldened, casting doubt on the ability of policy makers to preserve the central bank's independence, said Peter Rosenstreich, chief FX analyst at SwissQuote Bank in Geneva.

To Rosenstreich's thinking, that means the Swiss National Bank will likely have to back up its tough talk with action very soon: A test of the 1.20 franc level appears inevitable, he said.

In other words, questions about the central bank's credibility are effectively contributing to a stronger Swiss franc.

That's not the only thing that's topsy-turvy. The European Central Bank's decision to inject massive amounts of long-term liquidity into the euro-zone financial sector has been cited as a key factor in driving down peripheral euro-zone government bond yields.

The injections, much like the U.S. Federal Reserve's full-fledged rounds of quantitative easing, are credited with lifting investors' overall risk appetite. That should be bad for safe-haven currencies such as the Swiss franc and the Japanese yen.

But the Swissie and the yen have been rising even as so-called risk assets rally, indicating that some of the European Central Bank's long-term refinancing flows are also leaking into safe-haven assets, said Alan Ruskin, currency strategist at Deutsche Bank in New York.

"It is unlikely to be a coincidence that the SNB is finding it tough to limit Swiss appreciation after the ECB's generous liquidity additions," Ruskin said in emailed comments.

He notes that the normally positive correlations between the euro/Swiss franc pair and bellwether risk indicators like the S&P 500 index have turned negative in the last 30 days, while the correlation between euro/Swiss and Italian bond yields has turned positive, indicating a break in the link between risk appetite and the franc.

"This suggests that there is a bigger flow story here regardless of risk, that is going to force the SNB to again massively inflate its balance sheet, this time by being forced to follow the ECB's lead," Ruskin said.

While currency traders debate where exactly the Swiss National Bank will choose to intervene, Rosenstreich said the prospect for massive intervention has made the euro a good buy as it's fallen below CHF1.21.

With the euro hovering around CHF1.205, "we think it's a great buy with 50 pips on the downside and unlimited upside," he said.

But traders should be nimble and take profits when the Swiss National Bank's inevitable intervention arrives, he said. Over the long run, he questions whether the central bank can hold the line at 1.20 if the European debt crisis takes a decided turn for the worse.

In other words, subsequent interventions are likely to get less bang for the franc.

-William L. Watts; 415-439-6400; AskNewswires@dowjones.com [ 01-31-12 1329ET ]

title: UPDATE: Swiss National Bank Keeps EUR/CHF Floor At 1.20
text:
--SNB keeps EUR/CHF floor at 1.20

--SNB says Swiss franc still high at current level

--SNB ready to take action if growth outlook worsens, deflation risk rises

--SNB expects CHF to weaken over time

--SNB points to uncertainty, euro zone risks

--Uncertainty for exporters reduced since floor introduction in September

--SNB sees growth slowing to 0.5% in 2012

(Adds detail, comment.)

By Anita Greil

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss National Bank Thursday kept the minimum floor unchanged at 1.20 Swiss francs against the euro, even as it warned of a highly uncertain international economic outlook, saying that a further escalation of the European sovereign debt crisis can't be ruled out.

Even at the current floor, the Swiss franc is still high and should continue to weaken over time, the SNB said. The central bank reiterated that it will defend this level with "utmost determination," and was prepared to buy foreign currencies in unlimited quantities if need be.

Currency markets have been awash with speculation that the SNB may lift the floor to CHF1.25 or even CHF1.30, because the franc is still trading below purchasing power parity against the euro, and its high value against the euro renders exports expensive.

In recent days, however, most economists moved to predict an unchanged floor, saying the high-level of uncertainty in the euro-zone pressures the euro, which would make it tough for the SNB to defend a higher floor. What's more, Swiss government officials repeatedly urged exporters and parliamentarians to stop pressuring the SNB, saying it was important that the central bank can act independently.

If the economic outlook and deflationary risks so require, the SNB said it would take further measures.

"The central bank obviously highlighted the escalation in the European credit crisis," said Peter Rosenstreich, chief forex analyst at Swissquote, a medium-sized Swiss bank. "For us this was the key reason the SNB didn't adjust the EUR/CHF floor higher," he added.

At 0935 GMT, the euro traded at CHF1.2272, while the dollar was quoted at CHF0.9446.

The euro almost hit parity against the Swiss franc this summer, while the dollar was also trading at a record low. After the SNB set a floor against the euro on Sept. 6, the franc weakened against both currencies.

Even if the franc is still high at the current level, planning uncertainty for exporters has been removed because they can now rely on the euro no longer falling below CHF1.20. The SNB has been able to defend the level with surprising ease. Data on foreign exchange reserves suggest, that it didn't have to buy much foreign currency to defend the floor, as market participants stayed clear of testing it, knowing that the SNB would intervene.

The central bank noted that economic growth in Switzerland slowed considerably in the third quarter, but kept its growth forecast for this year at 1.5% to 2%. Next year, economic growth will slow to 0.5%.

"The international outlook continues to be highly uncertain," central bank President Philipp Hildebrand said. "A further escalation of the European sovereign debt crisis can't be ruled out."

This would have grave consequences for the international financial system. Moreover, given Switzerland's close relations with the euro zone, Switzerland's economic prospects are highly dependent on how the crisis develops, he added.

In the near future, there is no risk of inflation in Switzerland, the SNB said. There are, however, downside risks for price stability should foreign demand fall off more sharply than expected, the central bank added.

"In the short term, inflation will dip into negative territory sooner, owing to the effects of the earlier currency appreciation, which have been stronger than expected," Hildebrand said.

The SNB expects an inflation rate of 0.2% this year, a negative inflation rate of -0.3% next year, and inflation of 0.4% in 2013.

The forecast is based on three-months London Interbank Offered Rate at zero and a depreciating Swiss franc, Hildebrand said.

The SNB left the target for the three-months London Interbank Offered Rate at close to zero.

title: CORRECT: Swiss Franc Buckles After Swiss Price Growth Reverses
text:
("UPDATE: Swiss Franc Buckles After Swiss Price Growth Reverses," at 1016 GMT, misstated the date of the Swiss National Bank's meeting in the fourth paragraph, due to an error from the source. The correct version follows:)

-- Swiss franc falls sharply after Swiss price growth reverses

-- Traders fear further franc-weakening steps from the SNB

-- But analysts said the central bank will stay away for now


 
   By Eva Szalay 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LONDON (Dow Jones)--The Swiss franc fell sharply across the board Monday as traders fled the currency after inflation data from the country revealed that the strong currency is hitting retailers and pushing the economy towards deflationary territory, but analysts said the weak data print won't trigger more central bank intervention yet.

Price growth in Switzerland reversed in October and showed a 0.1% contraction, as the effects of the safe-haven franc took its toll on the export-led economy and increased fears that the country's central bank would take further steps to weaken the currency.

The euro spiked to CHF1.2394 after the data release, from CHF1.2294, while the dollar traded as high as CHF0.9033 from CHF0.8957, as traders braced for the chance that the Swiss National Bank could respond by lifting the euro's minimum level against the franc from the current CHF1.20 level.

"[Inflation] is one of the metrics they're looking at and I think people will be looking to see what [SNB chairman Philipp] Hildebrand has to say after the Dec. 15 central bank meeting," said Chris walker, a currency strategist at UBS in London.

Walker added that as the market is so easily spooked by intervention fears, the SNB will likely let the market sell the franc of its own accord, before the SNB raises the floor in the euro's value against the franc from the current CHF1.20 level.

"We have to bear in mind that it takes at least three months for currency effects to filter through to the economy," said Sara Yates, a currency strategist at Barclays Capital in London. "I don't think today's print will change monetary policy."

Yates added that while Barclays Capital expects the SNB to raise the floor in the longer term, it doesn't think the central bank would plunge in just yet but instead it will likely keep the market nervous. The SNB implemented a price floor under the euro's value at CHF1.20 against the franc in September, after the franc appreciated around 20% against the European currency from start of the year to September.

Traders have since been fearful of yet more intervention steps and regularly sold the franc against the euro when market chatter intensified. Comments like those from SNB Chairman Philipp Hildebrand Sunday noting that the currency is still too strong have also kept market participants on their toes.

title: FOREX  FOCUS: Japan Suffers For Having A Weak  Central Bank
text:
--Intervention power remains in political, not BOJ's, hands

--Investors not impressed with Japan like they are with SNB

--BOJ JGB purchases may help cap yen a little for now

By Nicholas Hastings

A DOW JONES NEWSWIRES COLUMN

LONDON (Dow Jones)--Currency markets are one place where reputation matters.

And Japan is finding this out the hard way.

The country is currently under the kosh with growth forecasts being cut and exporter share prices tumbling sharply.

Why?

Because the yen is at the strongest level it has been against the dollar since the Second World War and there is nothing the Japanese can do about it.

What is particularly galling for the Japanese is that the Swiss have had the same problem with their currency, the franc, but they have been able to resolve the issue for now.

How come? Because currency markets respect the Swiss National Bank.

The difference between the SNB and the Bank of Japan is clear. The former has a long reputation for managing the Swiss currency with market intervention when needed.

When the SNB said a few weeks ago that it would cap the franc's rise come what may, the markets listened and investors stopped buying the currency despite its attractions.

The new Minister of Finance Jun Azumi has tried a similar threat, but investors have just kept on buying the yen.

This is because, unlike Switzerland, the power for intervention to manage the currency in Japan lies in the hands of the Ministry of Finance. The Bank of Japan may control every other aspect of monetary policy but the control of the yen is political.

And investors aren't impressed.

Azumi may rant and rave about the yen's strength but having just been appointed to his position this summer, the markets really aren't listening.

And even if Azumi does unleash intervention to stop the yen from rising, investors will more than likely just take the opportunity to buy the currency cheaply, assuming that it will continue to rise again anyway.

Just look at Capital Economics' updated forecast. It is looking for a dollar down at Y60 in 2013 now. Before, it was looking for a dollar up at Y95 from just under Y76 now.

Part of the problem for Japan isn't only the safe-haven role the yen has been given during these times of global uncertainty but also the recent weakness of the dollar.

A sharp decline in U.S. Treasury yields, driven by increased speculation of further monetary easing in the U.S., has helped to widen the yield spread between 10-year bonds even more in favor of the yen.

A move by the Bank of Japan to narrow this spread, through the purchase of long-term Japanese government bonds, would help to reduce upward pressure on the yen in the near-term at least given the close historical correlation between 10-year yield spreads and the dollar/yen exchange rate.

However, any longer-term resolution to the yen's strength through market intervention, as achieved by the SNB in capping the franc, is highly unlikely while the power to intervene remains in the hands of the Bank of Japan's political masters rather than in the hands of the bank itself.

title: WSJ(9/27) Nissan Keeps Up Pressure On Japan
text:
(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL) 
   By Chester Dawson 

YOKOHAMA, Japan -- A Nissan Motor Co. senior executive on Monday urged Japan to take "decisive" action to prevent the strong yen from hollowing out the country's industrial base, saying he hopes Tokyo can learn from Switzerland's intervention in foreign-exchange markets to weaken its currency.

The remarks are the latest in an increasingly vocal campaign by Nissan and other Japanese auto makers to push Tokyo into doing more to combat the yen's strength.

"The situation requires very determined and decisive action by the government," John Martin, a corporate vice president at Nissan, said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal.

"We're very confident that [Japanese Prime Minister Yoshihiko Noda] is going to learn from this issue with the Swiss franc," said Mr. Martin, referring to the Swiss central bank's decision to set a ceiling for the franc against the euro.

The yen has risen to "abnormal" levels that are beyond the ability of any single company to cope with, he said.

The comments are the latest warning from Japanese auto industry executives over the strength of the yen, and come after Nissan's chief executive, Carlos Ghosn, said last week that Japanese car makers may be forced into a major strategic rethink if the yen stays near its recent record levels.

In a press release on Monday, Nissan Executive Vice President Colin Dodge also piled pressure on the Japanese government, urging Tokyo to take bold monetary policy steps to halt the yen's rise.

"We're praying for the Japanese government to do something in terms of quantitative easing," Mr. Dodge said, referring to steps to slow the yen's ascent by adding liquidity to financial markets.

The Japanese currency has been under constant upward pressure amid increasing global economic uncertainties, trading near its record high of 75.94 yen against the dollar marked in August. Late Monday in Tokyo, the dollar was at 76.39 yen. The yen was trading at 120 to the dollar as recently as five years ago.

Mr. Martin said the success of the Swiss move this month to cap the safe-haven franc's exchange rate against the euro has caused a flight of speculative capital into the yen. That has added to the urgency to switch to using more foreign-made parts at Nissan's domestic assembly lines. A stronger yen makes components made in Japan less price-competitive against those sourced overseas, particularly for use in export vehicles.

Nissan plans to increase the percentage of imported parts in models assembled in Japan to as much as 40% for some models produced at its factory in Kyushu, southern Japan, by 2013, up from an average of 28% currently, the executive said. Many of those parts will come from China and South Korea, he said.

Mr. Dodge also said in his statement that while Nissan's annualized global production as of the end of August was 150,000 vehicles greater than at the same time last year, output is still 3.7% below the company's own target. He said he expects Nissan to make up the 80,000 vehicle gap between current production and the company's internal goal "unless there is a massive change in consumer sentiment in the next six to eight weeks."

Nissan's shares finished down 3.6% at 620 yen ($8.10) on trading Monday in Tokyo due to continued concerns over the yen's rise and the health of the global economy.

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Japan can't act like Swiss on  currency  rise-MOF
text:
WASHINGTON, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Japan cannot curb rises in its currency like Switzerland has done by setting a cap on its currency and pledging to defend it with intervention, as that would effectively mean abandoning monetary policy independence, a senior Japanese finance ministry official said on Friday.

Deputy vice finance minister Masatsugu Asakawa also said the country's priority should be to beat deflation which is keeping upward pressure on the yen.

"Logically speaking, as long as deflation goes on, there will be continuous pressure for the yen to rise," Asakawa said in a seminar hosted by the International Monetary Fund.

He declined to comment on the appropriate level of the yen and shrugged off the view Japan should be as bold in countering currency rises as Switzerland, which like Japan saw its currency appreciate on safe haven demand from risk-shy investors.

"Switzerland decided to abandon its independence on monetary policy. In Japan, that is simply not an option to take," he said.

The Swiss central bank earlier this month decided to set an exchange rate cap on the soaring franc and promised it would defend it with unlimited currency purchases.

Japan also intervened last month to stem sharp rises in the yen, but just for one day spending roughly 4.5 trillion yen.

That has not prevented the yen from hitting a record high against the dollar and multi-year highs against the euro, moves policy-makers fret could hurt the export-reliant economy.

Tokyo has repeatedly threatened to step into the market again to counter yen rises. But as a G7 member committed to market-determined exchange rates and with an economy much bigger than Switzerland's, Japan feels it cannot intervene unlimitedly even if rises in the yen were a concern. [ID:nL3E7KD46X]

Asakawa also warned against complacency on Japan's huge public debt, saying it would be dangerous to assume that bond yields will stay low as long as Japanese government bonds (JGBs) are held mostly by domestic investors.

title: REFILE-BOJ FOCUS-BOJ to resist pressure to be as bold as Swiss
text:
(Repeats story filed on Tuesday, adds dropped word in paragraph 3)

 TOKYO, Sept 13 (Reuters) - The Bank of Japan is relieved Switzerland's radical move to weaken the franc so far has not unleashed a flood of yen buy orders, but fears it will come under pressure from politicians to do something similarly dramatic if the yen spikes again.

 The Swiss central bank set an exchange rate cap on the soaring franc and pledged to defend it with unlimited currency purchases, fanning talk that some risk-averse investors who sought safety in the franc could turn to the yen instead.

 So far the yen has stayed below its record high hit in mid-August, but remains well above exporters' comfort levels and the Japanese central bank has signalled its readiness to ease policy again to help exporters as global growth falters.

 But it would probably do it by further expanding its asset buying programme and the central bank is already lining up arguments why "going Swiss" is neither possible nor necessary.

 "Japan is different from Switzerland because the yen is a G3 currency," said a source familiar with the BOJ's thinking.

 "Just because Switzerland is intervening does not mean it's become easier for Japan to do the same. It's not that simple."

 First, unlike the Swiss National Bank, the BOJ does not have jurisdiction over exchange-rate policy and only acts as an agent of the Ministry of Finance.

 Secondly, the Japanese economy is five times the size of Switzerland's and the yen's trading volume far exceeds that of the franc, which makes defending a pre-set exchange rate level in a globalised market close to impossible.

 Finally, as a member of the Group of Seven club of rich nations Japan has certain responsibilities, given the group's stated commitment to market-determined exchange rates.

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^  


Possible Japan response to Swiss move         	
Graphic on world rates       http://link.reuters.com/xuc92s   	
Fed, BOJ balance sheets      http://link.reuters.com/zum33s("http://link.reuters.com/zum33s")

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^	

 Finance Minister Jun Azumi probably found out himself how
difficult it is for Japan to gain consent even for unilateral
intervention when he met his G7 counterparts last week, some of
whom have expressed discomfort over Tokyo's action last month.	

 Some analysts suggest the BOJ could help weaken the yen by
adding foreign bonds to the list of assets it buys.	

 But the BOJ is loath to do this because any effective action
would require buying huge amounts, exposing its balance sheet to
considerable risk. Such action would also impinge on the finance
ministry's jurisdiction. 	

 NOT OFF THE HOOK	

 Japan's central bank has played down the possible impact of
Swiss efforts to curb the franc, and market action so far
suggests that a feared yen rally on safe-haven flows has not yet
materialised.	

 Still, jitters over Europe's debt crisis and expectations
that the U.S. Federal Reserve will further loosen its policy
could spur more flows into the yen.	

 While Japan has plenty of its own economic problems, the
depth of its financial markets and the relative stability of its
financing costs makes it an attractive option for those seeking
a safe home for their investments.	

 Another yen test of its record high could be more painful
for Japan than last month, with the global slowdown now seen as
more pronounced and no end in sight to Europe's debt crisis.	

 That could force the BOJ to abandon its forecast of a
moderate recovery by year-end when it issues long-term growth
forecasts next month.	

 A revision at a time when parliament will debate how to fund
the main batch of reconstruction spending could spur calls from
lawmakers for more aggressive central bank action.	

 Among the steps suggested by lawmakers, including senior
ruling party officials, are an aggressive balance sheet
expansion, increased purchases of long-term government bonds and
even direct underwriting of government debt.	

 Prime Minister Yoshihiko Noda, who as finance minister
avoided leaving the impression that he was leaning on the
central bank, may pay more heed to such calls and become more
vocal in demanding further monetary stimulus, some analysts say.	

 "The Federal Reserve may ease this month and the Swiss took
bold steps on currencies. The BOJ might end up being the only
major central bank not doing anything," said Takeshi Minami,
chief economist at Norinchukin Research Institute in Tokyo.	

 "If several events drive the yen up again, the BOJ will be
under pressure to act with Noda seeming very concerned about the
risk of yen rises on the economy."	

 There is a debate within the BOJ on what more it can do
beyond boosting its asset-buying programme, and some do not rule
out steps such as more aggressive bond buying as an option if
the economy worsens further.	

 But there is no consensus within the BOJ on whether the
benefits of such moves outweigh the drawbacks. Governor Masaaki
Shirakawa is among the sceptics and said after the last policy
meeting that the bank has already put powerful monetary easing
in place to hedge against potential risks.	

 Yet more market turmoil and fresh safe-haven flows may force
the BOJ's hand.	

 "If yen rises and a global downturn hit Japan at the same
time, the BOJ would be in a tight spot," said another source
familiar with the BOJ's thinking. "It is not complacent because
it knows the market's tide can change any time."	
	

(Editing by Tomasz Janowski)

title: Norway c.bank chief says could react quickly
text:
OSLO, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank governor said on Thursday the bank could react quickly to changes in the economic outlook after the Nordic country's currency strengthened due to Switzerland's decision to intervene on the foreign exchange market.

 "A too strong crown could over time lead to too low inflation and too low growth", central bank governor Oeystein Olsen said in a speech published on Norges Bank's website.

 "That would in that case be addressed by taking action through monetary policy," he said, adding that setting the deposit rate would be the tool in question.

  Olsen on Wednesday admitted the strong crown would have an impact on policy, but stressed he was in no danger of following Switzerland in intervening to weaken it. 

 "Monetary policy can react quickly to changes in the economic outlook," he said on Thursday.

  The crown weakened on Thursday and traded at 7.5748 against the euro at 0818 GMT after surging to new eight-year highs below 7.49 on the two preceding days.
