title: WSJ: Swiss Cap Move Riles Officials In Norway, Canada
text:
Norwegian and Canadian officials on Thursday criticized Switzerland's move this week to cap the rise of its currency, as the impact reverberated in currency markets world-wide.

The Norwegian krone soared against the euro after the Swiss National Bank said Tuesday that it would use "unlimited" spending to prevent the euro from falling below 1.20 francs. The move sent investors flooding into other currencies belonging to economies viewed as fiscally sound, with Norway among the top destinations.

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal website, WSJ.com.)

Norwegian central bank Gov. Oystein Olsen warned investors that a strengthening krone would stifle Norway's economy by hurting exports. A swift policy response--likely lower interest rates--is in the offing if the krone keeps rising, Mr. Olsen said.

The Federation of Norwegian Industries said Thursday that the krone's strength was putting pressure on Norway's companies. "It's a serious issue when the Norwegian krone is so strong," Knut Sunde, an executive of the federation said. "We hope that the Swiss effect will fade, but we are not sure," he said.

Canadian Finance Minister Jim Flaherty on Thursday said he is "concerned" about Switzerland's audacious move into foreign-exchange markets and worried it could ignite another round of so-called currency wars. Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega last year began referring to the prospect of "currency wars" among countries seeking to protect their economic growth by keeping the value of their currencies down.

Mr. Flaherty said he planned to discuss the issue at this week's meeting of Group of Seven finance ministers in France.

For months, funds have flowed into Switzerland and other supposedly safe countries as investors have sought havens from Europe's financial crisis and the U.S.'s economic woes. In early August, the euro fell to near-parity with the Swiss franc, from 1.50 francs at the start of 2010.

Such flows are the latest example of floods of capital leaving the world's sluggish economies--especially the U.S. and the euro zone--and entering faster-growing economies such as Canada and Brazil.

What Norway, Sweden, Japan and other refuges have in common is big current-account surpluses, which means they rely less on international investors for financing and seem safer to investors.

Japanese officials this week quashed speculation that Japan would follow Switzerland in curbing the yen with a ceiling. However, Norway's pushback is making investors wonder again where to run when markets turn turbulent.

"Investors are saying, if you're taking away one of our safe havens, where's the next one?" said Thanos Papasavvas, an analyst at Investec Asset Management in London, which manages around $100 billion in funds. The Norwegian krone "doesn't have the liquidity and the history of the Swiss franc," he added.

It is also possible traders' preferences for Switzerland and Japan won't change much, especially if Switzerland's intervention effort eventually fails, as many expect. The euro traded at 1.2149 francs late Thursday in New York--close enough to the ceiling to indicate there is still investor demand, traders said.

--Katarina Gustafsson and Paul Vieira contributed to this article. [ 09-08-11 1908ET ]

title: Canada Fin Min "Concerned" About Swiss  Currency  Action
text:
OTTAWA (Dow Jones)-Canadian Finance Minister Jim Flaherty said Thursday he's "concerned" about Switzerland's audacious move into foreign-exchange markets and worried it could reignite tensions in currency markets.

Flaherty said this will be one of a few "frank" discussions he'll have with his Group of Seven peers as they gather in Marseille for a meeting Friday. He said he'll argue to maintain fiscal-austerity plans and further warn Europe of the need to move boldly and quickly to address its debt woes.

Flaherty also told reporters Thursday of his unease with Switzerland's move to intervene in foreign-exchange markets and its announcement that it will acquire "unlimited quantities" of euros in an effort to place a cap on the Swiss franc's value. He said he's worried this could ignite another round of so-called currency wars, as penned by Brazil's finance minister last year. That could have an impact on the Canadian dollar, which remains at an elevated level and is acting as a drag on the country's exports.

"We were concerned when Japan moved unilaterally, and we are also concerned about Switzerland acting unilaterally. That's a discussion I am sure we are going to have," Flaherty said before attending a Conservative Party caucus meeting.

The Group of Seven finance and central bank officials are expected to discuss how far they are prepared to go to support flagging growth and avoid a double-dip recession. But Flaherty reiterated the need for major industrialized countries to adapt robust, medium-term deficit-fighting plans, as agreed to at last year's Group of 20 leaders' summit in Toronto, and warned of tension at the G-7 as others argue for a different course.

"Our view is the G-20 commitments to move toward deficit reduction and balanced budgets are essential and we want to stay the course. There are some [in the G-7] that have a different view. So we will have an engaging discussion in Marseille."

Flaherty is the longest-serving G-7 finance minister, and for months has been calling on Europe to take decisive action to deal with sovereign debt woes to avoid a severe spillover into financial markets. He said he will continue making that case, especially in light of growing doubts about the ability of European policymakers to prevent sovereign defaults.

"It is fraught with danger to keep kicking the can down the road. Delay is the enemy," he said, reminding Europe of the bold and quick action the U.S. took in the fall of 2008 to address the credit crisis.

While at the G-7, Flaherty plans to hold bilateral meetings with his newly-minted French and Japanese counterparts.

Canada had been one of the strongest G-7 economies up until recently, when data showed output shrank in the second quarter. In an interim economic assessment released Thursday, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development said Canada would recover from the second-quarter contraction to lead expansion among G-7 nations in the fourth quarter.

-By Paul Vieira, Dow Jones Newswires: 613-237-0669; paul.vieira@dowjones.com [ 09-08-11 1140ET ]

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  slip on surprise Swiss move
text:
* Swiss widen "currency war" with plan to defend franc

* Central bank action becoming uncoordinated - economists

* Brazil's real, Chile's and Colombia's pesos weaken

* Mexico's peso little changed against U.S. dollar

(Updates prices, adds Mexico peso context)

By Jeb Blount

RIO DE JANEIRO (Reuters) - Most Latin American currencies weakened against the U.S. dollar Tuesday as a widening world "currency war" prompted investors to sell emerging market assets and buy more liquid, less risky ones.

The battle over exchange rates -- which pits central banks against each other in an effort to promote economic growth and trade -- reached a new level on Tuesday with Switzerland's decision to cap the value of its soaring franc at 1.20 to the euro.

With the threat of government and central bank intervention


-- some expect Japan to follow Switzerland and protect the yen
-- many investors will opt to hold dollars, gold, or U.S.


Treasury bonds rather than the Brazilian real, Mexican peso or other Latin American assets, said Andre Perfeito, economist with Gradual Investimentos, which manages about $1.1 billion of assets in Sao Paulo.

"We are entering what is clearly a currency war, a period of absolute lack of coordination between central banks and international political leaders," Perfeito said. "In a moment like this the move will be to liquidity, safety, away from Latin America."

Brazil's real weakened 0.37 percent to 1.6557 to the U.S. dollar, its weakest close since March 28, after plunging as much as 1.05 percent to 1.6670, its weakest intraday level since March 18.

Perfeito expects the real to trade weaker to about 1.70 to the dollar in the coming weeks before tracking back to about 1.60 at the end of the year.

"The immediate move will be weaker, but in the end, 


Brazil's fundamentals -- a high interest rate, stronger growth
than in the developed world, robust exports -- will keep cash


flowing to the country," he said.

The action by Switzerland shows that "the world economic train has no driver and there is no coordinated approach," said Alberto Ramos, Latin America economist with Goldman Sachs in New York.

Until some action is taken to halt the currency war, get growth going in developed countries and resolve Europe's sovereign debt problems, investors should be prepared for wide swings in the value of Latin American currencies against the dollar, he added.

Chile's peso fell 0.24 percent to 463.80 to the dollar and Colombia's peso weakened 0.46 percent to 1,791.20 to the dollar.

Argentina's official peso , which is managed by regular central bank intervention in the market, weakened 0.12 percent to 4.2075 to the dollar. Argentina's unofficial or parallel peso firmed 0.11 percent to 4.4125 to the dollar.

Mexico's peso traded 0.13 percent firmer at 12.5100 to the dollar in a day of see-saw trading that saw the Mexican currency slide as much as 0.38 percent.

Investors were divided between those seeking dollars and other less risky assets and those who sought pesos to invest in higher-yielding Mexican assets, said Jorge Perez-Duarte, a managing director at TD Securities in Toronto.

Mexico's peso slumped by more than 5 percent in August, its worst monthly drop since 2009, on concern the the United States, which buys around 80 percent of Mexican exports would slip into recession for the second time in two years.

Even as the peso traded weakly against the dollar, Mexican 10-year "bonos", a government bond in pesos, rose 0.54 to 104.92 percent of face value. The yield fell seven basis points to 6.02 percent. A similar 10-year U.S. Treasury

yields 1.98 percent a year.

"The situation against the dollar is also pretty negative," Perez-Duarte said.

At the same time, higher returns, faster growth and investment-grade credit ratings available in Mexico and other Latin American countries have led some investors to consider emerging markets as safe havens against slow growth and near-zero interest rates in the United States, Europe and Japan, he added.

"Emerging markets are more or less seen as safe assets to some extent, since that is where the growth is coming from," Perez-Duarte said.

(Additional reporting by Jean Luis Arce and Michael O'Boyle in Mexico City; Editing by James Dalgleish)

title: UPDATE 2-Model-driven hedge funds among losers in SNB shock
text:
* FX Concepts was short CHF pre-SNB, but loses on options

* Many CTAs, macro funds long Swiss franc, likely hit

* Some funds went short the franc before central bank move

* Swiss fund of funds came out ahead

(Adds FX Concepts' Taylor comments, details)

By Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss and Laurence Fletcher

NEW YORK/LONDON, Sept 6 (Reuters) - Hedge funds, betting on global markets and driven by computer models, were among those hardest hit by Switzerland's shock intervention on Tuesday to reverse profitable bets on the Swiss franc's "safe-haven" status.

The Swiss National Bank surprised investors with an exchange rate cap, saying it would no longer tolerate a rate below 1.20 francs per euro and would defend the target by buying other currencies in unlimited quantities. For details, see [ID:nL5E7K61FL]

The news sent the franc tumbling nearly 10 percent against the euro <EURCHF=EBS> on trading platform EBS. In late trading, the euro was still up 8.7 percent against the franc on the day to change hands at 1.2047.

John Taylor, chairman and chief investment officer of the $8 billion currency hedge fund FX Concepts in New York, was able to get the direction right as his fund sold the Swiss franc last week. But he was hit by the sharp drop in the euro/Swiss franc volatility in the options market.

"We made money on the outrights because we were short Swiss francs, but because vols were so high, we were happily pocketing the premium for a while and that cost us a bunch of money today because volatility dropped," Taylor said.

"So net-net, our fund is down," Taylor added.

One-month implied volatilities -- a measure of the market's view of the extent of future currency movements -- in the euro/Swiss franc dropped to 9.95 percent on Tuesday from 22 percent on Monday. Vols hit a record high of around 30 percent in early August.

Overall, the FX Concepts chairman thinks 1.20 francs is a feasible entry level to buy the Swiss currency against the euro, especially if the euro zone's sovereign debt situation worsens.

Managed futures funds, which latch onto market trends and which have been among the few winning hedge funds strategies in a tough 2011, had hopped on board the franc's appreciation from more than 1.32 per euro in April to just above parity last month. [ID:nL5E7JO2LY]

"Obviously, any directional fund will be down today," said Axel Merk, who manages the $750 million Merk Hard Currency Fund in Palo Alto, California.

Merk lost after the SNB move since he had a 1.5 percent exposure on the Swiss franc in his portfolio, but he said he managed to offset those losses by buying the Norwegian crown. In fact, Merk said he bought more crowns last Friday.

The Norwegian crown gained 1.2 percent against the euro <EURNOK=> on Tuesday.

The SNB move notwithstanding, Merk said he will still buy the Swiss franc, although it may be too early to purchase it right now since the central bank has obvious political backing to implement its target.

"But at some point, I will definitely buy it again since the SNB has made the Swiss franc cheaper," he said.

GLOBAL MACRO FUNDS' PAIN

Some macro funds -- a strategy made famous by the likes of billionaire investor George Soros -- may have suffered after profiting this year from bets that the Swiss franc and Australian dollar will rise.

"I'm sure it will hurt," said one fund of hedge funds manager who spoke on condition of anonymity.

"It's a massive move. It doesn't have to be that big (a position in a fund) to be painful ... CTAs are highly likely to be hit by that." Commodity trading advisors, or CTAs, is another term for managed futures funds.

Among computer funds that may have been hit is Man Group's flagship $23.9 billion AHL fund. An AHL fund manager told Bloomberg Television last month it had a small bet on the franc.

Winton Capital, which manages $22.4 billion in assets and whose main fund is up nearly 8 percent so far this year, declined to comment on specific currency movements.

Man Group and Bluecrest also declined to comment.

One computer-driven fund manager, who was short the euro against the franc as the Swiss National Bank announced it was setting a minimum exchange rate target, said his fund has closed out all its positions in the Swiss franc.

"As it was a central bank move, we decided to square our positions and now have no market exposure to the Swiss franc," he said. "We have squared our position in the Swiss franc for the future because we will not be able to capture that risk in the quantitative models."

Other funds profited from the SNB move. Quaesta Capital, a $3-billion currency fund of funds in Zurich, Switzerland, said currency managers it oversees have gone short Swiss franc this week, posting the biggest outflow as well.

In an earlier interview, Pablo Frei, portfolio manager and senior market analyst at Quaesta, said their currency managers have become concerned about the Swiss franc's overvaluation against the euro.

Aviva Investors went long the New Zealand dollar versus the Swiss franc in the past few weeks and has seen an 18 percent move. It has also gone long in the Norwegian crown against the franc. [ID:nL5E7K61UO]

Hardeep Dogra, Currency Fund Manager at Schroder Investment Management in London, said they had been neutral on the franc.

It was "precisely because of this quandary," Dogra said. As "much as you like the currency, valuation is a problem and the central bank had been making repeated comments about its position, that it was aiming for some currency weakness."

title: WSJ/The Source: SNB  Intervention  May Not Be Enough to Boost Exports
text:
(This article has been posted on The Source, the Wall Street Journal Online's site for European real-time analysis http://blogs.wsj.com/source)


 
   Posted by Goran Mijuk 
 

The Swiss National Bank's attempt to cap the franc at 1.20 against the euro should ease pressure on exporters. But many Swiss firms still face an uphill battle as Europe's persistent debt troubles inflict continued pain on companies.

"All will depend on how the European debt crisis will evolve," said Danske Bank analyst Kasper Kirkegaard. "If the troubles increase, especially if global growth slows, more problems could be ahead," he said.

Although the central bank said it will enforce its minimum currency rate "with the utmost determination," failure to live up to its word could spell trouble for the economy, said Tobias Straumann, economic historian at the University of Zurich.

"Potential difficulties include that the SNB isn't credible enough and will run out of ammunition and there is the danger that the euro assets it will buy to support the franc may be worthless," Straumann said. But overall, the move is "important for exporters and importers to have a certain guidance," he said.

Export-dependent companies greeted the SNB decision with a great sigh of relief. "This measure gives us some planning security," said Dominik Werner, spokesman for Swiss chemicals maker Lonza.

Lonza had suffered greatly from the strong franc during the past few months, urging it to take over U.S. peer Arch Chemicals Inc to spread its cost base outside of Switzerland, where it incurs some 40% of its costs today.

Even companies that are less dependent on the Swiss franc welcomed the SNB action. "Today's intervention by the SNB can only be supportive for ABB's exports from Switzerland and for Swiss industry in general," said ABB Chief Financial Officer Michel Demare, noting that only a minor part of ABB's cost base is in Switzerland.

Economists believe the SNB's intervention should help the overall economy going forward and reduce the risk of bankruptcies and massive job cuts in the months ahead.

A majority of Swiss economists expected until recently that gross domestic growth in Switzerland will halve to 1% due to the strong franc. Swiss think tank EconomieSuisse had warned of some 25,000 job cuts if no action was taken.

"Many companies are currently planning the budget for 2012 and the fact that they are able now to reckon with a stable franc is making their lives easier," said David Marmet of Zuercher Kantonalbank. "It could help the economy going forward."

Exporters are a main growth driver in Switzerland, contributing more than 30% to the country's annual gross domestic product of around CHF550 billion. Failure to support this sector had risked putting Switzerland into recession, Zurich-based consultancy Wellershoff & Partners said recently.

But Europe's debt trouble might still cause problems here and even at the current franc level exporters will struggle.

"The franc level is still too high," said Lonza's Mr. Werner, echoing similar comments by Swiss business group Swissmem, which called for more central bank and government action.

Rudolf Minsch, chief economist at think tank EconomieSuisse, said that a fair value of the franc to the euro was at about 1.3 francs to 1.4 francs. Below that level, many Swiss exporters will continue to struggle although they have learned to survive, he said.

title: WSJ UPDATE: Switzerland Caps The Franc Amid Threat Of More Action
text:
ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss National Bank set a limit on how far it will let the Swiss franc rise against the euro, the bank's most aggressive attempt yet to rein in the soaring Swiss franc.

The SNB said it would buy euros in "unlimited quantities" should the single currency fall below 1.20 francs, setting the stage for what could be a long battle by the bank to defend its action in the face of surging concerns about debt problems in the euro zone and the U.S.

The SNB said Tuesday that it would "no longer tolerate" the euro falling below the minimum rate. In a statement, it said will enforce the limit with "the utmost determination and is prepared to buy foreign currency in unlimited quantities."

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal website, WSJ.com.)

The euro surged 10% to CHF1.22 on the news. Prior to the news, the euro had sunk to about CHF1.10, after hitting a record low of CHF1.001 in early August. The Japanese yen also weakened, as investors wondered whether the Japanese central bank--which intervened early last month to rein in the Japanese currency--might follow the Swiss.

Even gold, which has hit repeated highs this summer, lost some of its safe-haven shine, falling 2% early in the European day.

In its first comment on the Swiss bank's efforts to rein in the franc, the European Central Bank said it took note of the decision to set a floor against the euro. In August, ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet urged countries to intervene in currency markets in tandem, rather than going it alone.

In August, the SNB slashed interest rates to close to zero and flooded the market with liquidity in an effort to pull down a franc that has threatened to choke off Swiss growth. The franc gained 27% between November 2010 and early August against the euro, with investors viewing Switzerland--with its strong growth and solid public finances--as a haven from the euro zone's festering debt crisis.

The SNB's August moves helped drive the euro nearly 20% higher against the franc, but in recent days a deteriorating outlook for the global economy and the euro zone have sent the franc higher again. That may have prodded the SNB to take further action, say foreign exchange strategists.

The relentless strength of the franc has already pushed some weaker Swiss exporters into bankruptcy, and sent others scrambling to slash prices to hold onto business. Swiss export prices fell 6.2% in the first half of the year. The Swiss government expects 1.5% gross national product growth in 2012, down from 2.1% this year and 2.7% last year.

For the last month, the Swiss government and business leaders have been appealing for bolder action by the SNB to weaken the currency, particularly amid signs that growth elsewhere in Europe and in the U.S. could hit the skids. In its Tuesday statement, the SNB said the franc "poses an acute threat to the Swiss economy."

Having drawn a line in the sand, the SNB could now face an endurance test in defending its euro-franc limit, as investors increasingly worry whether key euro-zone members such as Italy will execute a credible plan to get their enormous debt under control.

Recent experience is not encouraging. When the franc began surging in early 2009 in the early days of the euro-zone crisis, the SNB regularly intervened to buy euros. But it abandoned the effort in June 2010 in the face of widespread criticism. Between March 2009 and June 2010 the euro fell from CHF1.48 to CHF1.32, and the SNB posted 2010 exchange-rate losses of CHF32.7 billion. The losses sparked calls for SNB President Philipp Hildebrand to resign.

This time, the SNB will be fighting a sharp slowdown in the U.S. economy as well as the deep debt crisis among its euro-zone neighbors, in particular Italy. The ECB recently warned Rome that it may not be doing enough to get its debt under control, and a general strike Tuesday in Italy highlighted the difficulty of reforming public finances there.

"This could be a bloody battle for the SNB over the next few months," said Jane Foley, currency strategist for Rabobank. "It's a battle of the SNB against the search by investors for safe havens."

Others point to the strong language in the SNB's Tuesday statement as a sign of the bank's determination, which could bolster its credibility in the market. The language is far starker than the bank's communiques to the market during its 2009-2010 interventions.

"The SNB is now completely committed," said Alessandro Bee, currency strategist with Bank Sarasin. "There is no going back. They will do everything to defend this. They have to resist the pressure. Otherwise, they can just close the SNB."

Bee expects the euro to stay quite close to the CHF1.20 level in the coming months, and then appreciate to around CHF1.30 next year if the euro-zone debt problems ease.

Should the SNB have to intervene for years, it could risk driving up inflation. But economists see virtually no short-term risk of rising prices; Swiss inflation has been around 0.5% over the last year. Instead, if the SNB posts further losses due to currency intervention, it could cause tensions with the local leaders of Switzerland's 26 cantons, which have traditionally received a large portion of the central bank's profits. However, early comments from politicians in Bern were supportive of the SNB's move.

Meanwhile, Swiss business welcomed the news, although some said a euro-franc exchange rate of 1.20 still leaves them under pressure.

"We think a fair value would be 1.30 to 1.40 francs, but taking into account the serious debt crisis in Europe and the problems in the U.S., we believe 1.20 francs is a level that can be easily defended," said Rudolf Minsch, chief economist for Swiss business lobby Economiesuisse in an interview. "There is a trade-off in order to convince the market that this level is defensible."

-By Deborah Ball, The Wall Street Journal; Deborah.Ball@dowjones.com [ 09-06-11 0837ET ]

title: SNB, Swiss Government Act To Curb Franc Amid Calls For Stronger Measures
text:
--SNB boosts liquidity for third time to weaken franc

--Swiss government agrees to CHF2 billion aid package

--SNB fails to mention peg or limit for franc gains

--Market disappointed about measures, questions SNB

--SNB ready to take further measures if necessary

By Goran Mijuk and Neil MacLucas

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

The Swiss National Bank and the Swiss government Wednesday took separate steps to limit the impact of the strong franc on the country's economy, but their latest measures failed to impress the market and triggered calls for more decisive action to restrain the currency.

The SNB took a third attempt in as many weeks to curb the franc by boosting liquidity, lifting sight deposits by two-thirds to 200 billion Swiss francs ($253 billion). But even as it warned of further action, its latest move failed to rein in the franc and disappointed market participants who questioned the institute's credibility as many had expected a peg of the franc to the euro.

In a separate move, the government said it will provide the economy with a CHF2 billion aid package partially aimed at helping exporters and the tourism industry. Both sectors risk losing business to foreign competitors and may shed thousands of local jobs, said Economy Minister Johann-Schneider-Ammann. The aid package will be financed out of the country's expected budget surplus this year, he said.

Despite the latest measures, the franc remained high versus the euro and the dollar, trading at CHF1.1406 and CHF0.7894, respectively. This unnerved investors who had expected a peg, said Sebastien Galy, currencies analyst at Societe Generale. "Everybody is shaking their heads at this. The SNB implicitly told the market that there would be a peg, and now the market is disappointed," he said.

As a result, traders, economists and lobby groups in Switzerland called for more action, including asking for a temporary peg or a floor of the franc to the euro. "Some sort of targeted limit for the franc against the euro would be the most appropriate measure in these difficult times," said Rudolf Minsch, chief economist of influential business lobby group EconomieSuisse. "The Swiss economy simply can't live with a [the current franc rate], and it will have serious consequences for exports and employment."

While some left-wing political groups such as the Swiss Federation of Trade Unions have called for a Swiss franc peg to the euro at CHF1.40, economists say that the SNB is much more likely, if at all, to target a lower level that reflects the fair value between the pair. According to Nicolas Wiedenmann, economist at Bank Vontobel, the franc's purchasing-parity fair value against the euro stands at about CHF1.28. To achieve this target, economists say a series of SNB interventions would be needed.

Such steps, even if contested by some economists as they are considered risky and costly, are still possible even as the central bank Wednesday failed to use this tool after the bank's director Thomas Jordan last week said that temporary currency market interventions were in line with the bank's mandate, which raised hopes for a peg.

But the expectations for more direct action remained alive as the government said it plans to set up a task force, a move that was interpreted as a potential signal that more measures may be envisaged. "We are in a special situation, which requires a special response," said Economy Minister Johann Schneider-Ammann, warning that the current financial turmoil is likely to curtail global growth and add further stress to the Swiss economy.

Since the outbreak of the financial crisis, the government has launched several aid packages, which have helped the economy weather the crisis well and reach growth rates of more than 2% and keep a lid on unemployment. Schneider-Ammann, however, made it clear that the government won't interfere with the central bank when it comes to monetary decisions.

The SNB, which once again said that the franc was "massively overvalued," left the door open for more action as it warned that the central bank "will, if necessary, take further measures against the strength of the Swiss franc." In its previous two moves, the SNB cut interest rates close to zero and added liquidity to money markets, effectively pressuring short-term interest rates into negative territory. The SNB had in the past said that the liquidity boost needed time to take effect.

While the market expects more action, timing is considered to be decisive and an intervention or peg could come in the weeks or months ahead. "The SNB can still take more decisive action and it may be that at the current levels they don't yet want to use more drastic measures in order to remain flexible," said Commerzbank strategist Antje Praefcke.

But for such a step to have effect, the situation in Europe needs to improve, economists say. "The current SNB measures should continue to have an effect on the franc, even if the real medicine is probably a return of confidence in the neighboring euro zone," said Julien Manceaux, economist at ING.

Still, pegging the Swiss franc to the euro seems unrealistic for UBS, which said that "imminence of any such project [is] overblown." Although the political establishment in Switzerland has changed its view about direct currency interventions, prior SNB intervention moves in 2009 and 2010 had inflated the bank's balance sheet and led to hefty book losses. The consideration of a peg, critics say, could trigger an avalanche of Swiss franc buying and put further pressure on the SNB and trigger renewed political criticism.

-By Goran Mijuk, Dow Jones Newswires; +41 43 443 80 47; goran.mijuk@dowjones.com [ 17-08-11 1747GMT ]

title: *DJ Swiss Job Market Depends On CHF, Global Economy - Official
text:
8 Aug 2011 04:11 EDT *DJ  Swiss Govt Offical: Economic Facts Not As Bad As Sentiment

8 Aug 2011 04:15 EDT DJ  INTERVIEW: Swiss Job Market Hinges On Franc, Global Economy

-- Swiss job market depends on franc, global economy

-- Economic facts aren't as bad as sentiment

By Goran Mijuk

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

ZURICH (Dow Jones)--Failure by the Swiss National Bank to act to prevent the franc from rising and a worsening of the global economy are likely to badly hit the Swiss job market, the Swiss government's Director of Labor Serge Gaillard said Monday.

"The impact of the strong franc would be grave should the currency remain at current levels and if the SNB would fail to achieve a change of the trend," Gaillard told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview.

"It could hit many sectors such as the tourism and banking industry," said Gaillard, who heads the Labor Directorate at Switzerland's government State Secretariat for Economic Affairs, or SECO. "But it would be most felt with exporters."

Switzerland's jobless rate is currently at a two-and-a-half year low of 2.8%, but still off the level reached before the financial crisis when the figure stood at around 2.5%. Concerns are growing that a rising Swiss franc, which is trading at record levels against the dollar and the euro, could badly hit the country's exporters, a main source of economic growth in Switzerland.

Many economists expect the SNB to intervene in foreign currency markets after the central bank last week said it will take action if needed. While some economists believe the SNB could introduce negative interest rates to stem the flow of safe-haven buys, others believe that direct foreign-exchange interventions are possible even though the central bank's interventions in 2009 and 2010 left it with huge losses, which sparked political criticism.

But despite the challenging situation, Gaillard said the institute is yet maintaining its 3.1% jobless rate expectation for 2011 as the global economy is still in a healthy shape. "As far as growth is concerned, the situation in economies in Northern Europe and the U.S. is solid. The facts aren't as bad as the sentiment," Gaillard said.

Switzerland's unemployment rate remained unchanged in July at 2.8% compared with June. But analysts noted that forward-looking figures were somewhat less strong compared with earlier this year.

"While the number of job seekers continued to decline, the number of open positions was down by a pronounced 9.6% on the month, following a decline by 2.9% month-on-month in June," said Credit Suisse. "Meanwhile, the number of short-time workers continued to head lower and is now only slightly above pre-crisis levels."

title: WORLD  FOREX : Euro Suffers Brunt Of Massive High-Yield  Currency  Selloff
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--It was the euro, not the dollar, that bore the brunt of Standard & Poor's downgrade of the U.S. credit rating to double-A-plus Monday. Rattled traders ran to the Swiss franc and the yen, abandoning riskier currencies more closely tied to economic growth.

The euro was the focal point of a massive move away from nearly all higher-yielding currencies, at one point trading down as much as 3% against the safe-harbor Swiss franc, hitting a new all-time low of CHF1.0619. The dollar and U.K. pound also hit new all-time lows against the franc, though their declines were milder.

Many analysts believe the euro is still stronger than it should be, given that most of the currency's gains came on projections of strong global economic growth. With the U.S. potentially slipping back into recession, and even emerging markets showing some signs of slower expansion, the euro could stand to drop to its true value estimated of $1.20, rather than Monday's $1.42.

The euro zone's debt problems also appear to be worsening, further undermining the common currency. On Monday, French credit-default swaps widened significantly on fears that France also faces a downgrade from its triple-A rating. Traders view such a development as possibly the next serious stress point for the euro zone because France's triple-A rating helps back a triple-A rated European Financial Stability Facility. That fund is viewed as an essential emergency bailout fund for the euro zone's most vulnerable economies should they run into fresh troubles.

"The French AAA underpins the AAA rating of the [European Financial Stability Facility] and any downgrade would put the entire rescue mechanism in question," said Steven Englander, head of G10 strategy at Citigroup in New York.

That French news overwhelmed news that the European Central Bank also bought Italian and Spanish bonds for the first time, driving yields on Italian and Spanish debt sharply lower.

Late Monday, the euro was at $1.4180 from $1.4275 late Friday, according to EBS via CQG. The dollar was at Y77.79 from Y78.42, while the euro was at Y110.27 from Y112.01. The U.K. pound was at $1.6320 from $1.6394. The dollar was at CHF0.7548 from CHF0.7675.

The ICE Dollar Index, which tracks the U.S. dollar against a basket of currencies, was at 74.852 from about 74.598.

While it was U.S. debt that was downgraded on Friday, the dollar retained enough appeal as a relatively stable "safe haven" to attract nervous investors on Monday. Fears of an already fragile U.S. fiscal picture getting worse feeds into existing concern that the U.S. economy could drag down other healthier economies on the globe. With the U.S. debt-ceiling talks and any imminent debt default out of the way, the dollar could again resume its function as a safe-haven currency along with the franc and the yen. Aside from the U.S. currency being backed by the world's largest economy and government debt market, the dollar--recent low-yield and Washington in-fighting aside--has traditionally acted as one of the world's safe-haven currencies based on the fact that it is the world's reserve currency, and the most actively traded currency in the foreign-exchange market.

"Traders are increasingly taking into account a U.S. recession," said Paresh Upadhyaya, head of Americas G10 FX strategy at Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch in New York.

Other safe havens also face the threat of government intervention. Central banks in Japan and Switzerland have both recently attempted to halt their currencies' rise, without much success so far.

On Monday, investors ignored the threat of further Japanese intervention by selling off the dollar by 1% against the yen. Commodity-linked currencies also weakened as the price of oil and stocks continued to fall throughout the day. Both the Australian and New Zealand dollars fell nearly 2% against the U.S. currency.

title: US Stocks Stumble At Open, Oil And Euro Fall As Gold Soars
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Investors roiled by recessionary fears exited from risk-related assets Monday, seeking shelter in safety instruments as fallout from the credit dowgrade of the world's largest economy continued to reverberate in global markets.

On the heels of a decision by Standard & Poor's to strip the U.S. of its triple-A credit rating, markets around the world trembled. Equity markets in Asia, Europe and the Middle East suffered steep losses in offshore trading, while high-yielding assets such as oil and the euro skidded lower, while gold--a haven for nervous investors--surged to new record highs.

Europe's own debt travails and a torrent of data suggesting that the world's economy is decelerating sharply have unsettled investors, and left some analysts weighing whether S&P's move could become the tipping point for a global recession.

"We're clearly in the midst of an all-out panic," said Bruce McCain, chief investment strategist at Key Private Bank. "There's nothing that says this better than the fact that U.S. credit has been downgraded and we're running up the price of U.S. Treasury bonds."

In recent trade, the benchmark 10-year note rose 1 4/32 in price, pushing the yield down by 12 basis points to 2.429%. The yield tumbled to 2.334% Friday, the lowest level since October. Bond prices move inversely to their yields.

The 30-year bond was 1 3/32 higher to yield 3.765%. The two-year note was 3/32 higher to yield 0.248%.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average had dropped 319 points, or 2.8%, to a session low. The Dow posted its biggest weekly point loss since the financial crisis in 2008 last week, falling 5.8% as investors fretted about the slowing U.S. economy and Europe's spreading sovereign-debt crisis.

The Standard & Poor's 500 stock index was off 3.4%. The technology-oriented Nasdaq Composite was down more than 3%.

The S&P downgrade was largely telegraphed ahead of time, allowing investors to consider a world where the U.S. was no longer a triple-A country. As a result, Treasurys and the dollar began Monday on a relatively strong note.

Europe, however, is not much better off than the United States, with European officials struggling to contain a raging debt crisis. As a result, the euro was roundly battered by risk aversion, and fears that the European Central Bank's efforts to safeguard Italy and Spain from contagion risks through purchases of their debt would fall short of what analysts believe is necessary.

The ECB "is going to be facing a huge battle about how much they are going to buy" in Italian and Spanish debt, said Brian Kim, currency strategist at RBS Securities in Stamford. Meanwhile, "the dollar is doing better than people thought it would be."

The euro shed more than two cents from its Asia trading high against the dollar to change hands around $1.4175. The dollar set a new record low against the Swiss franc at CHF0.7629 and fell nearly one per cent against the yen to Y77.70, but its losses were limited amid fears of intervention by the monetary authorities of Japan and Switzerland.

Commodities linked to global growth tumbled Monday, with declines spread among oil, copper, grains and other agricultural products. Crude oil was recently down $3.82, or 4.4% at $83.06 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange, flirting with eight-month lows. Copper fell 0.7% to $4.0865 a pound.

The declines reflect fears that a possible second recession due to political deadlock in the U.S. and a worsening sovereign debt crisis in Europe will eventually curtail demand for raw materials.

"Nobody knows what will happen and as a result they prefer to limit losses," said Remy Penin, commodity market strategist at Societe Generale.

The uncertainty has sent investors flooding into gold, with spot prices hitting record highs above $1,700 a troy ounce in Europe Monday. Gold futures for December delivery, the most actively traded contract, were recently up 3% to $1,700.80 a troy ounce, after hitting an all-time high of $1,714.30.

High-grade corporate bond prices fell, and an index tracking risk in the market rose to its highest level in 10 months. Risk premiums--the added yield that investors demand to own corporate debt instead of safer Treasurys -- shot up significantly on each of the five most-active bonds in the secondary market. The premium on Capital One Financial 4.75% bonds due 2021 rose by 22 basis points and Citigroup 8.5% bonds due 2019 widened by 32 basis points. The CDX index that measures risk in the market rose by four basis points to 107. A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point.

But many think the dislocation will be a temporary one and some surmise the action might actually be beneficial for higher rated bonds. "Very highly rated corporates, including the three triple A rated companies (Exxon, J&J, and Microsoft) as well as strong double A rated firms, may actually see spreads narrow as investors look to high quality alternatives to Treasuries," according to Guy LeBas, chief fixed income strategist at Janney Montgomery. He also notes that lower- rated credits could tread wider due to volatility brought on by greater risk aversion.

-By Javier E. David, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-4564; javier.david@dowjones.com

--Steven Russolillo, Min Zeng, Kellie Geressy, Jerry Dicolo contributed to this article. [ 08-08-11 1035ET ]

title: FOREX -US dollar could weaken as Fed meeting looms
text:
* Fed meeting, assessment of economy will be key focus

* Swiss franc, yen stay in favor on economic worries

* Investors on alert for more currency intervention

(Recasts; add comment, updates prices)

By Wanfeng Zhou

NEW YORK, Aug 5 (Reuters) - The U.S. dollar could fall next week, especially against the Swiss franc and Japanese yen, as investors look to a Federal Reserve meeting for hints of further easing as worries about the global economy grow.

Stocks sold off and safe-haven assets, like the Swiss franc, soared this week after weak data fueled fears the world economy is slipping back into a recession. That sentiment persisted even after data Friday showed U.S. job growth accelerated more than expected last month.

The Swiss franc climbed to record highs against the dollar and euro on Friday, before easing back. The dollar last traded up 0.2 percent at 0.7665 franc <CHF=EBS>, while the euro rose 1.5 percent at 1.0960 francs <EURCHF=EBS>.

For the week, the dollar lost about 3.0 percent against the Swiss currency and the euro dropped 3.7 percent.

Against the yen <JPY=>, the dollar was last at 78.49, down 0.7 percent on the day, but rose 1.2 percent on the week after Japan intervened and eased monetary policy to weaken the yen.

Sharp moves in financial markets and the spike in volatility prompted aggressive policy actions by several major central banks in recent days, including a surprise interest rate cut by Switzerland, yen-selling intervention by Japan, and a resumption of bond buying by the European Central Bank.

"With markets already on the defensive and the macroeconomic picture deteriorating, (Fed Chairman Ben) Bernanke cannot afford to be tight-lipped about further quantitative easing," said Ashraf Laidi, CEO of Intermarket Strategy Ltd. in London.

"They have to continue signaling their readiness to introduce further measures, regardless of the Fed's opinion about the cost-benefit analysis of further quantitative easing," he added.

The U.S. Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's policy-setting panel, is slated to announce its decision on interest rates at 2:15 p.m. EDT (1815 GMT) on Tuesday.

With no change in rates expected, investors will scrutinize the accompanying statement for the central bank's assessment on the economy and the outlook for monetary policy.

Any hints that the Fed could introduce news measures to stimulate a slowing economy could further erode the dollar's traditional role as a safe haven, driving investors to the Swiss franc and Japanese yen.

"Even if the Fed doesn't talk about QE3 next week, the market is going to continue to leave it as a possibility," said David Watt, senior currency strategist at RBC Capital Markets in Toronto. "The only thing can turn the U.S. dollar trend is we start seeing a string of upward surprises in U.S. economic data."

INTERVENTION WATCH

Japanese Finance Minister Yoshihiko Noda said he was closely watching yen moves on Friday, signaling a readiness to continue selling the currency. For details, see [ID:nL3E7J467X]

"There is a good likelihood they will intervene again as they will want to make it clear to the markets that they will not be tested and they were not one-off interventions," said Andrew Cox, currency strategist at Citigroup in New York.

But with worries about a global economic slowdown, analysts doubted actions by central banks will spark a trend reversal.

The euro last traded up 1.3 at $1.4290 <EUR=EBS> but was down slightly on the week. It got a boost after Italy's Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi pledged on Friday to speed up austerity measures and bring the country's budget into balance by 2013. [ID:nR1E7IF02F]

Sources told Reuters the European Central Bank had demanded such measures in exchange for buying bonds to ease the pressure on Italy, which has come under market attack.

But Andrew Busch, senior currency strategist at BMO Capital Markets, said any positive sentiment would fade.

"Seriously, can the markets or the ECB trust Italian PM Berlusconi to put through reforms?" he said. "Remember, the Europeans have yet to implement their last rescue scheme for Greece and the ratings agencies are still likely to downgrade Italy and Spain."

title: SNB: Swiss July  Currency  Reserves Drop To CHF182.08 Billion
text:
ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The value of the Swiss National Bank's currency reserves slipped to 182.08 billion Swiss francs ($234.8 billion), central bank data showed Thursday.

The value of its foreign currency holdings fell from an unrevised CHF196.3 billion in June, according to data posted on the SNB's website.

Switzerland's central bank intervened repeatedly from March 2009 through June 2010 as it sought to check the franc's excessive gains against the euro to head off the danger of deflation.

The SNB last month reported a first-half consolidated loss of CHF10.8 billion, with "losses on foreign currency positions amounting to CHF9.9 billion due to exchange-related valuation losses of around CHF11.7 billion".

The book-loss followed franc gains of about 2.5% against the euro and almost 11% against the dollar during the first half of the year as investors sought shelter from the debt crises in the euro zone and the U.S.

title: DJ FOCUS:  Forex  Traders Still Skeptical As SNB Ups Pressure On Japan
text:
--Trader eyes turn to Japan following SNB move to tame Swiss franc

--Like the Swiss franc, yen has been strengthening due to its safe-haven status

--Japanese authorities seen struggling to tame yen 


 
   By Clare Connaghan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LONDON (Dow Jones)--Currency trader eyes are turning to Japan and to whether the monetary authorities there will follow the lead taken by the Swiss National Bank Wednesday by also acting to counter strength in their country's currency.

Yet despite widespread expectations for intervention in support of the yen and for more monetary easing by the Bank of Japan, skepticism abounds in London--easily the world's biggest foreign-exchange market--that any such action will succeed in turning the tide of yen strength.

Like the Swiss franc, the yen has appreciated significantly of late, moving on Monday to within a whisker of its all-time high against the dollar as concerns over global economic growth and the euro-zone debt crisis sent foreign-exchange investors scrambling for the relative safety of the Japanese currency.

To date, Japan's monetary authorities have done little except crank up the verbal intervention rhetoric. But now Switzerland's central bank has broken ranks and introduced measures to stem the relentless appreciation of its currency, pressure on Japan to do something is building.

"Rhetoric only has a short shelf-life and they [Japan's Ministry of Finance and Bank of Japan] know that," said Neil Mellor, a currency strategist at Bank of New York Mellon.

After fretting for months over the relentless appreciation in the Swiss franc, the SNB finally ran out of patience Wednesday and said it will trim its key three-month London Interbank Offered Rate target to as close to zero as possible. The bank said it will also increase the supply of liquidity to the Swiss franc money market by expanding banks' on-call cash deposits.

Such measures raise the stakes for Japan but are still unlikely to spur them into action any time soon, London market participants said.

"Its very unlikely we're going to get intervention," said Jane Foley a currency strategist at Rabobank in London.

It is also difficult to know which additional measures they could introduce, because there is already so much liquidity in Japan anyway, Foley said.

Nonetheless, Japan's export community is hopeful of some kind of remedial action soon, with all eyes on the central bank as it prepares to start a two-day policy meeting.

If it is prompted by the Ministry of Finance to intervene directly to suppress the yen, now could be the time to do it as thin summer liquidity conditions could result in a bigger immediate market reaction.

But, ultimately, unless sentiment towards global economic growth improves sharply, any measures introduced are seen by traders in London as likely to have a limited impact.

At 1635 GMT, the dollar was trading at Y76.860 against the yen, compared with Y77.14 in New York Tuesday.

title: Swiss right-winger wants SNB's powers crimped-paper
text:
* Blocher wants SNB only to focus on price stability

* Swatch Group CEO urged more currency intervention

ZURICH, July 31 (Reuters) - Switzerland's right-wing former justice minister launched a fresh attack on Swiss National Bank chairman Philipp Hildebrand in a Sunday newspaper interview and urged the central bank to focus exclusively on its task of maintaining price stability.

The SNB on Friday reported a 9.9 billion franc loss on its foreign exchange holdings for the first half of the year due to the surging franc. That follows a hit of 26.5 billion francs last year that led to the central bank reporting its biggest annual loss.

National elections are schedule for Oct. 23

In an interview with Der Sonntag, Christoph Blocher, mastermind of the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP), stepped up the rhetoric against Hildebrand, having earlier this year called on him to resign.

"It's untenable. He's been elected by the government -- it should now act," the paper quoted him as saying. "Hildebrand behaves like a speculator and is therefore not qualified for this job."

The SNB accumulated vast foreign currency holdings between March 2009 and June 2010 because it stepped into markets to cap the franc's rise and stave off the risk of deflation.

Blocher said the SNB should not be allowed to expand its balance sheet to such an extent without government approval.

"The job of the central bank is money supply and price stability -- here it should be independent. It should not be totally independent when it doesn't involve its main objective."

Hildebrand, whose term runs until 2015, became the subject of political sparring earlier this year, in part because Switzerland's 26 cantons (states) may not get their customary dividend from the SNB this year, pressuring their budgets.

Blocher's proposal would require a change to the Swiss constitution, which enshrines an independent central bank whose mandate is to ensure price stability.

The populist SVP, which in 2009 spearheaded a vote to ban the construction of new minarets, looks set to hang on to its lead as the biggest party in parliament's lower house.

MORE INTERVENTIONS

While Blocher has said he wants to clip the winsgs of the SNB, the Social Democrats (SP), the second-biggest party in parliament's lower house, have called for more currency interventions.

The safe-haven Swiss franc has risen some 14 percent against the dollar and 7 percent against the euro since the start of the year, drawing complaints from exporters.

Forward-looking indicators such as the KOF barometer have pointed to a slowdown in momentum.

One of the companies which has been most outspoken about the impact of the strong franc has been Swatch Group , famous for its colourful plastic timepieces, which has said its turnover target for the year may be a challenge due to the currency.

In an interview with the SonntagsZeitung, Chief Executive Nick Hayek said many of the problems due to the rampant franc had not yet become evident, that the SNB would simply have to endure the criticism, and that a new round of interventions was warranted.

"The SNB didn't intervene long enough. The SNB should now signal to the markets that it will not accept a further appreciation without action, and will intervene," he said.

The SNB has said it still has the means to act if deflationary risks were to resurface.

"(Hildebrand) should not allow the criticism -- from the politicians, the cantons or the journalists -- to intimidate him," Hayek said.

"The national bank must set an exchange rate goal of 1.35 and defend it. That would finally be a clear signal," he also said, and re-stated that in a few years Swatch Group would achieve 10 billion francs in annual revenue through organic growth.

The franc is currently trading at around 1.13 per euro

.

(Reporting by Catherine Bosley; Editing by David Cowell)

text:
13 Jul 2011 12:57 EDT DJ  Jordan: Swiss CentraL Bank Watching Franc Developments Closely

ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss National Bank is closely watching currency markets for developments involving the Swiss franc and euro, the vice chairman said Wednesday.

"We are of course concerned about the debt crisis in the euro region" and its impact on the franc, Thomas Jordan said during a panel discussion on how the euro-zone debt crisis could affect Switzerland.

The franc has gained sharply in recent weeks versus the euro as investors seek a refuge from the ongoing debt crisis in the euro region.

The Swiss currency has risen about 11% versus its European and U.S. counterparts in the past three months, undermining the competitiveness of Swiss exports in its most important markets.

Both the Swiss central bank and the economics ministry have warned the strong franc is likely to slow the pace of growth in one of Europe's best-performing economies this year.

13 Jul 2011 13:14 EDT *DJ  Jordan: Franc-Euro Peg Idea Would Mean Loss Of SNB Autonomy

13 Jul 2011 14:40 EDT DJ  UPDATE:SNB Watching Swiss Franc Closely; Rejects Euro Peg Idea

(Recasts throughout, adding detail and comments.)

By Neil MacLucas

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss National Bank is watching the Swiss franc's strong appreciation closely but Vice Chairman Thomas Jordan on Wednesday rejected suggestions it should peg the franc to the euro.

"We are of course concerned about the debt crisis in the euro region" and its impact on the franc, but calls for the SNB to peg the franc to the euro would mean the loss of its own autonomy, Jordan said during a panel discussion on how the euro-zone debt crisis could affect Switzerland.

The SNB intervened to try to check the franc's gains between March 2009 and June 2010 but stepped back from this policy, citing the disappearance of the danger of deflation.

The franc has gained sharply in recent weeks versus the euro as investors seek a refuge from the ongoing debt crisis in the euro region, and various ideas have been proposed to try to offset the effects of a strong currency on the Swiss export sector.

One proposal is for the SNB to peg the Swiss currency to the euro, but Jordan said this would mean the SNB surrendering its mandate and autonomy to the European Central Bank.

"We would need a change in the SNB's constitution to allow such a move," Jordan said.

Still, the SNB isn't powerless in the face of currency-market developments, and if signs of deflation emerge in Switzerland, it can take measures, Jordan said. He declined to say whether such measures included intervention, and stressed the SNB's main goal is the preservation of Swiss price stability.

Jordan said it is in everyone's interest that the European Union find a solution to some countries' debt problems and that if the situation worsens, then Switzerland, too, would have large problems.

The Swiss currency has risen about 11% versus its euro-zone and U.S. counterparts in the past three months, undermining the competitiveness of Swiss exports in the country's most important markets.

Both the Swiss central bank and the economics ministry have warned the strong franc is likely to slow the pace of growth in one of Europe's best-performing economies this year.

title: European Trader: Swiss Franc: Overheating
text:
(From BARRON'S) 
   By Jonathan Buck 


A sharp rise in the value of the Swiss franc means bad news for the Swiss economy, but it offers intriguing possibilities for investors.

The franc is soaring largely because it is considered a safe harbor by investors. At a time when the euro zone is grappling with a consuming debt crisis and parts of the Middle East are in turmoil, investors want to park their cash in low-risk locales, and Switzerland is considered one such destination. Since the start of the year, the lure of the franc has pushed up its value by 24% against the euro and 12% against the dollar. Adjusted for inflation, the Swiss franc is trading at its highest level in 30 years.

"It has gone beyond what you would normally expect," says Paul Robson, senior currency strategist at RBS in London, who says he fears for the health of the Swiss economy in the next 12 months.

Switzerland's cabinet discussed the strong franc last week, and its impact on the economy, noting that the currency is in "an overvalued phase." The government forecasts gross domestic product will grow by 2.1% this year, after trimming its 2012 forecast last month to 1.5% from 1.9%.

Typically there is a lag between exchange-rate appreciation and the effects on the economy. Butalready there are signs in Switzerland of a slowdown in the export sector, and corporate profit margins are coming under pressure. Zurich's benchmark SMI equity index has lost more than 3% in value since the start of the year. In contrast, Germany's blue-chip DAX index has risen more than 8%. The impact on equities may be muted due to the global nature of Swiss companies' businesses, says Frances Hudson, global strategist at Standard Life in Edinburgh. Food giant Nestle (NESN.Switzerland), with 458 factories around the world, said first-quarter sales were reduced by 10% due to the strength of the franc. Its shares are down about 3.6% this year.

Previous efforts at intervention by Switzerland's central bank have been ineffective in curbing the franc's rise. "For the short term, the strength of the franc is justified," says Hudson. "Long- term, it is questionable."

The franc is likely to remain strong against the euro if the euro-zone problems intensify, but could depreciate swiftly if the European Central Bank soon finds a solution to Greece's woes. That seems unlikely for the moment. Barclays Capital strategists believe the base case is that the euro zone's issues recede but not quickly, and the value of the euro rises to close to 1.40 Swiss francs in four years from about CHF1.20 Friday.

Hudson suggests the Swiss franc could get some relief against the dollar if the U.S. Congress reaches a budget deal before its Aug. 2 vote on raising the government's debt ceiling. She notes investors can earn "positive real yields" on Swiss franc bonds. RBS's Robson suggests that investors short the Swiss franc and buy Asian currencies, particularly the Singapore dollar, which he describes as "a good trade over the long term."

European markets sank Friday after the release of disappointing U.S. June jobs data. The Stoxx Europe 600 closed at 273.76, down 0.8% on the day and 0.4% on the week. One group that came under increased pressure: Italian banks, on speculation that many would fail the latest round of European stress tests. Unicredit (UCG.Italy) ended Friday at 1.23 euros, off almost 8%.

Since the start of the year, the lure of the franc has pushed up its value by 24% against the euro and 12% against the dollar. Adjusted for inflation, the Swiss franc is trading at its highest level in 30 years.

"It has gone beyond what you would normally expect," says Paul Robson, senior currency strategist at RBS in London, who says he fears for the health of the Swiss economy in the next 12 months.

Switzerland's cabinet discussed the strong franc last week, and its impact on the economy, noting that the currency is in "an overvalued phase." The government forecasts gross domestic product will grow by 2.1% this year, after trimming its 2012 forecast last month to 1.5% from 1.9%.

Typically there is a lag between exchange-rate appreciation and the effects on the economy. Butalready there are signs in Switzerland of a slowdown in the export sector, and corporate profit margins are coming under pressure. Zurich's benchmark SMI equity index has lost more than 3% in value since the start of the year. In contrast, Germany's blue-chip DAX index has risen more than 8%. The impact on equities may be muted due to the global nature of Swiss companies' businesses, says Frances Hudson, global strategist at Standard Life in Edinburgh. Food giant Nestle (NESN.Switzerland), with 458 factories around the world, said first-quarter sales were reduced by 10% due to the strength of the franc. Its shares are down about 3.6% this year.

Previous efforts at intervention by Switzerland's central bank have been ineffective in curbing the franc's rise. "For the short term, the strength of the franc is justified," says Hudson. "Long- term, it is questionable."

The franc is likely to remain strong against the euro if the euro-zone problems intensify, but could depreciate swiftly if the European Central Bank soon finds a solution to Greece's woes. That seems unlikely for the moment. Barclays Capital strategists believe the base case is that the euro zone's issues recede but not quickly, and the value of the euro rises to close to 1.40 Swiss francs in four years from about CHF1.20 Friday.

Hudson suggests the Swiss franc could get some relief against the dollar if the U.S. Congress reaches a budget deal before its Aug. 2 vote on raising the government's debt ceiling. She notes investors can earn "positive real yields" on Swiss franc bonds. RBS's Robson suggests that investors short the Swiss franc and buy Asian currencies, particularly the Singapore dollar, which he describes as "a good trade over the long term."

European markets sank Friday after the release of disappointing U.S. June jobs data. The Stoxx Europe 600 closed at 273.76, down 0.8% on the day and 0.4% on the week. One group that came under increased pressure: Italian banks, on speculation that many would fail the latest round of European stress tests. Unicredit (UCG.Italy) ended Friday at 1.23 euros, off almost 8%.

title: SNB: Swiss June  Currency  Reserves Steady At CHF196.03 Billion
text:
ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The value of the Swiss National Bank's currency reserves was steady in June at 196.03 billion Swiss francs ($233 billion), central bank data showed Wednesday.

The value fell slightly from a revised CHF196.08 billion in May, according to the SNB.

Switzerland's central bank intervened repeatedly from March 2009 through June 2010 as it sought to check the franc's excessive gains against the euro to head off the danger of deflation.

The SNB posted a CHF1.9 billion profit in the first quarter, after a CHF19.2 billion book loss last year, as the euro gained around 3% versus the franc in the three months through March, boosting the value of its euro holdings.

title: SNB Pushed To Peg Swiss Franc; Seen Asserting Independence
text:
--SNB pushed to peg Swiss franc by left wing

--Industrial lobby backs calls for temporary Swiss franc peg

--SNB seen resisting franc peg, other currency moves

--Swiss franc has gained 8.9% against the euro this quarter

By Katharina Bart

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss National Bank is under pressure from Switzerland's left-wing party to consider pegging the Swiss franc to the euro to dampen the Swiss currency's rapid appreciation.

It's an unconventional step which reflects growing political support for the country's increasingly vocal exporters.

Left-wing calls for Switzerland's central bank to temporarily fix the Swiss franc to the euro in case the Swiss currency strengthens further underscore the increasingly politically sensitive nature of the franc's strength against the euro and the U.S. dollar. The Swiss franc has strengthened 8.9% against the euro thus far this quarter, and 9.3% against the U.S. dollar.

The call for the franc to be pegged garnered support from Swiss industrial lobby group Swissmem, which echoed its calls for the SNB to intervene on behalf of Switzerland's exporters.

Still, the SNB is unlikely to be pressed into the unconventional step--even as an emergency, temporary measure--because it would mean compromising its independence on monetary policy decisions, according to experts.

"I cannot envisage this being feasible politically, because one of the SNB's greatest virtues is its ability to act independently in currency and monetary policy issues and react to Swiss inflationary and economic developments as it sees fit," Bank Sarasin strategist Ursina Kubli said.

The SNB is also likely to be too bruised from its unsuccessful 2009 interventions to consider a peg, according to currency experts. The Swiss central bank's balance sheet is bloated from spending billions of francs attempting to curb the franc's surge against major currencies like the U.S. dollar and euro. As a result, the SNB posted a 21 billion Swiss francs ($25.3 billion) loss in 2010.

The franc has Switzerland's exporters up in arms because a strong Swiss currency eats into their profit margins. Still, the SNB isn't likely to be swayed by what is turning into an increasingly political issue, the experts said.

"I think this is more a political platform to prepare the ground for the upcoming campaign for the fall elections," Wellershoff and Partners senior economist Felix Brill said.

Leading left-wing politician Christian Levrat Sunday warned Switzerland risks losing 100,000 jobs because of the Swiss franc's strength against the euro. Switzerland's political establishment is gearing up for October 23 parliamentary elections, and criticizing the SNB after the ill-fated currency market intervention is proving fertile ground.

SNB president Philipp Hildebrand has already come under attack from former justice minister Christoph Blocher, who remains a prominent and influential right-wing politician. Blocher called for Hildebrand to resign recently, arguing the central bank had speculated with public funds when it attempted to limit the franc's rise by buying euros.

In calling for a peg, the left-wing is playing to Switzerland's exporters, who are watching their profit margins dwindle under the strong franc. Data from May showed a rise in Swiss exports, though prices for exported goods continued to drop due to the strong franc. Switzerland's exporters have been particularly vocal about demanding action from the SNB.

A franc peg such as the one China maintains to the U.S. dollar would mean Switzerland would also give up its independence over its monetary policy, something Swiss authorities are seen as loathe to do. The Chinese central bank currently allows the yuan to float up to 0.5% above or below a daily central parity rate against the dollar.

Last Friday, SNB president Hildebrand forcefully asserted the SNB's right to act independently, saying its flexibility had been a valuable asset during the financial crisis, when it issued SNB bills to mop up excess money-market liquidity.

A spokesman for the SNB didn't comment Monday.

Swiss business lobby Economiesuisse rejected the idea of a franc peg, saying the instrument would do little to ease exporters' current pain.

"The main problem is that we have an overvalued franc, but if we pegged a clearly overvalued franc at current levels, it would effectively perpetuate this overvaluation, which certainly isn't the best thing for Switzerland's exporters," Economiesuisse chief economist Rudolf Minsch said.

A study released Monday suggested Switzerland's exporters are adapting to the franc's strength more nimbly than their chorus of protests would lead one to believe. Specialization and continued high demand for Swiss products are reducing the impact of the rising Swiss franc on the country's exporters, according to the study, carried out by think-tank KOF.

text:

21 Jun 2011 13:00 EDT *DJ  SNB Hildebrand: Fincl Crisis Showed SNB Flexibility Valuable

21 Jun 2011 13:00 EDT *DJ  SNB Hildebrand: Guided Solely By Mandate In Decision-Making

21 Jun 2011 13:00 EDT *DJ  SNB Hildebrand: SNB's Independence Not "Unconditional"

21 Jun 2011 13:00 EDT DJ  SNB Hildebrand: To Keep Using Suitable Instruments For Mandate

ZURICH (Dow Jones)--Swiss National Bank President Philipp Hildebrand signalled Tuesday the central bank will continue to keep its options open in pursuing its mandate to ensure price stability.

Hildebrand also backed the institution's right to act independently, in prepared remarks to a business audience.

"We are continually analyzing developments and constantly drawing conclusions with a view to our future actions. Based on this, the SNB will continue to use the instruments we judge best suited and necessary for fulfilling our mandate in the interests of the country as a whole, to the best of our ability," he said.

While not detailing specific options open to the SNB, Hildebrand started his speech by mentioning the 21 billion Swiss franc ($25 billion) loss the SNB posted in 2010, when it spent billions of francs attempting to curb the Swiss franc's surge against major currencies like the US dollar and euro.

Hildebrand said the SNB, which generally pays profits out to the Swiss federation and its cantons, may suspend those payments as it repairs its swollen balance sheet--a result of past interventions.

"Very volatile results may be expected in the next few years because of the current size of the balance sheet and the uncertain situation in the capital markets," Hildebrand said.

The central bank had already flagged possible future losses in January 2011, when it disclosed its 2010 loss.

Hildebrand also issued a passionate defense of the SNB's independence, which right-wing politicians have argued in favor of clipping.

Hildebrand said the SNB's independence is "particularly valuable" in Switzerland because monetary, and not fiscal, policy was mainly used during the financial crisis to stimulate the alpine nation's economy.

He also emphasized that the SNB's flexibility in deciding on instruments of monetary policy proved to be a "huge advantage" during the crisis, such as when it issued SNB bills to soak up excess money-market liquidity.

The Swiss government has repeatedly spoken out in favor of the SNB's independence when the central bank came under attack from the Swiss People's Party, or SVP--Switzerland's largest party--for intervening on the franc.

Hildebrand's remarks are noteworthy because he appears not to explicitly rule out more currency interventions--something most economists see as unlikely--and because the remarks are among his most political yet in quieting his detractors, and asserting the SNB's independence.

Last week, the SNB delayed curbing its expansive monetary policy, citing the recent surge in the franc as adding to the risks facing the Swiss economy.

The central bank kept the target range for its benchmark three-month Swiss franc London interbank offered rate on hold at 0.0%-0.75%.

The SNB is targeting a three-month Libor rate of 0.25%, a record low in place since March 2009.

The strong franc appears to have been a major factor in the SNB's decision to keep rates on hold for at least another quarter, in an effort to avoid lifting rates earlier than the European Central Bank.

title: UPDATE 1-Swiss franc hits record highs vs struggling euro
text:
* Swiss franc soars to record high vs euro

* Brushes off SNB comments about strong franc and growth

* Traders expect euro/Swiss franc to extend losses

LONDON, June 16 (Reuters) - The Swiss franc hit a record high against the euro on Thursday, shrugging off central bank concerns about franc strength and buoyed by demand for the safe haven currency due to growing concerns about euro zone debt.

The euro <EURCHF=> fell more than one percent on the day to hit a record low of 1.1957 francs on trading platform EBS, with traders saying losses had accelerated as stop loss orders were triggered on the break below 1.1970 francs.

It failed to break lower, however, with traders saying there were bids at 1.1950 francs.

"It feels like momentum in euro/Swiss franc is accelerating to the downside," said Kathleen Brooks, currency strategist at FOREX.com.

Implied volatility in euro/Swiss franc spiked higher, reflecting a perceived risk in the options market of further weakness in the euro/Swiss franc spot price.

One-month euro/Swiss implied volatility <EURCHF1MO=> traded above 12.0 percent, up from around 11.2 percent on Wednesday. One-month risk reversals <EUCH1MRR=ICAP> revealed an increasing demand for bets on euro losses versus the Swiss franc.

The Swiss National Bank left interest rates unchanged, stressing risks to the economy from a strong franc, with Chairman Philipp Hildebrand expressing concerns about exporters' margins. [ID:nLDE75E1S8] [ID:nWEA6270]

But analysts said intervention looked unlikely given that Switzerland was not facing deflation, adding that authorities would have a battle to prevent currency strength with risk aversion sparking demand for francs and weighing on the euro.

"It doesn't look like the SNB will intervene, and if they did they would be trampled on in the current risk-averse environment," Brooks added.

SNB board member Jean-Pierre Danthine said the Swiss economy was doing well enough that there was no reason at the moment for interventions or extraordinary measures. [ID:nWEA6294]

Between March 2009 and June 2010 the SNB intervened in foreign exchange markets to stave off deflationary risks.

The Swiss franc also gained against the dollar, which was down 0.5 percent at 0.8491 francs <CHF=>.
