title: SPECIAL REPORT-The trials of Philipp Hildebrand
text:
Refiles to fix name in para 4, add reporting credits

 By Emma Thomasson

 ZURICH, June 14 (Reuters) - Philipp Hildebrand learned the value of perseverance at an early age, when as a freestyle champ he narrowly missed qualifying for the 1984 Olympics. It's an experience he's drawn on in a rocky chairmanship of the Swiss National Bank since he took up the post in January 2010.

 The 47-year-old former hedge fund manager has faced down calls for his resignation after he risked state funds to try to halt the rise of the Swiss franc last year, an effort which cost the central bank 26.5 billion francs. The currency has since gone on to hit more record highs against the dollar and euro, and such huge foreign exchange losses mean Hildebrand is unlikely to take on markets again in a hurry. 

 But he has not been cowed. Swimming is a very good learning process for life, points out his former coach Anthony Ulrich. "It's an endurance-oriented sport," he says. "You learn to lose and keep your head above water at the same time."

Central bank heads in post-crisis Europe face many stiff challenges. For his next test, Hildebrand -- one of a new generation in  Europe taking over as familiar figures like Jean-Claude Trichet, Axel Weber and Nout Wellink move on -- has set his sights on another ambitious target: big banks. Pushing tough plans to force banks like UBS and Credit Suisse to be more prudent than their global rivals, he's made enemies at home. Internationally, he's building an image as a trail-blazing regulator.

 "He's one of the best central bankers around," said Charles Wyplosz, economics professor at Geneva's Graduate Institute, who taught with Hildebrand up to 2007. "He is up against two very big Swiss banks. These are some of the most powerful lobbies in the world. That takes a lot of personal courage."

 MARKET FORCES

 Hildebrand remembers the start of the financial crisis quite clearly. It was August 2007 and he was on the last day of his summer holidays in the Swiss Alps when his phone rang. It was the SNB's trading desk, calling to tell him global risk premiums had jumped, signalling the start of a liquidity crunch as banks stopped trusting one another. It was also the start of a steep climb for the safe-haven Swiss franc.

 Since then, the world's sixth most traded currency has gained over 20 percent against the dollar and almost 30 percent against the euro. Investors worried about the United States' fast-growing debt and the euro zone's failure to fix its problems have piled in. Swiss manufacturers were already complaining about squeezed profits on exports and having to compete against cheaper imports. 

 By early 2009, when Hildebrand was vice chairman, the Swiss economy was in its worst recession since World War Two and the SNB had already slashed interest rates to rock bottom. The bank was so concerned about the risk of a deflationary spiral it decided to act, buying euros in the foreign currency markets. That worked, at least for a while, and by December the SNB had decided the economy was on the mend and the currency had stabilised. 

 Then in January 2010, Philipp Michael Hildebrand took over as the youngest president in the history of the century-old bank.  Born in the Swiss capital of Bern, he had studied -- mostly politics and international relations -- in Toronto, Florence, Harvard and Oxford. 

 Though he was no economist, Hildebrand knew the territory. His first real job had been with the World Economic Forum in Geneva, organising speakers from the financial services industry for its annual talkfest at Davos. They included George Soros, who had made his fortune betting against the Bank of England, and who helped him get a position at New York-based hedge fund Moore Capital Management, which specialised in speculating on interest rate futures and monetary policy. 

 As a young hedge fund manager, Hildebrand had in 1996 written a letter to influential Swiss newspaper Finanz und Wirtschaft, demanding that the SNB intervene to weaken an overvalued franc. "The markets are powerful but they often also allow themselves to be led," he asserted at the time. (He declined to comment on the record for this report.)

 Scarcely had he settled into his new office at the edge of Lake Zurich -- hanging a favourite black and white photo of childhood idol Mohammed Ali on the wall -- when he was called into action. With the franc soaring again during the euro zone debt crisis, to around 1.4 per euro, Hildebrand ordered another round of massive interventions. Between February and May 2010, the SNB bought 147 billion francs in foreign currency, about a quarter of Swiss GDP. The markets sensed the SNB's desperation as it tried to move the market in thin Asian trade. 

 "The SNB wanted to make the biggest splash they could," one trader said.  "They wanted to take the speculators out of the game by squeezing their positions." A month later, with the franc still rising, the SNB ditched the policy. 

 That year the bank booked a 20 billion franc loss, the biggest in its history. It may yet have to suspend an annual payout to local governments, prompting belt-tightening that the wealthy Swiss have so far largely avoided.

 It was a hard lesson. "Historically, central bankintervention has a short-term effect but in the long run it always loses," said Geoffrey Baker, managing director and currency strategist at Insch Capital. "Hildebrand seemed to have more market knowledge than most and decided to throw in the towel." 

 DEUTSCHEMARK PROXY

 Retaining the habits of a hedge fund manager, Hildebrand still rises early to read the papers and keep an eye on the markets on the screen in his office. There he can see that he's up against profound forces and has only limited tools to check them. 

 The SNB is not the only central bank to have the problem of a strengthening currency. Last September, a bid by the Bank of Japan to weaken the yen failed after its intervention met global opposition: there were warnings of currency wars between rival exporting nations. The combined firepower of the Group of Seven rich nations did succeed in stabilising financial markets in March, when their first joint intervention since 2000 stemmed a sharp rise in the yen in the wake of the earthquake.

 But Hildebrand has had no such support. Since last June when he stopped intervening, investors on world markets have pushed the franc even higher. It hit a new record around 1.2004 per euro this week and a new peak against the dollar on June 7, its appreciation fuelled by Switzerland's stability -- and a low debt-to-GDP ratio of 53 percent according to the IMF -- as other parts of the world were hit by revolution and economic crises.

Rabobank market economist Emile Cardon says the SNB could not have predicted Japan's disaster, nor the ongoing weakness of the U.S. economy: "There used to be three safe havens, with the Japanese yen and the U.S. dollar, but after the earthquake and weak U.S. growth, the only remaining safe haven is the Swiss franc."

 Already last June, Mansoor Mohi-uddin, chief currency strategist at UBS, was arguing the franc is increasingly seen as a proxy for the old German mark: "Switzerland's currency already acts as an indicator of Germany's economy," he said in a report, noting that 20 percent of Swiss exports go to Germany.

 POLITICAL TARGET 

 Whatever the economic reality, the political recriminations for Hildebrand have been torrid, especially from Switzerland's right wing. They said the government should have been more wary of appointing a former hedge fund manager with no qualifications in economics. 

 "How hard is Hildebrand?" Weltwoche weekly wrote. "After a meteoric rise, sceptical voices are increasing. Is the man as hard as the currency which he has to direct through the euro crisis?"

 Christoph Blocher, mastermind of the right-wing Swiss People's Party, has kept up the pressure, calling on Hildebrand to resign and likening the losses to the folly that brought Switzerland's biggest bank UBS to its knees. "What the SNB did was megalomania or incompetence. At the beginning of 2010 they thought they could save the euro from collapse," he told Reuters. "Nobody can do that, not even the Americans." [20110614 085738 GMT]  

 Even SNB insiders and independent economists have been critical. Former SNB chief economist Ulrich Kohli -- who was still at the bank when the first interventions were launched in 2009 -- calls Hildebrand's effort a "total failure and a total waste of money ... It hasn't done anything to stop the Swiss franc appreciating. It's really money thrown out the window. I think he was wrong then and wrong now when it comes to the ability central banks have to manipulate the exchange rate."

 Hildebrand himself refuses to admit the interventions were a failure, saying they helped Switzerland become one of the first countries to return to pre-crisis growth levels. "The SNB's policy -- and that includes the foreign exchange purchases -- undoubtedly contributed to this positive outcome," he told SNB shareholders in April.

 Nonetheless, he's unlikely to try to weaken the franc again anytime soon, despite new calls from Swiss trade unions warning tens of thousands of jobs are at risk. "They got burned the last time," says Kohli, the former SNB economist. "They used up all the ammunition and the SNB's very much weakened."

 "FOLLOW THE SWISS LEAD"

 But if Hildebrand was brought down by the currency struggle, he's not out for the count. The Ali fan has turned his attention to what for him is a much bigger legacy of the crisis: weak banks. His forex intervention involved nearly a quarter of the country's GDP, but Swiss bank assets amount to at least six times the country's economy.

 Regulators in Europe and the United States are looking to increase the financial buffers banks must build to limit the call they can make on taxpayers if things go wrong. Hildebrand, who is credited with playing a central role in saving UBS from collapse at the height of the crisis, is pushing for new rules to go further than most. UBS and Credit Suisse will have to have a capital buffer nearly three times bigger than their global rivals. "Follow the Swiss lead to avoid another Lehman," he wrote in the FT last October. 

 He's been praised by the likes of Paul Volcker and Timothy Geithner and, along with Britain's top financial regulator Adair Turner, is seen as an innovator. The banks don't like it. They say high capital cushions will be costly to maintain and crimp lending. Switzerland is crazy to pursue more stringent rules than its global rivals, some say. 

 In his defence, Hildebrand points to the ultimate arbiter: the market. Swiss bank credit default swaps (CDS) -- a measure of demand for investors seeking insurance against unpaid debts -- have been trading at the lowest spread of all the majors.

"It is an interesting observation that the one market indicator that we have about the safety of banks, the CDS contracts, are telling us today that what we are trying to do in Switzerland may not have been so crazy after all," he said at a European Central Bank event in May. 

 "There is nothing wrong with a race to the top. What must be avoided in a global system, with global integrated markets, is a race to the bottom."

 BEYOND THE MOUNTAINS

 It's a line Hildebrand is pushing even though the domestic heat on him is unlikely to cool soon. As he sweats out the summer in his 3rd floor office, a listed building where air conditioning is banned, a fierce debate is underway over the rules he has championed. Some commentators say Hildebrand's critics have seized on his forex debacle to water down the regulatory aims.

 There are party politics to consider. Switzerland goes to the polls in October and Blocher's anti-immigrant, anti-European Union party, now the biggest in Switzerland, looks set to win. Blocher wants parliament to limit the SNB's powers beyond ensuring price stability. There would be no more currencyinterventions. 

 "Mr Hildebrand is very isolated in Swiss politics and in the popular mood," said Peter V. Kunz, professor at the Institute for Economic Law at Bern University. "Mr Hildebrand is not your average central banker. He is a very activist, self-assured national banker ... Swiss politicians can be very small-minded so an international star generally doesn't go down so well."

 Last year, Hildebrand was the world's highest paid central banker on 833,000 francs, and is rarely seen in anything but an elegant navy blue suit and luxury Breguet watch. Having spent much of his early adult life outside Switzerland, he lacks political allies at home. His towering 1 metre 94 stature gives him an aloof air, and his push for stronger regulations has raised hackles among a cosy Swiss elite more used to backroom deals and a strict code of preserving client secrecy.

 He has also been the subject of several glossy magazine profiles, which has jarred with a Swiss preference for modesty, particularly among public officials.

 HEAD ABOVE WATER

 But his opponents would be hard pressed to unseat him. The current term for the SNB's governing board ends in 2015: all three members can be reappointed by the government, and despite the tough talk, no government has yet forced a chairman out.

 What he lacks in terms of domestic support, Hildebrand more than makes up for on the international stage. He counts among his friends Mario Draghi, the Italian central banker who seems likely to follow Trichet at the head of the European Central Bank, former Brazilian central bank governor Arminio Fraga and Canadian central bank governor Mark Carney, with whom he studied at Oxford. 

 Hildebrand is already a member of the steering committee of the Financial Stability Board, the global regulatory body. He would make a convincing candidate to replace Draghi as chairman if, as expected, the Italian moves to the ECB. The committee which drew up the Basel III rules is also looking for a replacement chair for Dutch central bank governor Nout Wellink. He could do either job -- with both bodies conveniently located just an hour by train from Zurich in Basel -- alongside the SNB post. 

 If Hildebrand does end up joining the financial industry's global regulatory guard, he would undoubtedly be zealous. When times get tough, he recalls the words of former SNB chairman Fritz Leutwiler, who presided over contested interventions in the turbulent years following the flotation of the franc in 1973. 

 "He always said we are not there to be popular. If you think you can be popular for the whole cycle of a chairmanship then it is the wrong assumption about the job," Hildebrand told Swiss television. "What is a much bigger concern for me are the worries over whether we could stabilise the financial system, concern about the whole economy, where we are going, worries about the risks that are still in the system."

 Still, it would be a tall order to convince the world's bankers that keeping your head above water is more important than winning.

title: UPDATE: SNB Danthine: Sole  Intervention  Aim Was Price Stability
text:
(Adds comments from Danthine in 9th, 10th and 11th paragraphs and comments from Dewet Moser in the last paragraph.)

ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss National Bank's decision to intervene in currency markets in 2009 and 2010 was aimed solely at maintaining price stability with deflation being the main risk at the time, central bank Governing Board member Jean-Pierre Danthine said Thursday.

"At the start of 2009, the severe downturn in the global economy had translated into a very serious threat of deflation in Switzerland, and price stability was not assured," Danthine said in a speech prepared for delivery at a central bank conference in Zurich.

In addition, the "substantial increase in the Swiss franc's value since the start of the financial crisis represented an inappropriate tightening of monetary conditions when it was imperative they be kept as loose as possible," Danthine said.

The SNB intervened repeatedly between March 2009 and June 2010, amassing large foreign currency reserves, most of them denominated in euros, which then depreciated. This resulted in a book loss of 19.2 billion Swiss francs ($21 billion) last year, which drew some public criticism in Switzerland.

Danthine, whose speech focused on the SNB interventions carried out during that period, said the central bank judged the Swiss economy wouldn't have been able to withstand "a further violent appreciation of the franc [versus the euro]" at the time.

"By the end of May 2010, pressures on the franc started to subside, and the SNB considered in its June monetary assessment that the threat of deflation had largely disappeared," he said.

Danthine refuted suggestions the SNB "had been defeated by the [currency] markets" and said the interventions provided the economy with monetary conditions that have contributed to a "reasonably swift recovery from the financial crisis, while assuring price stability."

The downturn in the Swiss economy has been less severe than in other countries and output has been the first to reach its pre-crisis level, he said. Swiss gross domestic product grew 2.6% in 2010, after declining 1.9% in 2009.

Asked whether Swiss interest rates will remain near zero for longer than expected because of developments elsewhere in Europe, Danthine said there are already signs of inflationary pressure building in the eurozone, as well as the U.K.

"European Central Bank President Jean-Claude Trichet has warned about inflation picking up, and the U.K. may move on rates," he said.

As far as Switzerland is concerned, the SNB is evaluating the economic situation and the strength of the economy.

The SNB also reiterated that its interventions weren't aimed at achieving any particular exchange-rate target, but rather to provide the most appropriate monetary conditions.

"The primary indicator of the success of the SNB interventions is the inflation chart, and not the central bank's balance sheet," Danthine said. "Our foreign exchange interventions will only have been costly if they result in serious inflationary pressures two to three years from now."

Danthine said the SNB has, since June 2010, been absorbing the excess liquidity generated by the interventions through the use of reverse repos and bills of various maturities.

In a separate speech, Dewet Moser, alternate member of the governing board of the SNB, said that the SNB bills have helped to bind liquidity. He said that these steps are forming the base for a gradual normalization in the money market.

title: Swiss SVP seeks cap on SNB autonomy after losses
text:
* SVP to propose new rules in parliament next week

* Blocher already called for SNB head to quit

* Other parties accuse SVP of electioneering

ZURICH, March 6 (Reuters) - The popular right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) wants to limit the autonomy of the Swiss National Bank (SNB) on decisions outside its core mandate of price stability after big losses on currency interventions.

"If the SNB leaves its actual mission with large currency buys, one must be able to supervise the SNB bosses and if necessary stop them," Christoph Blocher, former justice minister and SVP mastermind, told the SonntagsZeitung newspaper.

Blocher has already called on SNB chief Philipp Hildebrand to resign after the central bank posted a 2010 loss of 19.2 billion Swiss francs ($20.74 billion) after ill-fated interventions to try to fight the currency's strength. [ID:nLDE71O14P]

The SVP, expected to remain Switzerland's biggest party in national elections in October, plans a motion proposing new rules in parliament next week to control the central bank.

"In extreme cases, currency buys can be necessary to secure price stability. That is why we need disciplinary supervisory rules to prevent the managing board contravening their core mandate and taking on unbelievable risks," Blocher said.

The SNB has repeatedly defended the interventions as being necessary to fight deflation risk from the soaring franc.

Blocher also accused Hildebrand of being too much in favour of more integration with the European Union.

"I have the suspicion that Mr Hildebrand wants to play a role at the European or even global level. He pleads for opening and integration which does not belong to his area of competency. He also doesn't rule out tying the franc to the euro," he said.

However, the other main parties in the coalition government that rules Switzerland have defended the SNB's currency interventions and the central bank's independence.

Economy Minister Johann Schneider-Ammann said in an interview with the Finanz und Wirtschaft newspaper on Saturday that the SNB had managed to dampen the franc's rise somewhat and said the situation had improved in the meantime.

Otto Ineichen from the liberal Free Democrats told the Sonntag newspaper the SVP was going too far with its election campaign and was defaming the SNB with "false accusations".

The safe-haven franc has soared to record highs against the euro and the dollar due to unrest in north Africa and the euro zone's debt crisis, prompting calls for the government to intervene as Swiss exporters suffer.

The Swiss government has announced measures to help firms to deal with the strong Swiss franc, including increased funding for the tourism industry and support for companies to boost innovation. [ID:nLDE71F1FO]

text:

By Neil MacLucas

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The value of the Swiss National Bank's currency reserves increased to 207.9 billion Swiss francs ($219.6 billion) in January reflecting the euro's rally last month.

The value of the foreign currency holdings rose CHF5.3 billion from an unrevised CHF202.6 billion in December, according to the SNB data. The euro appreciated by around 4% against the Swiss franc during the same period, boosting the value of those reserves.

"The higher reserve valuation is simply due to the slight rally we saw in the euro last month, pushing up the value of those common currency holdings," said Ursina Kubli, a currency analyst at Bank Sarasin & Cie. "It certainly doesn't suggest the SNB conducted any fresh currency purchases," she added.

Switzerland's central bank intervened repeatedly from March 2009 to try and stem the franc's excessive gains against the euro, though it appeared to step back from this policy in June last year, saying signs of deflation had disappeared.

The SNB is expecting to post a hefty CHF21 billion book loss for last year as the franc's 16% appreciation against the common currency eroded the value of its euro holdings.

The latest central bank data also show there was little diversification of its reserves in the final quarter of 2010, with its euro holdings slightly lower at EUR90 billion by the end of the year, and its dollar reserves little changed at $54.3 billion. The value of the SNB's Japanese yen holdings rose marginally to Y1.8 billion.

"I'm sure the SNB will diversify its reserves in coming months, taking advantage of any further euro gains to reduce its exposure to the currency," Kubli said.

The SNB's euro reserves climbed to EUR90 billion last year, from EUR37 billion at the end of 2009, while the dollar holdings increased to $54.3 billion from $27.6 billion.

text:

26 Jan 2011 11:01 EDT DJ  SNB Danthine: Bank Mandated To Preserve Price Stability-Report

title: Chile  Central Bank :  Currency Intervention  Program Working
text:
BASEL, Switzerland (Dow Jones)--Capital controls and currency interventions undertaken by a number of emerging nations are a by-product of the two-tier growth of the global economy, but they won't change the long-term course of these currencies, the governor of the central bank of Chile said Monday.

"There is so much tension in the foreign-exchange market that what we are doing in a way is to stabilize the sharp appreciation of the currency. But we won't change the long-term fundamentals...the adjustments will take place," Jose de Gregorio told reporters on the sidelines of a gathering of central bankers in Basel at the Bank for International Settlements.

Several emerging countries have imposed capital controls at their borders or intervened on foreign-exchange markets in order to curb the value of their currencies, pushed up by a surge in foreign capital inflows in search of higher remuneration against a backdrop of record low interest rates in the developed world.

At their meeting in Basel, central bankers agreed that these sharp inflows of capital are an issue for emerging markets. De Gregorio said they are a reflection of the "world's dual recovery," with emerging economies experiencing buoyant growth, while more mature ones are only witnessing a subdued pickup in activity.

The central Bank of Chile last week launched a $12 billion currency market intervention program in order to tame the peso's appreciation and prevent exports from being stifled.

De Gregorio said the program, which will beef up the country's foreign-exchange reserves, will help make Chile more resilient in the event of an external shock and is also giving the Chilean economy some breathing space to improve its competitiveness.

"The program is currently working," he said, adding that the Chilean central bank isn't targeting a specific level for the peso through the intervention.

France, which currently heads the Group of 20 industrialized and emerging economies, argues erratic capital flows can create currency volatility and disrupt the monetary policies of emerging countries. It wants the group to explore ways to better regulate them.

While De Gregorio said the central bank would consider any measure to further help stabilizing the Chilean economy, he stressed there was no need at the moment to expand the market intervention program or to use any other policy tools. He added that the currency intervention program will be assessed on an ongoing basis, and vowed it won't compromise the central bank's inflation target.

The program is designed in such a way "that we feel independent to move our interest rates as needed to fulfil our inflation objectives," De Gregorio told reporters.

title: WORLD  FOREX : Swiss Franc Continues Its Surge Vs Euro, Dollar
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The Swiss franc rose broadly Wednesday, hitting a record high against the euro as investors continued to seek safety from the euro zone's sovereign-debt crisis.

The Swiss currency moved as high as CHF1.2440 versus the euro, extending its rally this week. The franc also strengthened against the dollar to the highest levels since October when it touched the all-time peak against the U.S. currency.

"The Swiss franc benefits from both safe-haven flows driven by the debt problems in the euro-zone periphery and the strong Swiss economic outlook," said Gabriel de Kock, North American head of FX strategy at Morgan Stanley in New York. "It is a double positive for the franc and I am bullish on the currency."

De Kock said the Swiss National Bank, the country's central bank, is unlikely to intervene in the near term to stem the rise in the franc. The previous intervention earlier this year has left a huge overhang of liquidity in the economy and the Swiss National Bank doesn't want to further boost the money supply, he said, adding that the Swiss economy had a relatively shallow recession and recovered more rapidly than some other major countries.

Steven Englander, head of G10 currency strategy at Citigroup, noted that the franc's strength is due mainly to the euro-zone debt crisis, which means there are still many potential buyers desiring a haven. Englander said it may not be effective for Switzerland's central bank to intervene, saying that, even if intervention temporarily pushes down the franc, buyers could return to prop it up.

Some market participants noted that thinning liquidity near the end of the year exaggerated part of the price swings in the currency markets. Many companies and banks have already closed their books for the end of the year and such flows had little to do with the economic fundamental outlooks, they said.

Wednesday afternoon, the dollar was CHF0.9519 from CHF0.9563 late Tuesday, according to EBS via CQG. Against the euro, the franc rose about 0.8% to CHF1.2457.

The euro-zone debt worries continued to weigh on the euro, with the common currency weakening against the dollar and the yen.

The onslaught of credit warnings and downgrades of sovereign ratings over the past few days added to worries that borrowing costs in many euro-zone nations would be pushed up further, undermining their economic outlook at a time when governments are putting out fiscal austerity programs to cut budget deficits.

"We remain underweight the euro," said Englander.

The euro could fall to as low as $1.27 if it breaks below its late November low of $1.2970, said Hidetoshi Yanagihara, senior currency trader and strategist at Mizuho Corporate Bank in New York. "Probably the euro might be hit more against the majors--the dollar and the Swiss franc," he said.

The euro was at $1.3090 from $1.3096 late Tuesday. The dollar was at Y83.57 from Y83.75, while the euro was at Y109.38 from Y109.70.

The ICE Dollar Index, which tracks the U.S. dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, was at 80.692 from 80.718.

The pound was another big loser, touching a three-month trough against the dollar as a weaker-than-forecast economic report raised worries about the health of the British economy.

The U.K. pound was at $1.5380 from $1.5468.

The Australian dollar rose against its U.S. counterpart as a rise in U.S. stocks spurred some investors to buy higher-yielding currencies. The Australian currency has surged this year, benefiting from strong exports of commodities, thanks to strong demand from China.

The Australian dollar returned to parity against the U.S. dollar for the first time in a week. It rose about 0.27% to $1.0007, near the record peak of $1.0184 hit on November 5.

title: UPDATE 2-SNB says policy appropriate without  FX interventions
text:
* Hildebrand, Danthine: policy right given inflation f'cast

* Danthine says no legitimacy for FX interventions now

* Danthine says c.bank may act if shocks lead to deflation

(Adds further Hildebrand comment)

By Sven Egenter and Silke Koltrowitz

LAUSANNE/LUGANO, Switzerland, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank's expansionary policy is appropriate and there is no reason at present to intervene in the currency market given the inflation outlook, Swiss central bankers said on Thursday.

Speaking at an event in Lausanne, SNB board member Jean-Pierre Danthine said interventions earlier this year to fight a rise in the Swiss franc had been necessary to fend off deflation risks that had now eased. The SNB changed its stance in June.

"The current monetary policy is appropriate. In that context we have no legitimacy to go beyond standard monetary policy instruments," Danthine said at a conference, when asked about the SNB's stance on the currency.

"We are now projecting inflation which is comfortably in positive territory," Danthine said. At the same time, there were no inflationary pressures.

But as the Swiss economy was still vulnerable to external shocks and deflationary risks could resurface, the SNB would take the necessary measures, he added.

SNB chairman Philipp Hildebrand, at a separate event in Lugano, said it was important for Switzerland that Europe returned to stability and also issued a warning that the central bank was ready to take action against house price inflation if necessary, saying it was monitoring the real estate market closely.

"The main problem is the lack of confidence in Europe that has shown its effects via turbulence on the forex market that represents a difficult challenge for Switzerland," Hildebrand said.

The SNB dropped its intervention policy in June after spending some 200 billion Swiss francs in currency interventions. The franc has since hit record highs against the euro and the dollar, though it has softened in recent days <EURCHF=><CHF=>.

The SNB indicated at its last policy meeting in September that it was in no rush to lift its target rate for three-month Swiss franc LIBOR from the current ultra-low level of 0.25 percent as it sees a marked slowdown of the economy in 2011.

Danthine echoed the central bank's assessment, saying that following a number of strong quarters, the Swiss economy was now set to slow markedly, as the cooling of the global economy and the strength of the Swiss franc were taking their toll.

Switzerland emerged from the global downturn less bruised than many other European countries, and the SNB expects growth of around 2.5 percent this year. [ID:nLDE68D1IK]

A number of economic data and surveys have recently supported the SNB's view of a slowdown and markets will now closely watch the country's leading growth barometer, the KOF indictor, due on Friday <ECONCH>.

HOUSE PRICES

Hildebrand also said the SNB's expansionary monetary policy was appropriate, adding that the central bank's main focus remained ensuring price stability.

""The SNB will do everything to fulfill its mandate to preserve price stability. We do not want inflation above 2 percent and we do not want deflation," he said.

But he also emphasised that the real estate market was being monitored closely. The SNB could take action together with bank regulator FINMA, if necessary, while the SNB was also looking into macro-prudential measures to complement monetary policy.

"The longer monetary policy remains expansive, the bigger the risk of undesirable developments. Today some warning signs are already visible," Hildebrand said.

Hildebrand's remarks follow a warning from the SNB in June that mortgage lending standards could be too lax.

Similarly, SNB Vice Chairman Thomas Jordan said earlier this year that regulators might consider measures to tackle the real estate market if hiking interest rates was not an option.

Low mortgage rates combined with competition among lenders constituted fertile ground for growing risks, Hildebrand said.

"Even if the development of real estate prices until now seems to be supported by fundamentals, and the central bank in its base scenario sees a moderate development in the housing market for the coming year, from the perspective of risk there are indeed grounds for concern," he said. (Additional reporting by Catherine Bosley; Additional writing by Jason Rhodes; Editing by Catherine Evans and Susan Fenton)

title: =DJ UPDATE: Swiss  FX  Reserves Drop As SNB Reins In  Intervention
text:
ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss National Bank's currency reserves declined slightly in September, slipping for a fourth straight month, as the central bank refrained from intervening in the currency market.

The value of the reserves fell by 2.7 billion Swiss francs ($2.8 billion) to CHF215.3 billion at the end of September, according to SNB data released Wednesday. This signals the buying of euros to check its depreciation versus the franc continued to tail off from the levels seen earlier this year, and as the dollar lost around 4.5% of its franc value in September.

"This drop in the reserve valuation is no surprise and extends the trend seen in recent months," according to Ulrich Leuchtmann, currency analyst at Commerzbank AG.

Switzerland's central bank intervened repeatedly earlier this year to try and counter the franc's excessive gains against the euro, citing the danger of deflation, though it appeared to alter this stance in June, saying such risks had disappeared.

The central bank posted a hefty CHF2.8 billion book loss in the first half of the year as the franc's 10% appreciation against the common currency eroded the value of its euro holdings.

While the central bank has indicated the risk of deflation is diminishing, consumer price data Tuesday showed Swiss monthly inflation held at zero for a second month in September.

"The CPI report was weaker than expected, and while deflation isn't a threat right now, such risks may emerge next year," said Leuchtmann.

The SNB in September lowered its forecast for average Swiss inflation to 0.7% for 2010, and to 0.3% in 2011, and said the possibility of negative inflation at the start of next year can't be excluded.

title: Swiss firms must live with stong franc - bank lobby
text:
* Head of bankers' association says strong franc is to stay

 * Says Swiss industry needs to adapt quickly

 * Says systematic interventions to be challenged by markets

 ZURICH, Sept 16 (Reuters) - The Swiss industry needs to swiftly adapt to the strong Swiss franc, as its strength will last and central bank power to intervene is limited, the head of Switzerland's top banking association said.  "The Swiss franc has always been a problem in Switzerland and today we have a hiccup which could work to the detriment of some (sectors) of our export industry," Patrick Odier, Chairman of the Swiss Bankers' Association, said on Thursday ahead of a key Swiss National Bank rate-setting meeting.

 "The question is how swiftly can the Swiss industry adapt to the situation of the strong franc, which will last," he said.

 Odier noted that some sectors, like exporters, were more at risk from the strength of the Swiss franc.

 Others, such as the wealth management sector, have benefitted as nervous investors moved some of their assets out of the euro zone and into Switzerland.

 Odier said he did not expect the SNB, whose focus is inflationary or deflationary risks, to look only at specific sectors when taking monetary policy decisions.

 But he noted that the central bank had little room to intervene on the market to bring down the franc.

 "The way to intervene in the market to try and calm down the momentum on the height Swiss franc is limited, but it still exists," he said.

 "It is my view that whatever a national bank does massively and openly against or for a currency will be nearly always systematically challenged by the market," he added.

 "We should not exaggerate (the impact from the Swiss franc). We should watch the impact of the high franc on the industry in general and hope for a quick adaptation of some of these companies that may suffer the most."

title: Forex  Focus: The Waiting Game On  Switzerland  And Japan
text:
LONDON (Dow Jones)--Which central bank will intervene in the currency markets first: the Swiss National Bank or the Bank of Japan?

The chance that either will come into the market to tackle the soaring yen or franc is enough to put many traders off buying either currency against the dollar or the euro.

That means that buying one against the other in a "who will blink first?" trade is happy hunting ground for the brave.

This is, perhaps, a sign of how desperate currencies analysts are getting for good trades. Almost all major currencies [and indeed commodity-linked and emerging-market currencies too] are flashing bright red sell signals at the moment, so analysts and investors are forced to come up with some pretty creative ideas.

It does make sense, though, so it's worth weighing up the two.

By one measure, the Swiss are the more likely to take the plunge. After all, in real terms, the franc is stronger now than the yen, BNP Paribas pointed out in a note to clients last week. Some market-watchers believe that means the Japanese authorities will sit back and watch the yen climb much more--as long as it's a slow and steady move--before they try to flog it back down.

Still, even though the franc is now at an all-time high against the euro, which Monday sank below CHF1.2950 for the first time, few if any serious franc-watchers think a sting is coming.

That's partly because the Swiss economy keeps on proving itself perfectly capable of taking this strain, despite the risk to exports. Friday, the country's KOF index--a key leading indicator--did edge lower, suggesting that the country's economic recovery will slow for the rest of the year. Still, it was not a sharp pullback, and it comes after the index hit its highest level in four years in July.

If franc strength is seriously damaging, then that's not clear in the KOF think-tank's report, and the central bank is still reasonably likely to raise interest rates at some point late in 2010.

What's more, the SNB has already tried a heavy-duty program of franc selling this year, and it didn't exactly work, although one can argue that the franc would be much higher now if the central bank hadn't worked so hard to hold it down. The central bank's interventions, particularly during April and May when it was swimming against a heavy tide of euro weakness, "were a mistake," BNP Paribas said.

So, rule Switzerland out of the race to intervene, and buy the franc against the yen, the French bank concludes.

The chorus of political pressure in Japan for the central bank there to do something, anything, about yen strength is certainly pretty loud, and indeed, further easing measures are starting to emerge.

At an emergency meeting Monday, the Bank Of Japan's policy board voted to offer domestic financial institutions Y10 trillion of six-month loans at an ultralow rate of 0.1%. This was in addition to the Y20 trillion in three-month loans it had already been offering. We are constantly reminded that the authorities in Tokyo are watching the yen's climb with intense interest. Right now, though, the market is skeptical, and traders are continuing to push the currency higher.

Direct intervention, of the kind that is being threatened probably wouldn't work for long, particularly if Japan dived into the market without the help of the U.S. or the euro zone. It would also undermine international efforts to convince China to let the yuan climb. Still, a Japanese zap on the yen does seem somewhat more likely than a Swiss move. If the worst comes to the worst, and neither blinked, selling the yen against the franc in anticipation of such a development is a cheap bet to run.

In early European trading Tuesday, the currencies market was showing clear signs of nerves, with the yen and the franc--both seen as safe havens in times of stress--moving higher.

The euro was at CHF1.2940, according to trading system EBS, having dipped to a fresh record low of CHF1.2932 in Asian trading hours. It was at around CHF1.30 late in New York Monday.

The dollar was at Y84.12 against the yen, from around Y84.75.

The euro was weaker at $1.2643 from $1.2675, while sterling was also lower at $1.5431, from $1.5466.

title: =DJ SNB WATCH: Bank Faces Test Of Resolve As Euro Set To Slide
text:
ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss National Bank's claim of further leeway to intervene in currency markets could draw fresh scrutiny in coming days because the euro is expected to weaken to all-time lows versus the Swiss franc, according to analysts.

SNB President Philipp Hildebrand reiterated in a newspaper interview Saturday that preserving price stability remains its main goal, and that should the boundaries for such stability be breached, the bank could certainly act to prevent a further appreciation of the franc.

Analysts, though, are skeptical about the strength of the SNB's resolve to re-enter the currency markets after it signaled in June that purchases of euros would be halted because signs of deflation have disappeared.

"The intervention earlier this year and last was certainly necessary, but I don't think it is something the SNB will want to repeat right now," said Beat Siegenthaler, a currency strategist at UBS AG.

Hildebrand was adamant the SNB's earlier forays into the currency market were successful damage-limitation exercises, helping prevent a deflationary spiral and an unemployment rate of as much as 8% in Switzerland.

One consequence of the interventions, however, was a swelling of the SNB's currency reserves to CHF219 billion at the end of July, from around CHF95 billion at the end of 2009, resulting in a book loss of CHF2.8 billion as the value of those euro reserves slid.

With fresh concerns about a global economic slowdown resurfacing, and equity markets struggling to hold on to any significant gains, investors are increasingly likely to try to avoid risk by opting for the relative safety of the franc.

"Aversion to risky investments is raising its head again, and we are looking for the market to at least test the recent all-time low in EUR/CHF of 1.3072 in coming days," said Commerzbank analyst Antje Praefcke.

The euro managed to rally to just short of the CHF1.40 level earlier in August, but fears about slowing economic growth in the U.S. and Japan have put the skids under the common currency once more.

The euro was at CHF1.3142 by 0815 GMT, with technical analysts expecting a test of the 1.3072 level this week, and then the key 1.3000 mark.

UBS is doubtful the SNB will want to show its hand in the market right now because this tends to focus the spotlight on the franc, and attracts global speculative flows.

"Any SNB activity just stirs interest from the hedge funds, and then the speculation starts on potential intervention levels, which the SNB won't like," said Zurich-based Siegenthaler.

The Swiss central bank has cited the risk of deflation as the main reason for trying to check the franc's relentless rise to all-time highs versus the euro, though it conceded at its quarterly June policy meeting that such risks have now lapsed.

"Before the SNB undertakes any further intervention, I think they will need to issue fresh verbal warnings on deflationary risks developing," said Frankfurt-based Praefcke.

While UBS expects the euro to weaken to around 1.28 francs in the near term, the bank also forecasts that Swiss policy makers will lift interest rates when they meet Sept. 16. "We're out on a limb on this rate prediction, and certainly the stronger the franc gets, the less likelihood there is of a rate increase," Siegenthaler said.

Hildebrand reiterated that the SNB expects full-year growth in gross domestic product of 2%, though the pace of expansion is set to slow in the second half of the year and in 2011.

A poll of financial experts last week showed economic expectations in Switzerland rebounded in August from a one-year low, suggesting a more optimistic outlook for the rest of 2010, according to the ZEW institute and Credit Suisse Group.

Most other Swiss economic indicators also reflect robust growth, with the purchasing managers index hitting a record in July and the KOF barometer expected to hold near a four-year high.

title: SNB head warns against hiking rates too early-paper
text:
* Hildebrand defends SNB intervention policy

* Risk and uncertainty in world economy picked up since June

* SNB still sees 2 pct growth in 2010

* Pace of growth likely to ease in H2, 2011

ZURICH, Aug 21 (Reuters) - Switzerland's central bank chief warned against hiking rates too soon and said that risks to the bank's latest economic growth forecast had become more acute, in an interview with Swiss newspaper TagesAnzeiger.

The Swiss National Bank is sticking to its June growth forecast of 2 percent for 2010, but it still expects growth to slow in the second half of the year and in 2011, SNB Chairman Philipp Hildebrand was quoted as saying.

"The economic recovery, especially in the United States but also in China, has cooled off. In Switzerland the real appreciation of the Swiss franc will have an impact on exports, with a certain delay," Hildebrand said.

Markets expect the SNB, which stuck to its ultra-low 0.25 percent target rate in June, to make its first post-crisis rate hike in 2011.

"We cannot tighten too early, because we would then risk that the weakening trends would gain more prominence. On the other hand, we must also not wait too long, because this could endanger price stability in the long term," Hildebrand said.

The central bank has already unwound unconventional measures such as asset purchases and currency intervention.

HILDEBRAND DEFENDS FX INTERVENTION

The SNB faced sharp criticism in Switzerland for its intervention policy of selling Swiss francs for euros as part of a bid to prevent the franc from rising too sharply and thus stave off deflationary risks and protect the country's economic recovery.[ID:LDE66K04G]

"We were standing before the decision: Either we let the franc rise strongly, and then Switzerland would have to carry the costs in the form of a deflationary spiral and an unemployment rate of possibly 8 percent. Or we take aggressive action," Hildebrand said.

"Today we have growth of around 2 percent, falling unemployment rates, and price stability has not been endangered, but the SNB has a bloated balance sheet with the associated valuation risks. So for me, it is quite clear that we chose the right path," he said.

The Swiss franc rose some 10 percent against the euro in the first six months of the year and has risen strongly again in recent sessions, regaining much of the ground it lost in July and at the start of August. [EURCHF=]

The central bank said it made a loss of 2.8 billion Swiss francs ($2.7 billion) in the first half of the year, mainly because of losses on its currency reserves. [ID:nLDE67C067]

Hildebrand said the SNB was still able to take action despite the balance sheet risks.

"The limits for us are set where possible additional expansionary monetary policy would cause inflation in the long term," he said.

The Swiss economy, which is heavily dependent on exports, has emerged less bruised from the global recession than many other European countries, thanks to its resilient consumers.

(Reporting by Katie Reid, editing by Jane Baird)

title: UPDATE 1-Profit from UBS assets, gold limit SNB's H1 loss
text:
* Swiss National Bank reports 2.8 bln Sfr H1 loss

 * Gold, UBS asset fund gains counter some of currency losses

 * Makes provisions to pay potential gains from fund to UBS

 (adds details on UBS fund, background)

 ZURICH, Aug 13 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank made a loss of 2.8 billion Swiss francs in the first half, less than the central bank had estimated, as profit from a fund holding assets from bank UBS balanced some of its hefty currency losses.

 The SNB  said on Friday its overall loss totalled 2.8 billion Swiss francs ($2.65 billion), less than the 4 billion francs estimated in July.

 The central bank reported a loss of 14.3 billion francs on its currency reserves, built up through massive interventions, due to the euro's weakness.

 However, the central bank booked a profit of 1.3 billion on the fund, which holds toxic assets from UBS acquired as part of the bailout of Switzerland's largest bank in 2008.

 The SNB also made a revaluation gain of 6.8 billion francs on its gold reserves of 1,040 tonnes.

 The SNB said it set aside provisions in its consolidated accounts to cover potential payouts to UBS from the so-called stabilisation fund.

 Under the agreement with UBS, the SNB will get the first 1 billion francs in profits from the fund. Beyond this, UBS will receive half of the profit, therefore the need for the SNB to make provisions.

 The overall risk from the fund for the SNB was reduced to $19.2 billion. The SNB originally took over assets worth $39.1 billion as part of the rescue package for UBS, which ran up over $50 billion in writedowns during the financial crisis.

UBS officials have indicated in the past that the bank would like to buy the fund back, which the central bank has rejected repeatedly. A SNB spokesman reconfirmed the central bank's position, saying a sale to UBS was not on the table.

 The SNB said in its statement that its half-year result allowed only limited conclusions for the full-year as swings in currency, financial and gold prices had a large influence.

 The SNB has faced some criticism over its intervention policy in Switzerland where media and economists have raised concerns about losses on the large amounts of euros the SNB has acquired and the effectiveness of intervention.

 Traders say that the central bank has already started to diversify its currency portfolio, buying dollars, Canadian and Australian dollars against euros.

title: Swiss SNB  Currency  Reserves Fall To CHF219.3B At End July
text:
ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss National Bank's currency reserves declined to 219.3 billion Swiss francs ($208.2 billion) by end July from a downwardly revised CHF224.9 billion at the end of June, according to data released Thursday.

The CHF5.6 billion drop signals diminished buying of foreign currencies to check the franc's appreciation against the euro.

Switzerland's central bank has intervened repeatedly in recent months to curb the franc's excessive gains against the euro, though it appeared to step back from this policy in June, saying signs of deflation had disappeared.

In July, the central bank warned it expects a hefty CHF4 billion book loss in the first half of the year as the franc's 10% appreciation against the common currency eroded the value of its euro holdings.

At 0708 GMT, the Swiss franc was quoted at 1.3827 against the euro.

   (Adds detail, background, comments) 
 
   By Neil MacLucas 
   Of DOWN JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss National Bank's currency reserves fell for a second month running in July as the franc's recent falls against the euro allowed the central bank to step back from intervening in the currency market, analysts said.

The SNB's foreign exchange reserves slipped to CHF219.3 billion francs ($208.2 billion) by end July from a downwardly revised CHF224.9 billion at the end of June, according to data released Thursday.

"The CHF5.6 billion drop in reserves seems to confirm the SNB has stopped buying euros in recent weeks, and is using the common currency's recent rally against the franc to sell the accumulated euros at a better rate," says Thomas Steinemann, currency strategist at Vontobel.

Switzerland's central bank has intervened repeatedly in recent months to curb the franc's excessive gains against the euro, though it appeared to step back from this policy in June, saying signs of deflation had disappeared.

In July, the central bank warned it expects a hefty CHF4 billion book loss in the first half of the year as the franc's 10% appreciation against the common currency in that period eroded the value of its euro holdings.

The franc climbed to an all-time high around CHF1.3073 against the euro early July, but since then the euro has rebounded on renewed risk appetites and amid receding concerns about the euro-region's debt crisis.

At 0803 GMT, the franc was at CHF1.3820 against the euro, about 5.5% weaker over the past month.

"The SNB will be pleased at the recent franc declines, although we must not forget the central bank bought large quantities of euros when it was at 1.40 to 1.50 francs," said Zurich-based Steinemann.

The franc's falls against the euro will bring some respite to the SNB which has been facing the dilemma of balancing a robust economic rebound and the export-denting, inflation-boosting effects of a surging currency.

Switzerland's leading KOF economic indicator held near a four-year high in July, and the Purchasing Managers' Index climbed to a record, recent data releases show. The rate of unemployment is forecast to drop for a sixth straight month in July.

"August started with a bang, with the latest Swiss business sentiment indicator Monday topping the expectations of even the most optimistic forecasters of the Swiss economy," according to UBS AG economist Reto Huenerwadel.

UBS said an interest-rate increase at the SNB's next policy review in September cannot be ruled out, though most other observers don't expect any tightening until year-end, at the earliest.

title: UPDATE 2-SNB faces criticism as  FX interventions  lead to loss
text:
* Sharp Swiss franc rise resulted in 14 bln Sfr FX loss

* SNB's euro holdings soar to 120.5 bln by end Q2

* H1 loss will fuel public debate over SNB interventions

(Recasts, adds data from monthly report)

By Katie Reid and Sven Egenter

ZURICH, July 21 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank expects to post a first-half loss of around 4 billion Swiss francs due to exchange rate losses stemming from massive currency interventions, the central bank said on Wednesday.

The announcement is likely to fuel criticism of the SNB's intervention policy in Switzerland where media and economists have raised concerns about losses on the large amounts of euros the SNB has acquired and the effectiveness of intervention.

The SNB's monthly report for July showed that SNB's euro holdings more than doubled to 120.5 billion euros in the second quarter, taking the euro's share in the SNB's currency reserves to 70.5 percent.

The overall currency reserves have risen more than five-fold since the SNB launched its policy of fighting a rise in the franc in March 2009, hitting 226.7 billion francs at the end of June.

The SNB decided already in December to increase its provisions in order to take potential losses into account.

The SNB was applauded for its swift and drastic measures to mitigate the financial crisis, helping the Swiss economy to recover much faster than many other European countries.

But public criticism rose after it stepped up its interventions during the euro zone debt crisis before dropping its intervention pledge in June, saying deflation risks had largely disappeared.

EX-CENTRAL BANKERS CRITICISE

Switzerland's major broadsheet newspapers have run stories highlighting the risks of intervention. Former SNB chief economist Kurt Schiltknecht told one newspaper interventions had proven to be pointless in the past.

"That was a big mistake from the central bank," Schiltknecht, who worked for the SNB until 1984, was quoted as saying by Swiss financial newspaper Handelszeitung.

Another former SNB chief economist, Georg Rich, said he had agreed with the SNB's policy until this spring. "I started to feel uneasy in May when the central bank bought such large amounts of euros," Rich, who left the SNB at the end of 2001, was quoted by Handelszeitung.

The franc appreciated more than 10 percent against the euro between early January and the end of June and hit a record high in early July at around 1.3070 per euro<EURCHF=>. Since then, the franc has eased to around 1.36.

Losses on the currency reserves amounted to over 14 billion francs in the first half of the year, the SNB said.

"The income from foreign currency and Swiss franc positions and the steep rise in the price of gold limited the extent of the SNB's half-yearly loss, which is expected to reach approximately 4 billion Swiss francs," the SNB.

While the public debate has been on potential losses from the currency interventions, the central bank must also ensure that the franc liquidity created by the interventions is drained quickly enough to avoid a build-up of inflation risks.

The SNB increased the issuance and the range of maturities of its own debt -- the so called SNB bills -- and launched reverse repo operations in order to drain liquidity.

The SNB monthly report showed that the amount of outstanding debt certificates had risen to 73.3 billion francs by the end of June from 55 billion at the end of May.

The SNB is due to post its first-half results on August 13.

The bank said results from the stabilisation fund with toxic assets the SNB bought from UBS as part of the government bailout for the bank were not yet included in this first-half figure, but they were expected to make a significant positive contribution.

title: FACTBOX-SNB seen sticking to  FX interventions  at policy meeting
text:
(Repeats story filed late on Tuesday, with no changes)

ZURICH, June 15 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank is widely expected to stick to its policy of intervening to fight too sharp a rise in the Swiss franc at a quarterly policy review on June 17.

Here are some key facts about the SNB's current approach and past interventions:

CURRENT STRATEGY

* The SNB launched its interventions in March 2009 as part of a set of drastic measures to fight recession and deflation risks.

* The SNB relaxed its intervention stance in December saying it would fight an excessive appreciation of the franc decisively. It repeated the policy at its March review. Prior to December, it had said it would fight any appreciation.

* The franc has risen as much as 9 percent since the December policy meeting, hitting an all-time high against the euro at 1.3731.<EURCHF=>

Analysts assume that the central bank has turned to only slowing the franc's rise, seen as a matter of course given the problems in the euro zone.

* SNB Vice-Chairman Thomas Jordan was the latest policy maker to repeat the intervention message on May 20. Jordan also said there had been no excessive appreciation of the franc so far. [ID:nLDE64J1XQ] [ID:nWEA1715]

* SNB board-member Jean-Pierre Danthine said that there was theoretically no limit to the interventions.

* The SNB usually declines to comment on intervention talk.

* The SNB only confirmed the very first intervention on March 12, 2009, which sent the franc down by about 4 percent.

INTERVENTIONS

* Market participants assume the SNB has stepped in and sold francs many times since its December policy review.

* The central bank first opted to drive the franc down via large salvos into the market but has changed its approach on some occasions to buying euros steadily to keep the franc pinned at a given level. The SNB did this in April, locking the euro-franc rate in at around 1.43.

* On June 8 the franc quickly plummeted after hitting an all-time high against the euro, with traders citing the SNB's having stepped in. [ID:nWEA5363]

* Traders saw larger interventions on February 5, April 1 and May 19 this year.

INTERVENTION VOLUMES:

* Switzerland's currency reserves posted their sharpest rise on record in May with a 78.8 billion franc jump, reflecting the high intervention volumes.

* Overall, currency reserves have risen five fold since the beginning of the interventions in March to 232 billion francs at the end of May. [ID:nLDE6570WH]

title: SNB WATCH: Focus On Swiss Franc  Intervention , Less On Rates
text:
ZURICH (Dow Jones)--Switzerland's central bank will in all probability leave interest rates unchanged at its upcoming quarterly meeting but the focus will be on its stance on foreign currency interventions.

There is little doubt the Swiss National Bank will stick with its target of 0.25% for the three-month Swiss franc London Interbank Offered Rate at its quarterly policy review June 17, in line with recent no-change decisions by the European Central Bank and the Bank of England.

The SNB's expected decision to stand pat will come despite signs of a clear economic rebound, setting Switzerland apart from many European neighbors where economic activity is slow to revive. However, the effect on Switzerland of worsening concerns about government debts in part of the euro zone would make any hike in Swiss rates premature, most economists say. Plus, any rise in Swiss rates--a step most market watchers expect towards the year at the earliest--would put additional upward pressure on the franc.

Therefore, markets now focus on whether the SNB will alter its position on interventions on the foreign-exchange market, a tool it has used on a massive scale for more than a year to keep the franc under control.

The dilemma for the SNB twofold: It can't very well hike interest rates lest such a move propel the Swiss franc to further highs, nor is it likely to easily abandon its heavy-handed currency management for the same reason.

While many onlookers expects the SNB to renew its pledge to fight any excessive Swiss franc strength, there isn't a consensus. "The SNB is likely to announce the end of currency intervention, since it has been unable to keep the franc from appreciating strongly as investors seek haven assets," Moody's Economy.com economist Melanie Bowler said.

Since March 2009, the SNB has tried to prevent a massive strengthening of the franc against the euro, spending billions of francs to buy the common Europeancurrencyy. However, the policy has been only partly successful.

The SNB's currency reserves have swollen to CHF232 billion by the end of May from slightly below CHF100 billion at the end of 2009, leaving some market watchers wondering how much longer the central bank is willing to carry on with such unusual measures.

Mitsubishi UFJ Securities recently pointed out that Swiss reserves are now on a par with those of China relative to the size of the two countries' economies.

The current level of currency reserves is largely uncharted territory for the SNB and the current surge of euro holdings makes the central bank vulnerable to swings in the foreign-exchange market, some observers have said.

Peter Bernholz, a former economics professor at the University of Basel, recently suggested the central bank should build up its gold reserves rather than focusing on currency operations.

Gold, currently a vastly popular investment, has recently drawn interest from at least one central bank: In late 2009, the Reserve Bank of India bought 200 tons of gold from the International Monetary Fund, citing efforts to diversify its foreign-exchange reserves.

Meanwhile, the SNB has in the past few years reduced its gold holdings under a coordinated gold-selling program by several central banks. It currently owns 1,040 tons of gold.

Despite the SNB's robust efforts to manage the franc, the euro currently stands at around CHF1.39, close to a recent record low of CHF1.3746. The euro traded at CHF1.50 just a few months ago. But without the SNB's interventions, the euro could stand as low as CHF1.20, some economists have estimated.

The current level of exchange rates is a serious problem for the country's important export industry because the strong franc makes Swiss goods more expensive.

At the quarterly meeting on Thursday, the SNB will also provide an update of its forecasts for economic growth and inflation. Currently, it expects the country's GDP to increase at a rate of about 1.5% this year and forecasts average yearly inflation to stand at 0.7% in 2010, 0.9% next year and 2.2% in 2012.

-By Martin Gelnar, Dow Jones Newswires; +41 43 443 8042; martin.gelnar@dowjones.com [ 14-06-10 1426GMT ]

title: COLUMN-Swiss lessons in spitting in the wind: James Saft
text:
(James Saft is a Reuters columnist. The opinions expressed are his own)

HUNTSVILLE, Ala. (Reuters) - Looking at Switzerland's massive efforts to stem the effects of the euro meltdown on its economy, two things are clear: it is a ruinously expensive undertaking and the most direct beneficiaries are speculators.

Switzerland devoted the equivalent of 15 percent of annual gross domestic product in May alone building up reserves as it sought to reverse the rise of its franc against the euro. Only China, which has an economy 33 times the size of Switzerland, has ever racked up more than the Swiss National Bank's 67.7 billion francs in reserves in a month. The Swiss then have deployed something approaching 45 percent of annual GDP since the end of the year seeking to cap strength of the franc.

And the result? Well, the euro has only lost about 7 percent against the franc this year as against a far deeper loss against the dollar, but the trend has been inexorable. Time and again traders have challenged the Swiss authorities and met, after a time, with success.

This of course raises the question of what might happen should the Swiss think better of spending thousands per capita on lining the pockets of speculators, or investors if you please. The result, while perhaps inevitable, would not be pretty.

As ever with intervention, the problem is that authorities set the markets a target and supply it with a deep-pocketed trading partner. Unless intervention is coordinated across nations and truly massive, the result is often to attract more capital to take the other side of the trade. To be truly effective, a unilateral currency intervention probably has to be unsterilized, meaning that the central bank doing the intervention allows its money supply to balloon and risks losing control off its own monetary policy.

To understand the spitting-in-the-wind nature of Swiss currency intervention you only have to realize that Switzerland, in marked contrast to its euro zone neighbors, has both fiscal and trade surpluses. It also has a debt to GDP ratio that is a modest 45 percent. In other words, Switzerland has been doing more or less the right things.

Currency strategist Mansoor Mohi-uddin of UBS cleverly compares the Swiss franc to the German deutschmark of yore, and it certainly must on its fundamentals evoke a kind of nostalgia among Germans who remember the good old days of sound money.

So as ever, the speculators aren't really speculators but simply investors who recognize that there are strong fundamentals and an official buyer with plenty of money. In that way speculators are a bit like weeds, the definition of which is a plant that observer wishes was not growing there.

HUNGARIAN MORTGAGES

So, why are the Swiss spending all of this money trying to fix a problem that is not of their making and is probably far too big for their economy to effectively counter?

Besides making Swiss exports less competitive and threatening its recovery, an important threat of a strong franc is that by lowering the price of imported goods it may allow a self-reinforcing deflation to take hold. With Swiss official interest rates at 0.25 percent and consumer price inflation at 1.1 percent and falling that is no idle threat.

With interest rates so low and a small domestic bond market, the reserve accumulation is really a form of quantitative easing.

A strengthening Swiss franc, especially against central European currencies like the Hungarian forint, also causes problems for Swiss and other banks. In a desperate attempt to get on the property ladder many Hungarian borrowers took out mortgages denominated in Swiss francs, which then had much lower interest rates. This account for about 60 percent of the stock of outstanding Hungarian mortgages. That allowed them to buy far more house than they could really afford and also exposed them to currency risk. As the franc rises so does what they owe, though now that things are not looking as rosy in central Europe they may choose to default.

And while most of those franc loans were actually made by non-Swiss banks, the potential for contagion and damage is strong.

Switzerland's problems with a weak euro and potentially disintegrating euro zone are simply the problems of the rest of the world writ large. A falling euro will spread deflation, hit exports, depress consumption and further stress the banking system.

It would be dangerous to suppose that because Swiss intervention is not successful that the United States will be similarly toothless if they choose to wade in. If, and it is a massive if, the United States were able to convince European authorities that joint intervention were needed it would probably be successful. Would the European authorities cooperate? Perhaps.

The United States might choose to go it alone, but that risks the very destabilizing effects of failure. title: UPDATE: Swiss  Currency  Reserves Soar To CHF232.4B By End May
text:
(Adds background, analyst comments.)

By Neil MacLucas

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss National Bank's currency reserves climbed to 232.4 billion Swiss francs ($200.8 billion) by the end of May, according to data published on the Swiss Federal Statistics Office's website.

The Swiss central bank's reserves increased by CHF78.8 billion last month, from CHF153.6 billion at the end of April, signaling ongoing buying of foreign currencies to check the franc's appreciation against the euro.

A spokesman for the Zurich-based SNB said the data published by the statistics office is provisional and that official data will be released later in June.

"This is a clear indication the SNB was in the currency market last month buying euros in a big way," said Commerzbankcurrency analyst Antje Praefcke.

Switzerland's central bank has intervened repeatedly in recent months to curb an excessive appreciation of the franc against the euro, the currency of its main trade partner.

At 0935 the Swiss franc was quoted at 1.3790 against the euro, after earlier climbing to a record high of 1.3785 per euro.

title: FOREX -Euro edges up vs dollar; pound dips on debt warning
text:
* Investors stay jittery over euro zone debt crisis

* Euro hits lifetime low vs Swiss franc

* Fed policymaker says Europe's woes no big threat to U.S.

* Sterling slips on Fitch's UK debt warning (Adds details, changes byline)

By Steven C. Johnson and Vivianne Rodrigues

NEW YORK, June 8 (Reuters) - The euro rose on Tuesday as investors booked profits a day after the currency hit its lowest level against the dollar since early 2006, and the pound fell after a ratings agency urged Britain to cut its deficit.

The euro also hit an all-time trough below 1.38 Swiss francs but rebounded sharply, with traders citing Swiss National Bankintervention to weaken the franc. The SNB declined to comment. For details, see [ID:nWEA5363].

Against the dollar, the euro rose above $1.20 after tumbling to $1.1876 on Monday, its lowest level since March 2006. But analysts said the market was still anxious about debt levels in several euro zone countries and debt auctions this week from Portugal and Spain.

"The euro decline isn't over," said Marc Chandler, senior strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York. "There are supply concerns this week, and what we're seeing now is a brief respite. A rise above $1.20 would be a good chance to sell."

In late afternoon trading in New York, the euro was up 0.4 percent at $1.1954 <EUR=> after hitting a session peak at $1.2008, according to Reuters data. Analysts said it also saw support after euro zone ministers made final arrangements Monday to set up funds for countries facing debt problems. It was up 0.3 percent at 109.15 yen <EURJPY=>.

The euro has shed more than 16 percent against the dollar this year, and some economists worry this will hurt U.S. exports to the euro zone, a fear Chicago Federal Reserve President Charles Evans downplayed on Tuesday. [ID:nN08177384]

SWISS SPECULATION, UK DEBT WORRIES

The euro's abrupt rebound from a low against the Swiss franc earlier spurred talk of intervention by the Swiss National Bank.

Switzerland's central bank has intervened since 2009 to prevent excess franc strength but slowed its euro purchases recently as the euro fell below 1.40 francs.

The euro was last 0.6 percent lower at 1.3759 <EURCHF=>.

"Certainly the price action minutes ago seemed to suggest intervention. though we've no official confirmation," said one market participant at a U.S.-based bank about the euro's jump.

Sterling fell 0.3 percent to $1.4418 <GBP=D4> after Fitch Ratings said the UK was facing a "formidable" fiscal challenge and said Britain's public debt ratio had climbed more quickly than those of other top-rated sovereign credits. [ID:nWLA5820]

"It's more of the contagion fear that's been gripping markets for months now," said John Doyle, strategist at Tempus Consulting in Washington.

Against the yen, the dollar was flat at 91.34 <JPY=>. Earlier, new Japanese Prime Minister Naoto Kan chose a fiscal conservative as his finance minister. Kan has in the past advocated a weaker yen to help Japanese exports and fight deflation, but Chandler said that might be wishful thinking as long as markets are in crisis mode.

During times of risk aversion, the yen tends to rise as investors exit positions in riskier currencies and assets.

On Monday, technical analyst Robert Prechter told the Reuters Investment Outlook Summit in New York that the euro is likely to bottom out against the dollar within two weeks.

In the meantime, though, Citigroup strategists said they expect risk aversion to continue to hold sway in markets. [ID:nN07198050]

The single currency has yet to bottom out against the dollar and may eventually reach parity, Citigroup chief global currency strategist Steven Englander said at the Reuters Investment Outlook Summit in New York on Tuesday.

Englander sees the euro between $1.10 and $1.15 over the next one to three months. However, a weaker euro would help to offset slower growth in euro zone countries such as Greece and Spain, which will eventually help the currency recover.

In the long run, "I think time is on the side of the euro," he said, provided countries stick to austerity budgets.

(Additional reporting by Naomi Tajitsu in London; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

title: Swiss  FX  Reserves Rise To CHF153.6B At End Apr-Stats Office
text:
ZURICH (Dow Jones)-- The Swiss National Bank's currency reserves rose to 153.6 billion Swiss francs ($133.5 billion) by the end of April, according to data published on the Swiss Federal Statistics Office's website.

The SNB's reserves increased by CHF28.7 billion last month, from CHF124.9 billion at the end of March, signaling ongoing buying of foreign currencies to check the franc's appreciation.

A spokesman for the Zurich-based SNB said the data published by the statistics office is provisional and the official data will be published May 21.

Switzerland's central bank has intervened repeatedly in recent months to weaken the franc against the euro, the currency of its main trade partner.

"A similar increase in foreign exchange holdings excluding gold should lift Switzerland into the top 10 economies, with respect to foreign exchange reserves," said UBS AG economist Reto Huenerwadel.

"There is little evidence the SNB is to step away from their current monetary policy including currency interventions," he said.

title: Swiss econ min says SNB  interventions  important for now
text:
ST. GALLEN, Switzerland, May 7 (Reuters) - Switzerland's economy minister said on Friday the Swiss National Bank's interventions in the currency market were not for the long-term but that they remained important for now.

"I think that the activities of the central bank continue to be important and that it will intervene in the market because one knows exactly, if the difference is too big, our exporters and tourism will be hit badly," Doris Leuthard told journalists.

"It's not a long-term strategy, it's for the moment," said Leuthard, who is also the country's president."

She said the SNB did have the firepower for its policy.

"If we have the will, we have the means," she said.
