title: SNB Maintains  Currency Intervention  as Swiss Franc Gains -- Market Talk
text:
1254 ET - Investors reached for safe assets Monday, pushing the Swiss franc up 1.2% against the U.S. dollar, but it could be much stronger without intervention by Switzerland's central bank. As of Friday, the Swiss National Bank has likely spent about 2% of its gross domestic product on interventions this year, according to a Bank of America research report. One franc buys $1.0794, or EUR0.9419. "Without interventions, I think we would have seen parity [with the euro] already," said Nikolay Markov, a senior economist at Pictet Asset Management. The franc's increase has put the SNB in a tough spot as the Treasury recently added Switzerland to a watchlist of currency manipulators. The central bank has to weigh the potential label with its need to stem the currency's appreciation and counter low inflation. (caitlin.ostroff@wsj.com)

1223 ET - Bank of America Global Research says the ratio of the S&P 500 dividend yield over the 10-year Treasury yield has jumped to 2.5x, during the current cycle--overshooting some recent spikes. Analysts say the prior three peaks were followed by the S&P 500 outperforming the 10-year Treasury by 31 percentage points on average over the next 12 months. Since 1951 when the ratio was this high, BofA says, stocks have returned 19 times more than Treasurys. But BofA warns while the energy sector currently offers the highest dividend yield at 5.1%, "given continued risk to earnings, we recommend 'safer' yield sectors, such as Utilities (3.2%)." (patrick.sheridan@wsj.com)

1134 ET - Canada's budget planning process for 2020 is likely in upheaval with the unexpected plunge in oil prices. On Friday, Finance Minister Bill Morneau said he was prepared to inject fiscal stimulus as required, and would book a larger risk contingency in the coming 2020 budget plan to account for uncertainty related to the coronavirus epidemic. The 17% plunge to price in west Texas intermediate, to the $34 range, represents a fresh body blow to budget planning. Canadian crude from western Canada already trades at a sizable discount to WTI, due to pipeline bottlenecks among other things. Morneau has not provided a date at which time he will present his budget plan, which originally was to have a climate-change focus. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1111 ET - Slovakia, Slovenia and Malta are the eurozone's most exposed countries to supply-chain disruptions caused by the coronavirus. A report from ING examines the value chain of each eurozone economy in terms of overall exposure to China, South Korea and Italy, and concludes that those three nations have a higher chance of being affected as they depend more on countries worst hit by the epidemic. On the upside, the Netherlands, Latvia and Portugal are the least exposed and big economies such as Germany, France and Spain are in the mid-range. By sector, textiles, electronics and electrical equipment bear the highest risk, according to ING's ranking. (xavier.fontdegloria@wsj.com)

1059 ET - The dual impact of Covid-19 and the significant oil price shock will put pressure on some sovereign credit fundamentals and potentially ratings, Fitch Ratings says. In developed markets, the key drivers will be the effect on growth, if it persists, and the fiscal and monetary responses, the ratings firm says. Emerging markets face additional risks related to commodity export receipts, capital flows and exchange-rate pressures, it adds. Low oil prices weighed on ratings of major exporters in 2014-16 and will do so again if the oil price war leads to sustained lower prices, says Fitch Ratings , after oil prices had their biggest drop in nearly three decades after Saudi Arabia said on Sunday it would increase production and cut prices after talks with Russia on production cuts collapsed. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

1044 ET - The worst for the global economy is yet to come over the next several months, says Joachim Fels , global economic advisor at PIMCO. Fels says China's manufacturing and demand slump will affect activity in the rest of the world and demand for services will contract due to containment measures and fear. PIMCO expects the spread of the coronavirus outside China to peak in the next few months and foresees a U-shaped trajectory for global growth over the next few quarters. "However, this 'U' may feel initially like an 'I' as economic growth drops sharply, then like an 'L' as the economy finds a bottom but visibility remains low for some time, before growth inflects higher and the upward bend in the 'U' materializes," Fels says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1026 ET - Goldman Sachs expects a rebound in French and Italian production data from January, to be published on Tuesday. For France, Goldman Sachs forecasts a 1.5% rise in industrial production following a 2.8% contraction in December, reflecting the dissipation of disruptions related to strikes against pension reform. This forecast is below consensus because some recent economic releases indicate that disruptions to activity in some sectors were still observed in early January, Goldman Sachs says. In the case of Italy, Goldman Sachs expects a partial rebound after a sharp contraction in December. However, he bank says it won't be a sharp increase, as some of the decline seen in December was of a temporary nature and is unlikely to fully reverse. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1001 ET - The U.K.'s decision to leave the European Aviation Safety Authority lacks ambition and could threaten jobs as well as inward investment, says ADS Group , an aerospace and defense industry lobby group. ADS--which represents more than 1,100 U.K. companies--says continued participation in EASA is the best option to maintain global export-market access as well as the competitiveness of the U.K.'s GBP36 billion aerospace industry. "U.K. influence in EASA contributes to raising standards in global aviation, supports collaboration with our international partners and helps make our industry attractive to the investment it needs," ADS Chief Executive Paul Everitt says. "We're disappointed [the government] hasn't taken a more ambitious approach. It's essential it works with us to achieve a regime that doesn't put jobs at risk." (philip.waller@wsj.com)

0951 ET - "To respond to the price movement is the one thing you don't want to do." That is what Credit Suisse Chief US Equity Strategist Jonathan Golub tells WSJ he is advising clients this morning as stocks fall sharply amid worries about economic growth, profits and the spread of the coronavirus. For the year, the bank now expects weaker gains in the S&P 500, but Golub anticipates metrics like the yield on 10-year treasury notes, stock multiples and earnings to return to more normal levels by the end of the year. (micah.maidenberg@wsj.com; @MicahMaidenberg)

0937 ET - HSBC expects the European Central Bank to cut the deposit rate by 10 basis points to minus 0.60% at Thursday's meeting, with risks of a 20-basis-point move, but it sticks to the view that easing monetary policy will do little to shield the eurozone economy from the impact of Covid-19. The cut should be accompanied by an increase in the multiplier for the tiered reserves to eight from six, say HSBC's chief European economist Simon Wells and senior economist Fabio Balboni . The economists add that more QE is possible--it's currently EUR20 billion a month--, "but the political hurdle is higher and sovereign yields are at all-time lows for most countries," and therefore they expect the volume to remain unchanged. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0913 ET - The EU is unlikely to take a big economic hit from the U.K.'s exit, says RBC Wealth Management . If the EU loses access to the U.K. market due to the potential breakdown of negotiations over a new trade agreement, the impact would be modest as EU exports to the U.K. represent only 3% of EU GDP, RBC says. "Moreover, the damage would be partially offset by some diversion of trade, investment and skilled migrants away from the U.K. to the EU ," says RBC's Frederique Carrier. Brexit seems to have boosted support for the EU among its 27 remaining members and the loss of the U.K.'s contribution to the bloc's economy and budget should be manageable, he adds. (philip.waller@wsj.com)

0911 ET - Against a backdrop of rising pressure on major central banks to loosen policy in response to coronavirus, Capital Economics now expects the Riksbank to cut its repo rate back into negative territory at its April 28 decision, if not before. "However, as in other countries, any monetary response to the virus is likely to come alongside more targeted measures on the fiscal and regulatory fronts." Capital Economics notes that it's possible the Riksbank may start to buy corporate bonds, but the recent bond market rally has weakened the case for additional purchases of government debt. "Meanwhile, although mortgage-backed bonds offer a huge stock of assets to buy, we doubt that the bank will go there for fear of being seen as stoking the housing market." (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

By Caitlin Ostroff and Paul J. Davies 

This article is being republished as part of our daily reproduction of WSJ.com articles that also appeared in the U.S. print edition of The Wall Street Journal (February 24, 2020).

The Swiss franc has climbed to its highest level against the euro in more than four years, leaving Switzerland's central bank with a dilemma: Do nothing and potentially damage the economy, or intervene to curtail the rise and risk angering the U.S.

The Swiss National Bank has so far kept mum on its intentions and investors are torn. Some seem convinced the franc will keep rising: Hedge funds betting on further strengthening have increased their net long positions since the start of the year, according to data on futures markets from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Others warn such a gamble is foolhardy.

"If you try to play games with the SNB, it's very dangerous for you," said Thomas Stucki, chief investment officer at St. Galler Kantonalbank and former head of asset management at the SNB. "They will not hesitate to intervene in the market."

Weekly data from the SNB, which analysts monitor as a proxy for currency intervention, suggest it has been acting to stem the franc's rise already this year, buying foreign currencies and selling the franc. Its efforts have so far failed to hit its main target: The franc has risen more than 2% against the euro since the end of 2019 to EUR0.94.

"If they don't really manage to turn the tide on the current trend, then they could risk having to throw in the towel," said Andreas Steno Larsen, global foreign-exchange and fixed-income strategist at Nordea Markets.

At the same time, the franc has fallen more than 1% against the dollar to $1.02. This is a problem because the euro matters more for Swiss trade and inflation, but the dollar will matter more to the U.S. Treasury, which last month added Switzerland to its watch list of potential currency manipulators.

The franc is nearly 7.5% below its fair value to the dollar, similar to the Chinese yuan, according to Steven Englander, head of global G10 FX research and North America macro strategy at Standard Chartered.

A strong franc is a problem for the SNB because it makes imports cheaper and lowers inflation, which the central bank has been trying to stoke with some of the lowest interest rates in the world. However, a weaker franc makes exports cheaper to the U.S., its second-biggest market. That risks attracting the ire of President Trump, who has been vocal in his views that the strength of the dollar puts the U.S. at an unfair disadvantage.

Washington judges currency manipulation on three criteria: the size of a country's trade surplus with the U.S., the size of its overall current account surplus and how much it has spent on currency intervention. The Treasury department has said Switzerland met the first two criteria.

Switzerland might not have a lot of wiggle room before it meets the third criteria. Investors pushed the franc higher after the Treasury's report, speculating the SNB might be more hesitant to keep its currency at bay.

The main proxy for intervention is the SNB's weekly report on sight deposits, or short-term franc deposits held at the central bank by domestic banks, the government and others. When these are growing, that is a sign that the SNB is selling francs, because the central bank would be buying foreign currencies from banks and others, who would end up holding more francs in their deposits.

Up until mid-February, these sight deposits grew by 5.5 billion francs ($5.6 billion).

The U.S. rule is that a country shouldn't spend more than 2% of GDP on currency intervention; with Swiss GDP this year forecast to be about 700 billion francs, that suggests it can spend up to 14 billion francs on holding back its currency. Simple math suggests it might be able to spend less than 9 billion francs over the rest of 2020 before crossing the Treasury's line in the sand.

The SNB appeared to launch a big intervention last summer: Sight deposits rose by 13.5 billion francs between mid-July and mid-September, then stopped. This was roughly equivalent to 2% of GDP, said Paul Meggyesi, a currency strategist at JPMorgan Chase & Co. in London.

"I don't agree with the strand of thought that it doesn't matter if Switzerland is labeled a currency manipulator," Mr. Meggyesi said. "This is a U.S. administration that is prepared to use the tools at its disposal to counteract what it sees as unfair trade relations."

It is uncertain exactly what being labeled a manipulator would mean for Switzerland. The SNB has spent much more than 2% of GDP on intervention in the past and has been on the currency watch list before. However, Mr. Trump has given American companies the power to pursue tariffs against foreign competitors who have benefited from currency manipulation in their countries.

Switzerland's problem continues to grow because it exports more than it imports, and attracts a lot of capital that is looking for a safe home.

These pressures eased while the Federal Reserve was raising interest rates in 2018 and the European Central Bank also looked like it might start unwinding its easy money policies. That ended last year, when both central banks reversed course amid concerns about global economic growth.

The SNB could make it more costly to hold money in Swiss banks by taking rates further below the current minus 0.75% level, which is matched only by Denmark. It might have to if the ECB goes deeper into subzero territory, said David Oxley, senior Europe economist at Capital Economics.

"The SNB is focused on maintaining that gap between European interest rates and their own," Mr. Oxley said. "They're kind of between a rock and a hard place."

title: Hedge funds test Swiss tolerance with franc gambit
text:
* Franc hits 4-1/2-year high vs euro

* U.S. in Jan added Switzerland to currency watchlist

* Some say SNB will eventually intervene, hitting franc

* Euro/franc at 1.05 seen as red line for SNB

By Tommy Wilkes

LONDON, Feb 14 (Reuters) - Hedge funds betting that the Swiss franc will climb further against the euro will soon meet their match, according to investors who are taking the other side of the trade.

The Swiss currency on Thursday climbed to a 4-1/2 year high of 1.061 francs per euro, fast approaching the point where its central bank will feel compelled to ensure currency strength does not harm the country's export-dependent economy, these investors argue.

A catalyst was Switzerland's inclusion last month into a U.S. Treasury watchlist for currency manipulation, which led many to bet the central bank would take a more hands-off approach to the franc.

Concerns about the euro zone economy have also contributed significantly to franc gains versus the euro, handing a 2%-plus profit to hedge funds that piled into the franc and sold the euro a month back.

But many reckon the SNB remains too concerned about franc strength pressuring inflation and exports to stop intervening altogether.

"We think the move downward (in the euro/franc exchange rate) has been overdone," said Van Luu, Head of Currency and Fixed Income Strategy at Russell Investments.

Luu said the Swiss National Bank would "continue to manage the FX as it has explicitly stated its role in monetary policymaking," adding that the franc was the most shorted currency in its $5.6 billion FX fund.

According to some measures the franc is now at least 4% overvalued. Yet speculators' net long position on the franc versus the dollar has swelled to the biggest since late-2016 .

These positions are at risk of a shakeout if the central bank intervenes suddenly.

Against the euro, hedge funds have focused on buying the franc and selling the euro on spot markets, often magnifying their bets with leverage. Option traders said volatility on euro/franc derivatives markets was low and trading volumes very thin.

What would it take to force the SNB's hand?

Ian Gunner, portfolio manager at hedge fund Altana Wealth, said headlines about franc strength was "the last thing the SNB wants to see.

"I'm looking for a sign that we have bottomed against the euro," he said, pointing to 1.05 francs as the level beyond which the SNB would have to act.

Investors interviewed for this article generally saw 1.05 francs per euro - just 1% from current levels - as the threshold.

Andreas Koenig, global head of FX at Amundi Asset Management, said the threshold had shifted from a range of 1.10-1.08 francs per euro before the watchlist was released to 1.08-1.06 francs today, a band it is close to breaching.

NOT SO STRONG

Still, the SNB may not be panicking just yet.

Despite the franc's gains versus the euro and outperformance compared to another safe-haven currency, the yen versus the dollar, its showing more broadly is less impressive even with safe-haven flows driven by China's coronavirus outbreak.

The franc is down 1% versus the dollar so far in 2020 .

And while the trade-weighed franc index has climbed, it is well off 2017 highs when the SNB called the currency 'significantly overvalued'.

The SNB denies its interventions aim to give Switzerland a trading advantage, instead noting the impact a highly-valued franc has on inflation.

But the symbolism of appearing on the watchlist may have taken on new meaning under U.S. President Donald Trump.

"It's a new environment. These are not empty threats. They (the U.S.) will follow through," said Stephen Jen, hedge fund manager at Eurizon SLJ Capital, describing the political capacity of Switzerland to intervene as "compromised".

Recent sight deposit data, a gauge of Swiss central bank activity, indeed suggests the SNB has not been intervening significantly.

The bank is - at least verbally - sticking to its guns. Chairman Thomas Jordan said last week the SNB would still intervene if necessary.

Amundi's Koenig is positioning for "tactical recovery" in euro/franc.

"The market thinks the SNB cannot do anything anymore. But the SNB is not at the end of its possibilities."

(Reporting by Tommy Reggiori Wilkes Additional reporting by Saikat Chatterjee in London and John Revill in Zurich Editing by Sujata Rao)

title: German PMIs and Ifo Index Point to Manufacturing Stabilization: HSBC -- Market Talk
text:
1139 GMT - Both the Purchasing Managers Index and the ifo survey indicate a stabilization of manufacturing activity, pointing to an end to the industrial recession in Germany, says HSBC's economist Rainer Sartoris. Although the ifo business climate showed an unexpected setback in January, there was a strong improvement in the industrial sentiment component. Signals in the service sector were mixed, with a marked improvement in the PMI but a decline in ifo. However, Sartoris says expectations in the sector still sit above the cyclical trough seen last year, so "one should not get too pessimistic." Despite the disappointment from ifo, "the worst days for the German economy now lie behind us," Sartoris says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1130 GMT - As the spread of the coronavirus spreads out of China fuels risk aversion, the euro could come under renewed pressure against the Japanese yen, says Societe Generale 's Kit Juckes. "EUR/JPY shorts bearing fruit again" and if the pair falls below the 120 level, it would "look significant on charts and for sentiment," he adds. EUR/JPY fell briefly to a two month low of 119.920 and is last at 120.00, according to FactSet.(lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

1123 GMT - Precious-metal stocks are among just a handful of FTSE 100 risers as fears about the coronavirus outbreak in China boost the price of gold and silver, as well as some safe-haven currencies such as the Japanese yen. Mexican silver miner Fresnillo is up 0.8% and Russia and Kazakhstan-focused gold and silver producer Polymetal International gains 0.6%. Gold and silver prices advance 0.5% apiece to $1,580 and $18.20 an ounce respectively. "We're seeing further demand for traditional havens, such as the yen and gold, as traders seek to shield themselves from the potential economic repercussions of this virus," says Josh Mahony at trading firm IG.(philip.waller@wsj.com)

1108 GMT - The Swiss franc rises to its strongest level against the euro since April 2017 as investors turn to the safe-haven currency due to fears about the spread of the coronavirus, with EUR/CHF hitting a low of 1.0687. Investors have further encouragement from U.S. pressure on Switzerland not to intervene in the Swiss franc to limit the currency's advance, Societe Generale says. "U.S. pressure on Switzerland not to intervene to hold the currency down has given the Swiss franc bulls another reason to be long," says Societe Generale 's Kit Juckes. The U.S. added Switzerland to the Treasury's watch list of currency manipulators earlier in the month as a warning to the Swiss National Bank . Speaking to Bloomberg at Davos, SNB's chairman Thomas Jordan denied the SNB was engaged in currency manipulation. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

1058 GMT - January's ifo index reading shows that for the time being, the economy remains stuck at the bottom, says Carsten Brzeski , chief economist at ING in Germany. The first drop of the ifo index since August 2019 is "a cold shower for all optimists," Brzeski says. According to Brzeski, the decline to 95.9 shows that the German economy, particularly the manufacturing sector, has still not bottomed out. "While the service sector has already gone through a real rebound since the summer, the manufacturing sector still looks paralysed, suffering from trade conflicts and the global manufacturing downturn," Brzeski says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1034 GMT - The decline in Germany's ifo business climate index for January comes as a bit of a surprise, says Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist for Capital Economics. The ifo business climate index came in at 95.9 points in January, below the 97.5 forecasted by Capital Economics . "This sounds a warning note for those expecting an impressive rebound in the German growth rate," Kenningham says. Capital Economics expects the German economy to grow "at only a very anemic pace" in the first half of this year. While the manufacturing component of ifo rose, the services component fell. Kenningham says this is in line with Capital Economics ' forecast of an improvement in the export-oriented manufacturing sector coinciding with a weakening of domestic demand. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1019 GMT - The Bank of England is unlikely to restart bond purchases unless it brings interest rates, currently at 0.75%, to zero, says Roberto Mialich of UniCredit . Therefore, the BOE is unlikely to mention the possibility of quantitative easing at this Thursday's policy meeting. UniCredit expects the central bank to cut interest rates by 25 basis points to 0.5% on Thursday and its view is that the BOE will be more aggressive in loosening monetary policy than what the market expects but "not to the point to negative interest rates," adds Mialich. The 10-year gilt yield is last down almost 4 basis points to 0.530%, according to Tradeweb . (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

1017 GMT - Many market watchers neglect the risk of higher inflation, which could be a risk for bond markets in 2020, says Werner Kraemer, senior economic analyst at Lazard Asset Management. "Monetary expansion is entering its twelfth year, full employment prevails in many countries, wage costs are rising slightly, the state and the associated costs are expanding more and more, globalization is being increasingly restricted and the oil price is moving slowly but steadily upwards," he says. The rising gold price in recent years could also be an early indicator of inflation risks, he adds. "Therefore, it cannot be completely ruled out that the bond market, and thus the stock market, will run into difficulties again due to rising inflation rates," says Kraemer. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

1017 GMT - Rising sea levels are set to bruise the gross domestic product of G20 countries due to coastal flooding, even if they take ambitious action to halt climate change, says a study from the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis . IIASA projects that under two scenarios--one below 2 degrees Celsius of warming by 2100 and another overshooting the target--annual global economy-wide losses could hit more than 4%. "This confirms the importance and economic efficiency of adaptation in the long term: Making sure that coastal communities and their infrastructure are climate-resilient will affect economies across the globe much less than persistent climate impacts in the absence of climate action," says study author Thomas Schinko. (dieter.holger@wsj.com; @dieterholger)

1016 GMT - Data from the ifo Institute shows that the mood among German companies is somewhat gloomier again, says Friederike Koehler-Geib, chief economist at KfW Group. Although the fall in the ifo business climate index came as a surprise, Koehler-Geib says there are reasons for it. The agreement between China and the U.S., as well as the orderly withdrawal of the U.K. from the EU "merely eliminate the immediate downside risks, but they don't yet create any real stimulus for the economy," Koehler-Geib says. In Germany, Koehler-Geib says an end to the industrial recession "is only dimly visible," while construction and services are showing signs of fatigue at the beginning of the year. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

0950 GMT - The euro falls to an eight-week low of 1.1016 against the U.S. dollar on weaker-than-expected German Ifo Business Climate Index for January. The data came in at 95.9, down from 96.3 in December and expectations of around to 97, according to a WSJ poll of economists. "Sentiment among German managers is somewhat diminished" as companies are "more pessimistic outlook for the coming months," says Clemens Fuest , president of the ifo Institute. The single currency is last at 1.1021, having fallen to an eight-week low of 1.1017 after the announcement from 1.1029 beforehand, according to FactSet.(lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

0944 GMT - The regional elections in Italy will make an early parliamentary election in the country less likely, UBS says. The results in the Emilia-Romagna region showed a "surprisingly strong" performance by the center-left, led by the Democratic Party. The results could strengthen the position of the party, which is part of the ruling coalition in Rome, UBS says. "All in all, this result should push back the risk of an early election," the Swiss bank says. (pietro.lombardi@dowjones.com; @pietrolombard10)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: German Ifo Index Worth a Second Glance: Commerzbank -- Market Talk

The eight-month average in manufacturing business expectations is rising for the first time in two years and confirms the positive reading of the purchasing managers index, Kraemer says. This goes in line with Commerzbank 's forecast that the decline in industrial production should end in the spring. "Nevertheless, you shouldn't get over-optimistic, as the headwinds for the German economy remain strong," Kraemer says. Commerzbank expects the German economy to grow 0.8% in 2020 as a whole. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

The rebound in business expectations in the manufacturing sector supports the idea that the German economy will regain some momentum over the course of this year, Berenberg says. Economists Florian Hense and Holger Schmieding say the manufacturing sector has been at the core of the Germany-led downturn in the eurozone and a stabilization in its automotive sector--which continues to struggle--would be conducive to a rebound. Berenberg says German growth could return to its trend rate of 0.4% in the second half of 2020. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1139 GMT - Both the Purchasing Managers Index and the ifo survey indicate a stabilization of manufacturing activity, pointing to an end to the industrial recession in Germany, says HSBC's economist Rainer Sartoris. Although the ifo business climate showed an unexpected setback in January, there was a strong improvement in the industrial sentiment component. Signals in the service sector were mixed, with a marked improvement in the PMI but a decline in ifo. However, Sartoris says expectations in the sector still sit above the cyclical trough seen last year, so "one should not get too pessimistic." Despite the disappointment from ifo, "the worst days for the German economy now lie behind us," Sartoris says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

title: Market Talk Roundup: Coronavirus Hits Markets, Investors Seek Safety
text:
The Chinese coronavirus hits markets globally, causing equities, oil and base metals to fall sharply while investors flee into the perceived safety of gold, government bonds, the Swiss franc and the Japanese yen. The following is a selection of analysts' comments.

0754 GMT - Eurozone government bond yields drop as markets remain edgy over the impact of the Chinese coronavirus. "The spreading 'coronary angst' leaves scope for the safety bid to extend," says Commerzbank 's rates strategist Rainer Guntermann. He adds that with the macro backdrop still looking inconclusive and the flow pattern improving, setbacks in Bunds should remain better buying opportunities. He sees room for eurozone government bond spreads to tighten. The week will see a load of economic data from Germany and the eurozone, starting with the Ifo business climate index on Monday. The 10-year German Bund yield is trading 1 basis point lower at -0.37%, according to Tradeweb . (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0807 GMT - Brent crude oil is down 3.4% at $58.60 a barrel and WTI futures are down 2.3% at $52.93 a barrel, with both benchmarks following broader Asian markets lower amid intensifying fears about the impact the spreading coronavirus could have on Chinese oil demand. With many Asian stock indexes closed for Chinese new year, trading is thinner than usual but those trading are "rattled by the spread of coronavirus over the weekend as China steps up efforts to contain it," Oanda's Craig Erlam says. Despite the Saudi energy minister's remarks about the virus's "very limited impact on global oil demand" according to Reuters, "the supply/demand dynamics are not favorable right now so it was important the energy minister stressed OPEC 's flexibility and capability to do more," Mr. Erlam adds. (david.hodari@wsj.com; @davidhodari)

0820 GMT - Base-metal prices slump after Beijing extended the Lunar New Year holiday, compounding worries that the spread of coronavirus will dent demand for industrial commodities. Copper is down 1.7% on the London Metal Exchange , falling to $5,825 a metric ton, its lowest price in almost eight weeks. Nickel and zinc both drop 2.1%, to $12,705 and $2,290 a ton respectively. "This could be a very bumpy ride," says Malcolm Freeman, director of Kingdom Futures. Still, he says the decline could represent an opportunity to buy base metals at bargain prices, and suggests doing so using long-term call options. "Past experiences suggest that the impact of viral outbreaks can be large but also short-lived," says Liam Fitzpatrick, a metals analyst at Deutsche Bank. (joe.wallace@wsj.com)

0836 GMT - The U.K.'s FTSE 100 falls 116 points, or 1.5%, at 7470 as fears intensify over the speed at which the coronavirus is spreading. "The big risk right now for Europe and U.S. equity markets would be human-to-human [coronavirus] cases within continental Europe/North America," says Neil Wilson of markets.com. "Without that happening the focus will be more on the risk to global growth rates given the virus is hitting the drivers of global growth." Luxury goods producer Burberry, which has high exposure to China, falls 4.7%. Airlines drop, with easyJet down 4.7% and IAG down 4.1%. Heavyweight mining stocks also drop sharply, with Evraz, Rio Tinto and Anglo American all down by more than 4% while Glencore falls 3.9%. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

0838 GMT - USD/CNH market remains open this week, with 7.00 looking "touchable" as risk-off trade continues to dominate, Commerzbank says. Given China's priority of fighting the spread of the coronavirus, local governments will likely delay infrastructure projects, implying a weakening bias to economic-growth prospects in the short term, Commerzbank adds. USD/CNH is now up 0.7% at 6.9771, approaching both the 50- and 200-day moving averages on the FactSet chart. But with the stochastic oscillator way above the 80 threshold that some traders see as overbought, there is a risk that USD/CNH may trim its gains. (ronnie.harui@wsj.com)

0839 GMT - Gold prices rise as mounting worries about the outbreak of coronavirus hit stock markets and prompt investors to buy haven assets such as precious metals. Gold and silver futures are both up 0.4% in New York, at $1,578.10 a troy ounce and $18.18 a troy ounce respectively, after the news that the virus has infected more than 2,700 people and killed at least 80. Beijing said it was extending the annual Lunar New Year holiday by two days to Feb. 2 to delay the infection risk. As well as monitoring coronavirus, gold traders are awaiting the Federal Reserve 's monetary-policy decision on Wednesday. There is an 87% chance that the central bank keeps interest rates on hold, according to CME Group analysis of the federal-funds futures market. (joe.wallace@wsj.com)

0859 GMT - Reports of the coronavirus spreading rapidly causes European stocks to fall sharply as investors spy at an excuse to sell assets that many consider to be overvalued. "Some traders were questioning the lofty valuations of stocks, so now the fear surrounding the health crisis has acted as an excuse to take money off the table," says David Madden at CMC Markets . title: Swiss National Bank says  interventions  not aimed at trading advantage
text:
ZURICH, Jan 14 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank's currency interventions are not intended to give Switzerland a trading advantage by weakening the Swiss franc, the central bank said on Tuesday, after the country appeared on a U.S. watch list of currency manipulators.

"The SNB's interventions in the currency market are motivated purely by monetary policy considerations," the SNB said in a statement, citing the negative effects on inflation and the economy from a too highly valued franc.

"They are not aimed at bringing an advantage for Switzerland by making the franc undervalued," the SNB added.

The Swiss franc leapt to its strongest level since April 2017 after Switzerland was added on the semi-annual list which the U.S. says is intended to dismantle unfair barriers to trade. (Reporting by John Revill; Editing by Michael Shields)

title: UPDATE 1-For Swiss franc, only way to go may be up as  central bank  steps back
text:
(Updates with SNB policy meeting outcome)

By Elizabeth Howcroft and John Revill

LONDON/ZURICH Dec 12 (Reuters) - A strong currency that hurts exports and risks deflation, or a weak one that hobbles banks and annoys the U.S. -- that's the choice Switzerland faces. For now, at least, it seems to have picked the former.

The Swiss franc, backed by a huge balance of payments surplus, is the currency traders love to buy in times of trouble. With a global trade war raging, the franc has gained 9% versus the euro since last April and stands less than 1% below September's two-year highs .

The gains may be signalling a shift in the Swiss National Bank's currency policy. The SNB has dual mandates -- ensuring price stability and supporting the export-led economy -- that lead it to intervene to stem franc gains. In 2011, it even imposed a cap on the franc's value, abandoning it only in 2015.

Now the euro-franc rate is about to fall under 1.09 for the second time in a month, a level that triggered interventions over the summer.

But franc sight deposits at local banks, a proxy for measuring SNB interventions, fell to five-month lows of 587 billion Swiss francs ($588.65 billion) in the week ending Dec. 9, a 4.6 billion-franc net drop since October.

The SNB also refrained from following the European Central Bank's recent interest rate cut.

So, what's changed?

Neil Mellor, a currency strategist at BNY Mellon, said the SNB's challenge "is not down to a lack of policy tools per se, but rather the likely repercussions of using them."

He was referring to the U.S. Treasury's criticism of currency policies at its trade partners. A Treasury report in May 2019 report put Switzerland 12th on a list of currency manipulators, though it removed it from a monitoring list it was put on in 2016.

The dollar has gained 2% since mid-August against the franc. Since early 2018, it's up 7%.

The next Treasury report is due in December and many reckon the SNB is holding off intervening until then. https://reut.rs/35eKmYa

"They've not been intervening as much lately," said Marie Owens-Thomsen, chief economist at wealth manager Indosuez. "With respect to the U.S., my feeling is that they just want to try to fly below the radar."

In September 2017, the bank tweaked its language to call the franc "significantly overvalued", versus the earlier "highly valued".

The SNB did not comment. But Chairman Thomas Jordan told Swiss newspaper NZZ am Sonntag that the bank remained in close contact with the U.S. Treasury.

"Our interventions are never intended to weaken the franc at the expense of other economies," Jordan told the paper, adding the SNB only aimed at "combating an excessive appreciation".

On Thursday, the SNB left interest rates unchanged, as expected, but pledged to stay active in currency markets to ease upward pressure on the franc.

LIMITED ABILITY

Policymakers, including Jordan, would clearly prefer a cheaper currency; in an October speech, Jordan said https://bit.ly/36hJyBQ("https://bit.ly/36hJyBQ") further franc strength would cause a "gloomy scenario", slowing the economy and increasing unemployment.

A weak franc would help the SNB to avert deflation and boost exports, which make up 65% of Switzerland's annual output. The SNB has little room to cut its benchmark interest rate; at minus 0.75% it's already the lowest in the world.

The financial sector is warning of asset bubbles and damage to savers and pension funds from deeply negative rates. A majority of the more than 2,500 company executives and entrepreneurs surveyed by UBS recently said they were suffering from negative interest rates on cash and savings.

As for deflation, Switzerland has seen three rounds of deflation in the past decade -- in 2009, 2012 and 2015-16. With November inflation at 0.1% year-on-year, the threat is back .

Yet Salman Ahmed, chief investment strategist at Lombard Odier, noted this was a far cry from 2015, when inflation was minus 1.5%. The economy is also growing at double the euro zone rate.

"There was a fear of widespread deflation, but inflation is near 0%, so they still have some leeway," Ahmed said.

Finally, observers note Swiss exports such as luxury watches and drugs are not especially price-sensitive. Exports rose last year to record highs despite the franc's 4% rise. And franc strength would cut companies' import costs for raw materials such as metal, cocoa and chemicals.

The franc may strengthen to 1.07 per euro in the next three months, 2% above current levels, predicts Tom Flury, head of FX at UBS Global Wealth Management.

"They can't cut rates forever, and intervention is already a bit limited given that Switzerland might fall into the U.S. currency manipulator pocket, which would be something which, at least from the political side, we wouldn't appreciate too much," he said.

($1 = 0.9972 Swiss francs)

(Reporting by Elizabeth Howcroft in London and John Revill in Zurich; additional reporting by Saikat Chatterjee; editing by Sujata Rao and Larry King)

title: BUZZ-COMMENT-For dollar to do well next year, nothing needs to change
text:
For the dollar to do well next year, nothing needs to change. The U.S. economy is beating the competition and the trade deals demanded by the United States authorities should strengthen that advantage. Interest rates in the U.S. are higher than those for other major traded currencies and the Federal Reserve has been able to provide the U.S. economy with more support than the central banks have provided in other major nations, some of whom have done nothing. By contrast, a huge change is needed for the dollar to lose its advantage. That is unlikely -- interest rates would have to rise drastically. In Japan, the central bank is considering how it may do more to support the economy. The euro zone central bank resumed quantitative easing on Nov 1 . In Switzerland, the central bank continues to intervene to stave off unfavourable Swiss franc strength, and the UK is bogged down by Brexit. Chances are far better the dollar will gain advantage rather than lose it.

title: BUZZ-COMMENT-The Swiss National Bank is conspicuous by its absence
text:
The Swiss National Bank is conspicuous by its absence in foreign exchange markets that not so long ago would have seen the central bank actively trying to stem the Swiss franc's strength. Since early May, the franc has gained over 5 percent, yet sight deposits, which usually reveal intervention, have fallen over 10 billion francs. Perhaps Switzerland fears the consequence of currency manipulation, which at times in the past decade has dominated daily FX flows. Switzerland converts 35% of its 768 billion francs of reserves to dollars and 9% to yen. It clearly is supporting those currencies, in opposition of U.S. and Japanese wishes. Intervention now during a trade war wouldn't sit well with either. Nor would an even bigger reserve that could easily surpass 1 trillion francs just to hold EUR/CHF 12% below the old 1.2000 floor. With low unemployment, little inflation and a huge trade surplus, many would say Switzerland can afford a higher franc.

title: Trio of Central Banks Cut Interest Rates -- WSJ
text:
India, New Zealand and Thailand surprise investors with aggressive reductions 


By Brian Blackstone and James Glynn 

This article is being republished as part of our daily reproduction of WSJ.com articles that also appeared in the U.S. print edition of The Wall Street Journal (August 8, 2019).

Three central banks in the Asia-Pacific region lowered interest rates in a surprisingly aggressive fashion Wednesday as the fallout from the U.S.-China trade war intensified, suggesting the global rate-cut cycle will gather steam in the months ahead.

The trade war has hit markets hard in Southeast Asia, a fast-growing region deeply intertwined with global supply chains and dependent on trade with both the U.S. and China.

Two of the central banks that reduced rates Wednesday -- India and New Zealand -- were among the first to begin easing policy earlier this year and were a precursor to the Federal Reserve's rate cut in late July, its first since 2008. Thailand's central bank reduced interest rates Wednesday for the first time this year, reversing a late 2018 increase. The European Central Bank signaled in July that it will consider injecting fresh stimulus when it meets in September.

With banks in the Asia-Pacific region moving again, the global easing cycle may turn out to be longer and deeper than previously expected. The Philippines central bank is expected to follow its Asian peers with another rate reduction on Thursday. Investors increased their expectations for a rate cut from Australia's central bank in the wake of New Zealand's move.

"It's getting more and more difficult to make the case that central banks can fiddle around the edges on monetary policy," said Neil Shearing, chief economist at Capital Economics. "There will have to be more substantial easing."

One reason: With interest rates already ultralow or even negative in many parts of the world, central banks may need to be aggressive early on to have an effect on financial markets and exchange rates.

"There's quite limited ammunition left for many central banks; you want to use that very wisely," said Ben May, an economist at Oxford Economics. Central banks have a choice: either hold their firepower for emergencies or act early for a bigger effect, he said. The decisions out of the region Wednesday "suggest central banks are going down that second option," he said.

With central banks in big, developed countries either lowering rates or poised to do so, emerging-market central banks have greater flexibility to stimulate their economies without having to worry about capital fleeing from their financial markets to chase higher returns elsewhere. Central banks in Malaysia, Indonesia, South Korea and South Africa have also reduced policy rates in recent months.

Meanwhile, inflation is largely under wraps in many developing economies and well below the 2% annual growth rates that central banks in wealthy countries consider optimal. This means policy makers have little to lose by leaning on the forceful side with policy easing.

"There's not that kind of balancing act that central banks have had to do in the past," said Mr. May, referring to economic stimulus on one side and inflation fears on the other.

Most economists had expected New Zealand's central bank to make a one-quarter-percentage-point reduction. But it was double that size, to 1% from 1.5%. New Zealand "appears to be adopting the 'sooner is better' approach to monetary policy setting," said analysts at ING Bank, in a research note.

Thailand's central bank also surprised investors. The monetary policy committee cut its policy rate to 1.50% from 1.75%. Nine out of 11 economists polled by The Wall Street Journal had expected the central bank to hold steady.

India's central bank cut its key lending rate to 5.4% from 5.75%, deeper than investors expected and its lowest level in nine years as it tried to kick-start lending in Asia's third-largest economy.

Policy easing hasn't only involved interest rates. Switzerland's central bank appeared to have intervened in foreign-exchange markets late last month to weaken the Swiss franc, according to the central bank's weekly sight deposit figures and monthly foreign-exchange reserves figures. By stepping in -- which involves purchasing foreign assets with freshly created Swiss francs -- the Swiss can weaken the franc and provide a boost to exporters, effectively easing its monetary stance.

The Swiss National Bank's foreign reserves climbed by around 8 billion Swiss francs ($8.2 billion) to 768 billion francs in July, according to the SNB's monthly report Wednesday. But like many other central banks, its scope for action is limited. The SNB's foreign reserves exceed Switzerland's entire gross domestic product, raising doubts about how assertive the central bank could be if the franc, a traditional safe haven in times of global stress, were to strengthen significantly more.

The next phase of easing for Switzerland and other central banks in Europe depends critically on the ECB's next steps. The ECB sent a strong signal last month that it was preparing a cut in its deposit rate, currently minus 0.4%, and announce a fresh round of bond purchases as soon as its next meeting on Sept. 12.

Mr. Shearing said he expects a 10-basis point reduction in the ECB's deposit rate next month and a restart in new bond purchases -- which ended last December -- of EUR30 billion ($33.7 billion) in December.

But with German industrial production posting what Mr. Shearing called a horrific 1.5% monthly drop in June, "it's not going to take much" to move those bond buys forward, he said.

title: Swiss  Central Bank  Head Defends Negative Rates as 'Crucial' for Economy
text:
ZURICH--Swiss National Bank Chairman Thomas Jordan on Friday defended negative interest rates, saying the policy is "absolutely crucial" to ensuring price stability and keeping the Swiss franc from being too strong.

"Unfortunately, you can't have your cake and eat it, as the saying goes," he said at the SNB's annual general meeting, explaining that "you can't have higher interest rates and a weaker Swiss franc at the same time."

He acknowledged public concerns about the more-than four-year-old policy, in particular the effect on savers who have seen their deposit rates depressed after years of ultralow rates. "Some say that it runs contrary to economic logic, and creates major problems for savers and pension funds," Mr. Jordan said.

"We would not charge negative interest if we did not regard this as being absolutely crucial for us in fulfilling our mandate," Mr. Jordan said. Without that policy, in addition to the SNB's currency interventions to weaken the franc, "Switzerland would today be facing a different economic reality," with subzero inflation, weak growth and higher unemployment, he said.

The SNB has among the deepest negative policy rates in the world at minus 0.75%. It has held its deposit rate at that level since January 2015 in an effort to keep the Swiss franc from strengthening too much, which would damage exporters.

Most economists expect it to stay at this level well into next year at least. Like other European central banks outside the eurozone, the SNB is highly sensitive to what the European Central Bank does. With the ECB expected to keep its own negative policy rate unchanged into 2020, the Swiss are likely to stand pat as well. With annual inflation in Switzerland at just 0.7%, the SNB is under no pressure to raise rates anytime soon.

Mr. Jordan's comments were made at a meeting of the SNB's shareholders. The SNB is one of the only central banks in the world with listed shares. Its share price has risen about fivefold over the past three years even though the SNB pays only a tiny dividend and the small pool of private shareholders has no say in how the bank is managed. Mr. Jordan and the other governing board members don't own any shares, according to the SNB's annual report.

On Thursday, the SNB reported a first-quarter profit of 30.7 billion Swiss francs ($30.1 billion), which was largely driven by valuation gains on its massive holdings of foreign stocks and bonds.

title: Swiss  Central Bank  Swings to Loss -- WSJ
text:
This article is being republished as part of our daily reproduction of WSJ.com articles that also appeared in the U.S. print edition of The Wall Street Journal (January 10, 2019).

ZURICH -- One year after posting a record 54 billion franc ($55 billion) profit, the Swiss National Bank swung to a 15 billion franc loss in 2018, as a double whammy of weaker global equity markets and a stronger Swiss franc eroded the value of its massive holdings of foreign stocks and bonds.

The valuation loss reported Wednesday by the SNB underscores the interplay between central banks and markets. Usually, it is central bank decisions, or hints of changes in interest rates and other policies that cause stock and bond markets to fluctuate. But this has worked in reverse for Switzerland's central bank, whose finances are largely at the mercy of financial markets beyond its borders.

What sets Switzerland apart is that after years of currency interventions by the SNB -- creating francs to purchase foreign stocks and bonds in a bid to weaken the franc -- the bank has amassed over 700 billion francs worth of foreign assets, an amount that exceeds the country's entire gross domestic product. This makes it a major asset manager in addition to being a central bank.

"In terms of absolute numbers you have these high swings, but that comes from the huge size of the balance sheet and foreign exchange reserves," said Alexander Koch, an economist at Raiffeisen Schweiz bank.

This included over $3.5 billion in Apple Inc. shares at the end of the third quarter, according to Securities and Exchange Commission filings, $2.6 billion in Amazon Inc. stock and $2.7 billion in Microsoft Corp. The SNB's equity investments -- which comprise 20% of its foreign assets -- replicate broad indexes. The rest of the SNB's foreign-reserve portfolio is in foreign bonds. Euro assets comprise the largest share, followed by the dollar.

When equity markers rise, and when bond yields are low, the market value of the SNB's portfolio rises. A weaker franc amplifies those gains. These forces combined to push the bank's profit sharply higher in 2017. But they went in reverse in 2018.

The euro fell 4% against the franc last year, as economic and political uncertainties lifted demand for the Swiss currency, which is typically seen as a haven in times of global stress. The dollar was little changed against the franc over 2018, but has weakened in the past month.

Unlike other asset managers, the SNB can't hedge its currency exposure, because doing so would undercut its efforts to weaken the franc.

Given that limitation, "they've done quite a good job," said Mr. Koch, and the 15 billion franc loss only represents about 2% of the bank's roughly 800 billion franc balance sheet, including gold holdings.

Other central banks like the Federal Reserve and European Central Bank also have amassed large portfolios consisting primarily of bonds. But those assets are denominated in their own currencies, giving them a steady source of interest income without the foreign-exchange risk.

The good news for the SNB is that it can ride out market volatility, and its loss doesn't affect its ability to carry out monetary policy. Annual Swiss inflation was just 0.7% in December and with the franc still strong by historical measures, the SNB isn't under pressure to sell its foreign assets to strengthen its currency. It is expected by analysts to keep its key policy rate at minus-0.75% at least until late 2019.

The danger would come if Switzerland faced a sudden inflation shock that forced the SNB to sell its foreign assets at a loss. Repeated valuation losses could also damage the SNB's reputation at home.

Despite the 2018 loss, the SNB said it would still disperse two billion francs to the federal government and Swiss states, known as Cantons, under a profit-sharing agreement that runs through 2020. Because the SNB held on to the vast majority of its 2017 profit, it had a significant cushion to absorb last year's loss.

Its tiny pool of private investors didn't seem worried. Shares in the SNB jumped 20% Wednesday to 4,850 francs, although only around 500 shares traded hands, according to FactSet.

Unlike most central banks, the SNB has publicly listed shares, and it pays a small, legally capped dividend of 15 francs per share to those shareholders, who have minimal ownership rights, no say in how the bank is run or how it conducts monetary policy. The SNB itself has played down the importance of its shares. For these reasons, it is hard to pinpoint why the stock rises or falls, although confirmation that the SNB would pay its dividend may have helped shares Wednesday.

According to the SNB's last annual report, it had nearly 2,200 private shareholders at the end of 2017, who held 49% of its total 100,000 shares but only about 23% of voting shares.

The bank's share price attracted global attention in 2017 and 2018 when it rose more than fourfold and approached 10,000 francs a share last April. However, it has retreated since then and despite Wednesday's gain its share price was about 50% below last year's peak.

title: *S&PGR Affirms Switzerland At 'AAA/A-1+'; Outlook Stable
text:
18 May 2018 16:11 ET *S&P Expects Switzerland's Economy Will Expand at Sound Rates in 2018-2021

18 May 2018 16:11 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Affirms Switzerland At 'AAA/A-1+'; Outlook Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
Ratings: 
Foreign and Local Currency|U: AAA/Stable/A-1+ 
 
For further details see ratings list. 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
     -- We expect that Switzerland's economy will expand at sound rates in 
2018-2021, thanks chiefly to strong exports, and supported by easing pressure 
from the Swiss franc exchange rate. 
     -- We are affirming our 'AAA/A-1+' long- and short-term ratings on 
Switzerland. 
     -- The outlook is stable. 
 
RATING ACTION 
 
On May 18, 2018, S&P Global Ratings affirmed its unsolicited 'AAA/A-1+' long- 
and short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings on 
Switzerland. The outlook is stable. 
 
OUTLOOK 
 
The stable outlook on Switzerland reflects our expectation that the country's 
economy will continue to expand steadily over the next two to three years, and 
that Switzerland will maintain its institutional stability as well as its 
long-established fiscal and external buffers. 
 
We could lower the ratings on Switzerland if policymaking became significantly 
less predictable, for example through abrupt economic policy changes with 
severe economic repercussions. Potential adverse effects of the monetary 
environment on the financial sector or the Swiss economy could also weigh on 
the ratings. 
 
However, we currently view these scenarios as unlikely over our 2018-2021 
outlook horizon. 
 
RATIONALE 
 
Our ratings on Switzerland reflect the country's high prosperity levels and the 
demonstrated resilience of its economy. The high competitiveness, especially of 
its exports, and consequently high current account surpluses also support the 
ratings. Furthermore, our ratings reflect Switzerland's institutional stability 
and fiscal prudence. The Swiss franc's status as an actively traded currency 
and the Swiss National Bank 's (SNB's) monetary policy credibility also support 
the ratings. 
 
Institutional and Economic Profile: Switzerland's economy benefits from global 
demand for its exports 
     -- We think that the Swiss economy will benefit from a favorable global 
macroeconomic environment in the near term. 
     -- We consider that persisting global demand for Swiss goods will support 
the country's export-oriented manufacturing sector and fuel investments as well 
as domestic demand in the tightening labor market and low-inflation 
environment. 
     -- Switzerland's institutions will remain an anchor of stability, in our 
view, although the Swiss franc could appreciate again if global risk 
perceptions increase, due to the country's appeal as a safe haven. 
 
In our view, the Swiss economy is set to benefit from global economic growth, 
which drives demand for Swiss exports and in particular capital goods. At the 
same time, capacity utilization is increasing and is now slightly above its 
long-term average for the first time in seven years and, as a result, equipment 
investment is rising. The unemployment rate (national definition) fell to 2.9% 
in March from 3.4% one year earlier, which indicates rising pressure in the 
labor market on the supply side. We anticipate that higher disposable incomes 
will further underpin private consumption over our forecast horizon. The Swiss 
franc depreciated by around 10% relative to the euro over the past 12 months, 
reaching the level at which the SNB had capped the currency until January 2015. 
This alleviates one of the main constraints on the Swiss economy, the Swiss 
franc's appreciation over the previous few years. However, we've observed--as 
in past episodes of an appreciating franc--that the Swiss economy has 
maintained its competitiveness. Swiss companies' investments in product-quality 
improvements also support our forecast of a strong export contribution to 
growth, since we now forecast the exchange rate at EUR1 to Swiss franc (CHF) 
1.20 over the coming years. 
 
In addition, broad-based growth is supported by the increasing population and 
continued monetary accommodation. We hence forecast real GDP growth of 2.3% in 
2018 and 1.7% in 2019, before moderating slightly thereafter. 
 
Switzerland's institutional effectiveness remains proverbial, and the country's 
stability, rule of law, and business environment add to its reputation as a 
beacon of stability even during crisis periods. The Swiss political system has 
a long-standing tradition of incorporating popular referenda and initiatives 
(direct democracy). While the predictability of referenda outcomes is 
inherently prone to uncertainty, Swiss policymaking has a formidable track 
record of responding to economic and societal priorities, which in part 
explains Switzerland's top positions on various business-environment ranking 
tables. 
 
As an example of a popular initiative, in June 2018, a referendum will be held 
on whether to abolish fractional reserve banking and replace it by so-called 
sovereign money. If the referendum result favors changing the status quo, this 
would imply an untested and fundamental change to the country's monetary and 
financial system. More specifically, the central bank would be the sole creator 
of money, and commercial banks would be prohibited from creating electronic 
money, that is creating deposits through lending. All sight deposits would have 
to be backed by money created by the central bank. We think that the 
initiative's adoption could bring high uncertainty for the banking sector, the 
role of the central bank, and potentially the economy. But as we observed with 
previous referenda, the implementation of any changes could take a long time. 
 
Another important topic of public discussion in Switzerland is the limitation 
of immigration, and new referenda on the free movement of people could be on 
the agenda toward the end of our outlook horizon. These discussions touch on 
the six bilateral agreements that are connected to the agreement on the free 
movement of people within the EU . Ease of EU  market access is of crucial 
importance for Swiss companies and, as such, we have observed that Switzerland 
has adapted legislation to comply with the bilateral agreements. Switzerland is 
currently negotiating a framework agreement with the EU  to codify how 
Switzerland will adapt its own legislation to changes in EU  law. We note that 
Switzerland's relations with the EU  will remain a subject of national 
discourse, and we do not believe there will be any disruptions in Switzerland's 
relationship with the EU . 
 
Flexibility and Performance Profile: Monetary policy remains accommodative and 
conscious of exchange rate developments, while fiscal and external positions 
are solid 
     -- We project that Switzerland will post general government surpluses in 
2018-2021, reflecting the country's prudent fiscal policy. 
     -- We expect Switzerland's current account surplus will remain at a high 
7% of GDP on average in 2018-2021, bolstered by export strength. 
     -- While we believe inflation will remain well below 2% over the next few 
years, we anticipate that the central bank will be ready to intervene, if 
needed, to ease currency pressures. 
 
Switzerland's central government posted a sizable surplus of around 0.5% of GDP 
in 2017, which would have been even higher if the government had not made a 
provision for tax refunds it has to pay. Currently, tax payers choose to leave 
the money with the state to avoid negative interest rates on deposits. The 
fiscal results have been outperforming the budgets in the past years, and we 
expect general government surpluses will persist over the coming years. This is 
because of continued tax revenue growth, and previous years' savings measures 
and expenditure restraint, enacted even in times of solid fiscal performance. 
We expect fiscal prudence will continue, to comply with the Swiss debt brake 
rule and also to prepare for some potential fiscal pressures. For example, the 
reform of corporate taxation aims to abolish several corporate tax privileges 
that would no longer be internationally accepted, while retaining competitive 
tax rates. The reform, which is currently in the legislative process, could 
have an adverse effect on tax revenues and also trigger shifts in the Swiss 
intercantonal equalization system from 2020. We estimate that the potential 
impact on the federal government would amount to roughly CHF1 billion per year 
(0.1% of 2018 GDP). In that regard, we note that Swiss public finances are 
highly decentralized. Cantons and municipalities account for about one-half of 
total general government revenues and spending; however, we consider that the 
impact would be limited. 
 
As a result of a solid budgetary performance and economic growth, we expect net 
general government debt to decrease to about 16% of GDP by 2021 from 20% in 
2017 as net issuance reduces further in the coming years. 
 
One of the key pillars of the SNB's monetary policy, in addition to negative 
interest rates, has been its interventions in the foreign exchange markets. 
These measures intended to stem the strong appreciation of the Swiss franc 
following the decision to abandon the franc's cap against the euro in 2015. 
Although the Swiss franc had appreciated in 2007-2017 by about 20% in real 
terms, the currency recently depreciated vis-a-vis the euro, trading at around 
the level at which it was fixed before 2015. This has eased some of the 
economic pressures on corporate margins, labor demand, and the tourism sector. 
As a result of the SNB's interventions, foreign currency reserves increased to 
CHF738 billion (about $738 billion) in March 2018, from CHF522 billion in April 
2014. Due to the SNB's balance-sheet expansion, it has become more exposed than 
any major central bank globally to valuation shifts. Consequently, the recent 
trend of an appreciating euro against the franc has contributed to the further 
accounting-based increase in foreign exchange reserves, and we understand that 
the SNB has not intervened in the foreign exchange markets since last year. We 
do not expect the SNB to pre-empt any efforts by the European Central Bank  to

normalize monetary policy. Because the SNB is holding large amounts of eurozone 
government bonds and U.S. equities, any steps toward normalization would likely 
be carefully weighed regarding their potential market effects. Negative 
interest rates have had unintended consequences, including rich valuations in 
the property sector. Despite the SNB's efforts to tackle low inflation, 
consumer prices rose only slightly in 2017, following five years of deflation, 
and we expect inflation to climb gradually to 1.3% by 2021. This expectation 
could change, however, if the franc appreciates again, for example if external 
risks lead to safe-haven inflows into the franc and the SNB's foreign exchangeinterventions and negative rates did not suffice to counteract those potential 
pressures. 
 
We expect that Switzerland will continue to post a sizable and stable current 
account surplus of about 7% of GDP on average throughout our forecast horizon, 
owing to strong expected export performance. We also project the country will 
remain a net external creditor, well in excess of 100% of current account 
receipts (CARs) regardless of potential valuation effects on Switzerland's 
international investment position. By a narrower measure of external debt, net 
of public- and financial-sector external assets, we expect Switzerland will 
remain in a debtor position, averaging 14% of CARs during our forecast horizon. 
We view the franc as an actively traded currency. It holds almost a 5% share in 
spot foreign exchange transactions, according to the Bank for International 
Settlements ' Triennial Central Bank Survey in 2016. 
 
Switzerland has a prominent financial sector with total assets representing 
almost 5x GDP, mainly from the two largest Swiss banks, UBS AG  and Credit 
Suisse AG . Domestic assets denominated in franc are about 3x GDP. Since the 
financial crisis and substantial government support for UBS , the government has 
taken regulatory measures to reduce systemic risk and improve the resolvability 
of systemic banks, which should help contain future contingent liabilities for 
the sovereign. 
 
We think that growth in residential real estate prices and mortgage lending 
over the past several years could pose a risk, especially for Swiss banks 
focusing on the domestic market and with large exposures to the Swiss real 
estate market. We think that mortgage lending, which represents 85% of domestic 
bank lending, will increase by 2%-3% in 2018, although recent growth rates are 
considerably lower than in 2012-2015. We think that ongoing efforts by the 
central bank and Swiss regulator to contain mortgage debt, using 
macroprudential and self-regulatory measures, will constrain the growth of 
imbalances in this market. Another potential risk generally stems from the need 
to adapt to the negative-interest-rate environment. Under our Banking Industry 
Country Risk Assessment, we classify Switzerland in group '2' (on a scale of 
'1' to '10', with group '1' denoting the lowest-risk banking systems), one of 
the strongest worldwide. We currently view the government's contingent 
liabilities from its financial sector and government-related entities as 
limited.

title: SNB not beggaring neigbours by reining in franc - Jordan
text:
BASEL, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank's massive foreign currency purchases to weaken the Swiss franc are not a deliberate 'beggar-thy-neighbour' approach to gain unfair advantage at the expense of Switzerland's trade partners, SNB Chairman Thomas Jordan said.

The central bank has been selling francs for foreign currency in vast amounts for years to keep a lid on the soaring currency, whose rise has spelt danger for Switzerland's export-reliant economy.

The interventions -- which have inflated the SNB's foreign currency holdings to 742 billion Swiss francs ($747.76 billion) -- have attracted the attention of the U.S. Treasury looking to crack down on international currency manipulators.

Switzerland's current account surplus of around 10 percent of GDP - the seventh-largest surplus in the world - was another cause for concern for U.S. officials, who put Switzerland on a watch list along with China, Japan, South Korea and Germany.

Jordan said the SNB had to be active in the currency markets because reducing interest rates was not enough to steer monetary policy in the current low-rate environment.

"Our foreign exchange market interventions do not amount to a mercantilist policy at the expense of Switzerland's trading partners or a beggar-thy-neighbour strategy," Jordan said in remarks prepared for a conference in Basel on Thursday.

"Rather, this policy provides the SNB with a necessary instrument for ensuring price stability and for fulfilling its mandate."

Switzerland has been on the U.S. Treasury's monitoring list since 2016 and appeared again in October on the list which aims to curb what the U.S. calls "unfair currency practices".

Switzerland met two of its currency manipulation criteria -- having a material current account surplus at 10.3 percent of GDP and having engaged in a "sizeable one-sided foreign exchange purchases", the U.S. report said.

Switzerland's $6.6 billion first-half bilateral trade surplus with the United States fell short of the third criteria, which could have triggered bilateral talks aimed at correcting the situation.

"We are maintaining a constructive dialogue on this matter with the responsible government agencies in the U.S.," Jordan said.

Switzerland's high current account surplus was not due to currency interventions, he said, but to special factors like the country's ageing population and strong presence of merchanting and pharmaceuticals companies which were less affected by the currency's strength.

Despite a slight weakening of the franc, Jordan described the currency as "remaining highly valued." (Reporting by John Revill; Editing by Michael Shields)

title: FOREX -US dollar bounces back, bolstered by solid U.S. data
text:
* U.S. dollar rises vs euro, yen

* Dollar up more than 1.0 pct vs Swiss franc

* Graphic: World FX rates in 2017 http://tmsnrt.rs/2egbfVh("http://tmsnrt.rs/2egbfVh") (Updates to U.S. trading, new throughout, changes dateline, previous LONDON)

By Dion Rabouin

NEW YORK, July 27 (Reuters) - The U.S. dollar rallied against the euro and yen on Thursday after solid U.S. economic data, bouncing back from lows plumbed after Wednesday's Federal Reserve monetary policy statement.

U.S. durable goods orders rose more than expected last month and a fifth straight monthly increase in shipments suggested that business spending on equipment would support economic growth in the second quarter.

The good durable goods orders data was a welcome sign to dollar bulls, as U.S. economic data, including subdued inflation, and uncertainty surrounding U.S. President Donald Trump's proposed fiscal stimulus have sunk the dollar in recent months.

The euro on Thursday fell 0.5 percent against the dollar, slipping back below the $1.17 mark.

The dollar rose 0.3 percent against the yen to 111.50 yen.

"The most significant thing was the durable goods orders, those came in much better than expected," said Sireen Harajli, currency strategist at Mizuho Corporate Bank. "Especially given that the recent data releases in the U.S. have been coming in on the weaker side, I think that was welcome news this morning."

The dollar sank on Wednesday after the Fed's policy statement remained largely unchanged from June and suggested the Fed was in no hurry to raise interest rates again.

Soft U.S. data on inflation and consumer spending so far this year have pushed the dollar to multi-year lows against the euro, which has also been underpinned by the European Central Bank's talk of reducing its ultra-loose monetary policy.

The euro has risen more than 11 percent against the dollar so far this year.

Analysts also said investigations into the Trump administration's ties to Russia, and the inability of Trump's fellow Republicans to push through the president's promised repeal of the 2010 Affordable Care Act, have reduced the likelihood of tax reform and infrastructure spending plans being enacted soon also.

The Swiss franc was the biggest mover among major currencies, falling to its weakest since the collapse of an official cap in 2015.

The franc has held largely steady for the past two years as a result of capital seeking the security of Switzerland and a campaign of official intervention against the currency.

On Thursday the dollar rose 1.3 percent against the Swiss currency to 0.9618 franc.

LONDON, July 27 (Reuters) - The Swiss franc's fall to its weakest since the collapse of an official cap in 2015 dominated major currency markets on Thursday, and the dollar recovered from a fall to 2-1/2 year lows.

title: UPDATE 1-Swiss play down inclusion on U.S.  currency  manipulation list
text:
(Adds detail, comment, latest data on sight deposits at SNB)

By John Revill

ZURICH, April 18 (Reuters) - The Swiss government on Tuesday played down Switzerland's reappearance on a U.S. Treasury watch list of potential currency manipulators, saying the status would have no immediate consequences.

"The Swiss National Bank, according to its legal mandate, follows its own independent monetary policy," the Swiss finance ministry said in a statement.

"Their currency purchases are not aimed at devaluing the currency and raising the competitiveness of Swiss exports," it added. "Its goal is to limit the extent of the franc's overvaluation and prevent a strong downward push in inflation."

Switzerland, which was also mentioned by the Treasury last October, appeared along with China, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Germany on the latest list which aims to curb what the U.S. calls "unfair currency practices".

The Swiss qualified because for years they have used foreign exchange purchases to counter persistent inflows into the safe-haven franc. The SNB has also introduced negative interest rates to make the franc less attractive.

The SNB's foreign exchange reserves jumped by nearly 15 billion Swiss francs ($14.93 billion) in March to 683.18 billion francs, larger than Swiss gross domestic product.

Sight deposits at the central bank, a proxy for currency interventions, showed the SNB continued to sell francs ahead of the French presidential elections starting on Sunday, according to the latest data on Tuesday.

The SNB was not immediately available for comment.

Instead of market interventions, Switzerland should rely more on fiscal policy and interest rates to support its economy and ward off demand for the franc, the U.S. Treasury said in its report on Friday.

Switzerland met two of its currency manipulation criteria -- having a material current account surplus at 10.7 percent of GDP in 2016 -- and having engaged in a "sizeable one-sided foreign exchange purchases", the U.S. report said.

At $13.7 billion Switzerland did not however have enough of a bilateral trade surplus with the United States to meet the third criteria, which could trigger bilateral talks aimed at correcting the situation.

"As long as Switzerland is only on the watch list, it isn’t a problem," said David Marmet, an economist at Zuercher Kantonalbank. "Switzerland fulfils two of the three criteria, but it cannot be long before the trade balance means it meets all three, when it could become a problem.

"Still the Swiss will try to explain to the Americans their situation," Marmet said. "I think the SNB would prefer not to be on the list, but I don't think it will affect its monetary policy – what else can they do?" (Additional reporting by Angelika Gruber, Editing by Michael Shields)
