title: WORLD  FOREX : Dollar Rises Vs Euro As Debt Worries Linger
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The dollar extended its rally against the euro Friday morning in New York as renewed concern over sovereign debt problems in Europe overshadowed a mixed U.S. employment report.

Currency trading was choppy, with the euro briefly erasing most of its overnight losses before trading back around the $1.37 level, as investor digested the report showing the U.S. economy continued to shed jobs while the unemployment rate unexpectedly dropped in January.

"It's a mixed report," said Carl Forcheski, director of foreign exchange at Societe Generale in New York. "It's showing some repair, but there's certainly a lot of work to be done."

Because of the mixed nature of the report, currency markets have been unsure of how to trade the data, Forcheski said.

It's not unusual for currencies to fluctuate wildly in the immediate aftermath of closely watched data such as the monthly U.S. employment report. The knee-jerk reactions as investors make initial adjustment to positions don't always reflect the trend which later becomes dominant.

But, after traders digest the report, "there's no question that issues in the euro zone will remain," referring to the sovereign debt problems in Greece, Portugal and possibly Spain.

"The sovereign risk questions in Europe will begin to reassert themselves," he said. "The euro will remain on the defensive."

Friday morning in New York, the euro was at $1.3690 from $1.3741 late Thursday, according to EBS via CQG. The dollar was at 89.55 yen from Y88.94, while the euro was at Y122.57 from Y122.20. The U.K. pound was at $1.5673 from $1.5750. The dollar was at CHF1.0730 from CHF1.0655.

The Dollar Index, which tracks the greenback against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, was at 80.201 from 79.907. The index also traded near seven-month highs.

Demand for safer assets had picked up during Asian and European trading hours on the back of renewed concern over sovereign debt problems in the euro zone, forcing the Swiss National Bank to intervene to stem a spike in the Swiss franc against the euro, according to traders.

The Swiss franc fell to multi-month lows against the euro and dollar in Asia Friday as market participants said Switzerland's central bank made a rare and aggressive intervention to curb the rise in its currency.

The euro spiked around 0300 GMT to CHF1.4905, its highest since Dec. 28, from CHF1.4635. The dollar jumped to CHF1.0800, its highest since Aug. 18, from CHF1.0670.

Two dealers in the region said they saw franc-selling orders under the name of the SNB on the EBS trading platform. The central bank was bidding for euros at CHF1.49, far above the spot rate of CHF1.46, they said. The Swiss central bank didn't confirm the intervention.

Meanwhile, the cost of insuring Greek and Portuguese debt against default remained at record wide levels Friday. According to CMA DataVision, Greece's five-year sovereign credit-default swap spreads--a key measure of credit risk--stood at 446 basis points in early European trading Friday, up around 19 basis points from Thursday's record wide close of 427 basis points.

Investors are focused on a key vote in Portugal Friday. Portuguese lawmakers may vote for a regional finance law that could add to the budget deficit at a time when investors are growing increasingly concerned about the state of Portuguese finances.

The proposed Law of Regional Finances was approved Thursday by a parliamentary committee and would increase the funds sent to Portugal's Madeira and Azores regions by EUR50 million this year, and raise the amount each year until 2013 when the figure would hit EUR86 million, according to Finance Ministry calculations.

Jitters over the fiscal health of weaker members in the euro zone pushed the dollar index to its highest level since July 2009, while the euro sank to as low as $1.3648, a fresh eight-month low.

The euro is under increasing pressure over sovereign debt issues in Greece and other euro zone countries and "when you've got [anti-euro] momentum of this kind of scale, you need something to reverse it," said Daragh Maher, deputy head of global foreign exchange strategy at Calyon in London. The payrolls data didn't provide the impetus to stop the momentum, he said.

The U.S. unemployment rate, calculated using a household survey, fell to 9.7% last month from an unrevised 10% in December, the Labor Department said Friday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires had forecast the jobless rate would edge higher to 10.1%.

Nonfarm payrolls fell by 20,000 compared with a revised 150,000 decline in December. Economists had expected payrolls to be flat. The December figure was revised down sharply from an originally reported 85,000 drop.


 
    Canada Morning 
 

The Canadian dollar is higher after a volatile Friday morning that saw it rallying on positive domestic jobs data for January, surrendering some of its gains and then rallying again along with the euro after U.S. jobs data were released.

The U.S. dollar is trading at C$1.0684 from C$1.0729 late Thursday.

The U.S. dollar dropped in earlier trading after Statistics Canada reported in earlier trading that the Canadian economy created 43,000 jobs, substantially exceeding the expected 15,000.

While the greenback recovered partially, it then headed lower again after the release of U.S. jobs data, a move that traders linked to the U.S. unit's simultaneous decline against the euro.

A rebound in U.S. equities futures after the U.S. data encouraged market players to take profit on earlier risk aversion trades, said George Davis, chief technical analyst for foreign exchange at RBC Capital Markets in Toronto.

Strength in stocks could drive some further short-term weakness in the U.S. dollar, but the market remains nervous overall and could use a U.S. dollar retreat as a buying opportunity, he said. [ 02-05-10 0946ET ]

title: =DJ FOCUS:SNB May Hang Back On Policy Reversal, Despite Strong Data
text:
ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The predicted reversal of the Swiss National Bank's policy of currency intervention may take time, despite signs the Swiss economy could recover faster than originally expected, economists say.

Fundamental factors--such as rising demand for Swiss goods and a reduced threat of deflation--suggest an increase in interest rates and an end to extraordinary monetary policy measures could be in the cards this year. In Switzerland's case, these measures mainly consist of currency intervention.

But, some argue, given the paramount importance of the country's export sector, the central bank won't rush into abandoning the Swiss franc to the mercy of the financial markets.

A premature change in the SNB's policy of intervening to prevent excessive Swiss franc strength could choke off the expected economic recovery, Moody's Economy.com said.

"Currency interventions will end only once the economy shows clear signs of stabilizing and the risk of deflation has subsided further," economist Melanie Bowler at Moody's Economy.com noted.

"Against the backdrop of decreasing deflation risks and the improved export situation, there are few arguments to support the euro versus the Swiss franc," said Credit Suisse Group economist Fabian Heller. "However, the SNB will aim to continue to reduce volatility in the currency market," he added, pointing at the possibility of further intervention.

Hopes of a rebound in the Swiss manufacturing sector received a boost from purchasing managers' data Monday, but any recovery will hinge on the central bank's willingness to influence the franc, economists say.

The purchasing managers' index posted a 19-month high of 56 points in January, consistent with an economic growth rate of 2% for 2010, economists said. This would mark an impressive rebound from a contraction of around 1.9% last year.

BNP Paribas economist Eoin O'Callaghan said the result of the PMI, an important gauge of future economic development, was impressive considering the "very elevated level of the exchange rate."

The recent rally in the franc is one of the most pressing economic issues in Switzerland, a currency island in the vast euro zone. Given the small size of its domestic market--just 7.5 million residents--the country's economic fortunes hinge on exports. A strong franc puts a strain on exporters, and in times of economic stress, politicians and entrepreneurs are quick to call on the SNB to weaken the local currency.

The central bank did just that in March 2009 when the global economic crisis was at its worst, effectively making foreign exchange management a mainstay of monetary policy.

However, this was clearly a measure for extraordinary times. The SNB cut its key interest rate to a record low 0.25%, thereby depriving itself of the ability to influence the currency with more cuts.

The SNB intervened on further occasions last year, mostly without confirming it had been active.

Under the new leadership of Philipp Hildebrand, who took charge of the central bank last month, the SNB has renewed its pledge to prevent any excessive strengthening of the franc.

Traders say the SNB appeared to have sold Swiss francs last week--its first intervention this year. Friday, the euro jumped to CHF1.4770 from CHF1.4635 and the dollar to CHF1.0644 from CHF1.0548, following talk the SNB had intervened.

In line with its policy of reticence on interventions, the central bank Monday declined to comment.

On the foreign exchange market at 1552 GMT, the euro was at CHF1.4727 and the dollar at CHF1.0589.

title: UPDATE: Swiss PMI Up In January;Fuels Hopes For Quick Pickup
text:
(Adds background, economist comment.)


 
   By Martin Gelnar 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

ZURICH (Dow Jones)--The Swiss purchasing managers' index rose to a 19-month high in January, reviving hopes that the country's economy will quickly recover from last year's recession, figures showed Monday.

The indicator, a gauge of economic activity in the next few months, rose to 56.0 points from a downwardly-adjusted reading of 53.7 points in December, beating market expectations of 55.4 points.

The series rose above the 50-point level--the threshold that separates economic expansion from contraction--in September, but a slip in December temporarily broke the pattern of improving results.

The January advance reflects a rise in industrial output and orders, said Credit Suisse Group, which calculates the series with the Association of Purchasing and Materials Management.

However, the rebound is still fragile. The PMI remains well below levels of more than 60 points registered in periods of rapid economic expansion.

Economists said the figure is in line with improving economic prospects in Switzerland and elsewhere.

The spike in January shows the economy had a very good start this year, according to ING, with economist Julien Manceaux noting the level is consistent with growth in gross domestic product of 2% for 2010. He also highlighted a better-than-expected upward move in the forward-looking Swiss indicator KOF, released last week.

However, much will depend on the confidence of Swiss consumers, which is likely to be shaky as unemployment continues to rise. "For that reason, signs of a strong recovery are still to be taken with a pinch of salt," Manceaux said.

BNP Paribas SA economist Eoin O'Callaghan said the Swiss PMI data compare favorably with the 52-point reading recorded in the euro zone. "Switzerland continues to outperform the euro area on this measure of manufacturing activity. That continues to impress considering the very elevated level of the exchange rate," he said.

The PMI report came after a clear drop in the Swiss franc late last week, sparking speculation the central bank has intervened to prevent a further rise in the currency.

On Friday, the euro jumped to CHF1.4770 from CHF1.4635 in New York trading hours. The dollar made similar gains, leaping to CHF1.0644 from CHF1.0548.

Earlier this year, the Swiss National Bank renewed its pledge to sell Swiss francs to prevent any excessive appreciation of the currency. A fast rise in the Swiss franc against the euro, the currency of the country's most important trading partners, puts a strain on Switzerland's important exporting industry.

Last year, the SNB intervened several times to lower the franc.

On the foreign exchange market at 1015 GMT, the euro traded at CHF1.4718 and the dollar at CHF1.0580.

The SNB , which has kept interest rates at a record low of 0.25% since March 2009, is expected to maintain that level for some months to come.

title: Swiss prices post y/y rise, deflation risks remain
text:
* CPI posts first y/y rise in December since February

* Annual inflation lower than economists had expected

* Core inflation ticks down

ZURICH, Jan 7 (Reuters) - Swiss consumer prices rose for the first time year-on-year in ten months in December, data showed on Thursday, but the gain was smaller than economists expected, indicating that the risk of deflation was not fully overcome.

The consumer price index rose 0.3 percent from a year ago but was 0.2 percent lower compared with the previous month, the Federal Statistics Office said. Core inflation also declined month-on-month, the data showed.

"The index's (month-on-month) fall of 0.2 percent is chiefly due to sales in the clothing sector and lower prices for crude oil," the statistics office said in a statement.

For December, economists polled by Reuters had on average expected a yearly inflation rate of 0.5 percent.<ECONCH>

To fight the worst recession in decades and combat falling prices, the Swiss National Bank launched unconventional policy tools in March, including ultra-low interest rates, corporate debt purchases and foreign exchange interventions.

Switzerland emerged from recession in the third quarter of last year, and the SNB forecasts growth of 0.5 to 1.0 percent for 2010 and inflation of 0.5 percent.

Although the central bank has begun to unwind some of its unconventional measures, it has also cautioned that the recovery remains fragile.

The closely-watched KOF barometer, published on Dec. 30, indicated that the recovery was set to loose momentum this year. [ID:nLDE5BT0UK] (Editing by Andy Bruce)

title: WORLD  FOREX : Dollar Falls As Concern Eases Over Dubai's Debt
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The dollar tumbled against most rivals Tuesday as concerns over Dubai's debt situation receded, spurring investors to snap up global stocks, commodities and higher-yielding currencies.

Easing fears about Dubai's debt crisis spreading to other credit markets "is helping to relieve some concerns that had weighed on riskier assets," said Omer Esiner, senior market analyst at Travelex Global Business Payments in Washington.

The greenback remained under pressure versus other major currencies except the yen, which fell across the board on the announcement of a surprise meeting by the Bank of Japan.

Late afternoon Tuesday in New York, the euro was at $1.5086, from $1.5015 late Monday, according to EBS via CQG. The dollar was at Y86.68, from Y86.45, while the euro was at Y130.76, from Y129.80. The U.K. pound was at $1.6617, from $1.6456. The dollar was at CHF0.9994, from CHF1.0043.

The Dollar Index, which tracks the greenback against a trade-weighted basket of six currencies, was at 74.426, from 74.788.

"At least for now the market is under the impression that the Dubai situation is more or less contained," Esiner said.

Safe-haven currencies have therefore lost their appeal and investors have reverted to the previous trend of selling the dollar and buying commodities, stocks and emerging market assets, he said.

However, investor caution ahead of further details on the Dubai situation and Friday's key U.S. non-farm payrolls report should keep the dollar's losses in check, said John McCarthy, manager of currency trading at ING Capital Markets in New York.

To see the dollar moves against the yen, please see chart at:

http://www.dowjoneswebservices.com/chart/view/3118 ("http://www.dowjoneswebservices.com/chart/view/3118")

State-run conglomerate Dubai World broke six days of silence early Tuesday morning and announced details of its proposed debt restructuring, saying it was having constructive talks with banks over some $26 billion in affected debt.

That bolstered investor appetite for risk in global markets overnight, fueling a rally in oil, metals and stocks.

A weaker-than-expected report on U.S. manufacturing activity failed to damp investor sentiment. The Institute for Supply Management's November manufacturing index came in at 53.6, trailing economists' estimates for reading of 55.0, and less than the 55.7 reported in October.

Still, the index clocked in above the 50 threshold, indicating manufacturing activity remained in expansion territory.

Though the dollar declined against most of its rivals, it gained ground against the yen after a surprise overnight meeting of the BOJ. The dollar rose as far as Y87.54 on the news of the emergency meeting, but gave up most of those gains when the BOJ didn't announce specific measures to arrest the appreciation of the Japanese currency.

Instead, BOJ board members agreed to provide more liquidity to markets by lending up to Y10 trillion in three-month funds at the 0.1% policy rate. That was seen largely as a political gesture rather than a shift in policy.

Australia's central bank overnight bucked the ultra-loose monetary policy trend by announcing an expected increase in key interest rates by 0.25 percentage point, putting its key rate at 3.75%. Because analysts had expected the increase, the Australian dollar had already appreciated ahead of the announcement and actually lost some ground. It has since gained on the U.S. dollar.

Meanwhile, the Swiss National Bank said overnight it would continue to act decisively to prevent the Swiss franc from strengthening against the euro, SNB President Jean-Pierre Roth said.

The SNB first announced its strategy of acting against Swiss franc strength in the spring in an attempt to support Switzerland's export-driven economy, and is thought to have intervened in currency markets four times since then.

Several times in recent months the franc has appreciated to levels against the dollar and euro greater than what the SNB is thought to tolerate, but the SNB has not always intervened, keeping investors guessing.

2 Nov 2009 13:48 EDT DJ  SNB: Time For Exit Strategy Hasn't Yet Arrived - Jordan

BERN (Dow Jones)--The worst of the financial crisis has passed but it would be premature to hike rates, Swiss National Bank directorate member Thomas Jordan said Monday.

"The worst is behind us but there isn't enough stability to talk about an exit strategy as yet," Jordan said in a speech in Bern.

He added the biggest challenge for policymakers is the timing of any exit strategy--the return to a higher interest rate level consistent with long-term price stability.

The current stimulus stemming from record-low rates will have to disappear at some stage to prevent a surge in inflation in a few years' time, according to Jordan.

However, the path to a normalized monetary policy will be a stony one, he said.

"The timing of the exit strategy will be crucial, and it will also be tough to communicate," Jordan said, adding that the SNB's overriding goal remains price stability.

Among the positive recent signs are the fact that banks have begun lending to each other and that credit risk premiums haven come down. Also, there is no sight of a credit crunch in Switzerland.

He said the central bank's foreign exchange intervention policy begun last March has been successful. "As a consequence, the volatility in the Swiss franc has decreased.

He didn't comment on last week's speculation the Swiss central bank bought foreign currency to drive the Swiss franc lower.

UBS AG (UBS), the only Swiss bank that needed government support to survive the crisis, is on the path to recovery, Jordan said.

The risk to the SNB stemming from the so-called StabFund, a special vehicle for UBS's toxic assets, has halved to around $25 billion compared with some $54 billion earlier this year, according to Jordan.

Jordan added the dollar will in all probability remain the world's bellwether currency in the foreseeable future.

title: FUND VIEW-Correction in stocks to boost dollar-Capricorn
text:
NEW YORK, Aug 28 (Reuters) - The U.S. equity market is due for a pullback and this could support the dollar as an inverse correlation, in which the two assets tend to move in opposite directions, is intact, a Switzerland-based currency manager said.

Over the past few months, the dollar has tended to rise when stocks retreat as investors see the greenback as a safe store of value in times of market stress. The link, although somewhat weaker, is set to stay for some time.

"We're pretty bullish on the dollar over the medium-term," said Mikkel Thorup, chief investment officer of Capricorn, which manages assets of about $280 million.

"We believe the equity market in general is over-stretched and there will be a correction very soon," he said. "There's not an awful lot of buying going on. There's still a lot of money on the sidelines that's not willing to actually go in and buy at these current levels."

The S&P 500 has rallied more than 50 percent since it hit a 12-year low in early March as the United States appears to be emerging from its worst recession since the 1930s. There are concerns that the rally is overdone and that stock prices may have run ahead of fundamentals.

The recent sell-off in China's Shanghai composite <.SSEC> has reminded investors of significant risks and uncertainty facing the global economy and financial markets, Thorup said.

"Everybody is talking about China in terms of growth," Thorup said. "We've seen some pretty steep corrections already in China. (That) should definitely have an influence on the U.S. equity market."

He expects the dollar to climb to around $1.33 and $1.34 per euro by the end of the year. On Friday, the euro <EUR=> last traded at $1.4337, little changed on the day.

While the global economy may have hit bottom, the recovery is likely to be slow as banks are still reluctant to lend, consumer spending remains weak, and unemployment stays near 10 percent in the United States, Thorup said.

"Just in March, everybody was talking about a doomsday scenario. Then five months after, everything is really looking fantastic. That's what I just don't understand," he said.

"I think we're going to have a prolonged period where we'll actually see the markets (and the economy) moving not too far away from the bottom. I think we can call that an L-shape (recovery)."

STABLE SWISS FRANC

The currency manager expects the Swiss franc to be "relatively stable" against both the dollar and euro, noting that the Swiss National Bank is "very strong on the intervention side."

Switzerland's solid fundamentals have supported the franc, but the risk of intervention has limited the currency's upside. Earlier this week, SNB board member Thomas Jordan said the central bank does not accept a further appreciation against the euro. See [ID:nWEA8258].

On Friday, the euro slipped 0.2 percent to 1.5155 francs <EURCHF=>, while the dollar fell 0.2 percent to 1.0568 <CHF=>.

But Thorup said uncertainty surrounding the U.S. tax settlement with UBS will likely put pressure on the Swiss economy.

Switzerland earlier this month agreed to reveal the names of about 4,450 wealthy American clients of UBS to U.S. authorities, creating uncertainty about the ramifications for other banks. See [ID:nLJ718259]

"We've seen several of the biggest players in the Swiss market beginning to outsource or offshore a lot of their (wealth) management business and of course that's having an impact also on the Swiss economy."

BERNE (Dow Jones)--Switzerland's central bank Thursday said it is prepared to intervene in foreign exchange markets to cushion the impact of the economic crisis on the country's economy, and kept interest rates near zero.

Switzerland's economic and monetary policy situation is gradually normalizing but risks remain, Swiss National Bank president Jean-Pierre Roth said at a media conference.

"We consider that the time for a correction has not yet come, but that an additional relaxation of monetary conditions is not necessary either," he said.

After its quarterly monetary policy assessment, the Swiss National Bank said it continues to target 0.25% in the three-month Swiss franc London interbank offered rate, its rate benchmark. The decision was widely expected by economists, most of whom expect the SNB to maintain the target at the current record-low level for the remainder of this year.

The three-month Swiss franc Libor, set each day around noon along with other Libor rates by the British Bankers' Association, was 0.395% Wednesday.

Renewing its pledge for a generous liquidity supply through unconventional means known as quantitative easing, the central bank said it would continue to buy foreign currency to prevent an excessive strengthening of the Swiss franc if need be. The SNB started this practice in March, returning to the foreign exchange market as an active player after a 15-year absence.

The central bank didn't provide details of past forex interventions, but said they were effective partly because market participants didn't know which exchange rate level would trigger an SNB action.

According to currency traders, the SNB has in the past few months bought euros after the euro-Swiss francs exchange rates fell through a psychologically important level of 1.50.

SNB directorate member Thomas Jordan said the central bank also plans to continue liquidity-boosting measures such as the purchase of bonds. Under the SNB's bond repurchasing scheme launched in March, the central bank bought Swiss covered bonds for CHF2.5 billion and corporate bonds for CHF300 million.

The SNB said it expects the Swiss economy to contract 2.5% to 3% in 2009, unchanged from a previous estimate. Consumer prices are expected to decline 0.5% this year, and to rise 0.4% and 0.3% in 2010 and 2011, respectively.

title: SCENARIOS-What will the SNB decide at its policy meeting?
text:
ZURICH, June 15 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank looks set to stick to its ultra-loose monetary policy course at its next policy meeting on June 18, keeping up the fight against the worst recession in decades and the risk of deflation.

The Swiss economy shrank 0.8 percent on the quarter in the first three months of this year, its third quarterly drop in a row as global demand for Swiss products has collapsed and higher unemployment is slowing consumption.

Consumer prices fell one percent on the year in May, the steepest price decline since 1959.

"Against this background for Swiss growth, coupled with the threat of a deflationary spiral, it is clear that the SNB will be in no position to reverse their ultra-loose monetary policy stance in 2009," said 4Cast analyst Saara Tuuli.

Following are key scenarios for the outcome of the SNB's meeting:

MORE OF THE SAME

The Swiss central bank is most likely to stick to its set of drastic unconventional easing measures adopted at the March 12 meeting as the recession has deepened and the price declines highlight the risks of a deflationary spiral in Switzerland.

In a Reuters poll, all 41 economists expect unchanged rates and most bet on continuing unorthodox easing.[ID:nLAG003501]

The central bank lowered its target rate for 3-month Swiss franc LIBOR to 0.25 percent -- a level only seen in the 2003 recession until now -- as it forecast a 2.5-3.0 percent drop in gross domestic product 2009, the worst since 1975.

The SNB offered longer-term repos to bring LIBOR down.

It also intervened to stem a rise in the franc against the euro and started to buy corporate bonds in Swiss francs -- mostly covered bonds or Pfandbriefe.[ID:nLE924029]

SNB board member Thomas Jordan said in May the measures were showing the desired effects: credit spreads have narrowed, the franc is hovering in a range of 1.50-1.52 per euro and volatility has come down significantly.

Analysts hope for more details on the exact scope and size of the bond purchases and the currency interventions.

Click on [ID:nL2504822] for a Q+A on the SNB's unorthodox measures.

STEPPING UP INTERVENTIONS

Some economists have noted that monetary conditions in Switzerland have not really eased over recent months despite the SNB's drastic actions. The franc remains strong against a basket of the currencies of Switzerland's trading partners.

The SNB has called currency interventions its strongest instrument to fight deflation, and it may want to weaken the franc more actively to provide some relief for Swiss exporters.

However, this would contradict the SNB official's repeated pledge that they would not engage in a devaluation race. Therefore, a more activist intervention policy seems unlikely.

NEW MEASURES

Right after the March decision, board member Jordan emphasised the SNB had more aces up its sleeve if needed:

* The SNB could add riskier assets to its list of collateral accepted in the repo and more counterparties could be allowed to take part.

* The SNB could impose negative interest rates on banks' deposits with the central bank and in its liquidity operations.

* On the credit market, the SNB could buy bonds directly from the issuers or buy government bonds.

* As a final step on the currency front, the SNB could set a fixed exchange rate target and defend it with unlimited purchases of other currencies.

* The SNB may buy government bonds.

However, SNB officials have said patience is needed to allow the measures already taken to work.

Some analysts see a small chance of government bond purchases as yields have been rising.

TAKING BACK MEASURES

Taking back any of the unconventional easing measures is by far the least likely scenario, despite some more optimistic news on the global economy and first tepid signs that the economic slump maybe slowing in Switzerland, too.

The SNB officials said that a timely unwinding of the loose monetary policy was important, but they have given no indication that this would happen soon. "The inflation forecast will be the key instrument in determining when it is time to begin the exit strategy," Vice-Chairman Philipp Hildebrand said recently.

It is highly unlikely, however, that the SNB will sharply revise up its inflation forecast, which sees nearly unchanged prices in 2010 and 2011.

The Swiss National Bank was among the first central banks to highlight deflation concerns when it slashed interest rates to a historic low in March, and the economic picture hasn't changed since then. Given the lack of potential surprise over Swiss rates, market watchers will focus more on the SNB's economic and consumer price forecasts next week, and on any comments on the central bank's strategy to cope with the economic downturn.

The bank's repertoire of unconventional methods to increase liquidity also includes additional repurchase transactions and the buying of corporate and covered bonds.

title: Swiss economy will hit bottom by '10-new SNB member
text:
ZURICH, April 9 (Reuters) - The Swiss economy may have hit the bottom of the crisis by January 2010, Jean-Pierre Danthine, who will join the Swiss National Bank executive board at the start of next year, told a Swiss newspaper.

Asked whether he expects the worst of the crisis to be over by the time he takes up his new post in January, Danthine was quoted by Le Temps on Thursday as saying: "We could have seen the bottom, with the exception of unemployment."

"We will at that point make sure that the conditions for a recovery are the best possible, and that the biggest risk is inflation rather than deflation," he added.

The SNB has warned against the risk of deflation in Switzerland and said it was ready to use foreign exchange intervention as a way to defuse this threat.

Danthine, an economics professor at the University of Lausanne who also heads the Swiss Finance Institute, said he hoped the risk posed by Switzerland's largest bank UBS was over.

"We can now hope this (the risk) is now behind us," he said. "We are exploring several avenues -- capital requirements and the leverage ratio -- to avert this situation in the future."

He said he was also interested in the concept of "contingency capital", whereby institutions considered to pose systemic risks could get access to capital in specific situations.

"This can be a sort of insurance that would allow, in certain specific situations, an automatic injection of capital that could come from abroad," Danthine said. "The markets in their own entirety would contribute to this form of systemic insurance."

Danthine, whose appointment was announced on Wednesday, also appeared reluctant to support any heavy regulation of executive pay within the financial sector and said this was not a key responsibility for the central bank.

"Remuneration has played a certain role in the crisis, but we should not exaggerate," he said. "There is a need for improvement and if this is not done quickly enough, we may have to regulate."

"I would like to mention that socially responsible investment is a good way to introduce progress, possibly more effective than some big regulation, even if this does not grab newspaper headlines."

title: ANALYSIS-Japan unlikely to follow SNB in  FX intervention
text:
* Japan intervention unlikely, would spark big trade tensions

* Broad yen drop also argues against intervention

By Masayuki Kitano and Stanley White

TOKYO, March 13 (Reuters) - Based on the Swiss National Bank's intervention to weaken its own currency, Japan may appear to have reasons to do the same. But analysts say it is unlikely to do so.

Intervention from the world's second-biggest economy as the world scrambles to combat its deepest financial crisis in decades would cause much greater trade tensions than intervention by Switzerland, the world's 22nd biggest economy.

Earlier this decade Japan spent well over $350 billion to push the yen lower but has resisted the temptation to intervene so far during the crisis.

Such intervention now would hit a raw nerve, especially as the Group of 20 nations plan in coming weeks to tackle the global crisis that has been compared with the 1930s Great Depression -- a crash made worse at the time by competitive currency devaluations.

"Competitive currency devaluation is not likely in Japan now because the risks of sparking trade friction are too great," said Masahiro Sato, joint general manager of the treasury division at Mizuho Trust & Banking Co.

"The Swiss can get away with this because of the relatively small size of their economy and the limited role they play in the global economy," he said.

Takahide Nagasaki, chief forex strategist at Daiwa Securities SMBC, agreed:

"A simple comparison between the two countries cannot be made, and it is difficult to say that SNB's move will open the door for Japan to intervene," he said

The SNB announced bold steps on Thursday to fight deflation and underpin the economy. It cut interest rates virtually to zero, reflecting moves by the United States, Japan and Britain, but stunned markets by intervening to weaken the Swiss franc.

That made the SNB the first major central bank in the world to intervene in currency markets during the crisis, raising the prospect its actions could spark a round of competitive currency devaluations as governments move to protect their economies.

In response to the SNB's actions, the euro posted its biggest one-day gain against the Swiss currency and heads turned towards Japan.

LEGACY

Switzerland and Japan face similar economic difficulties that a weaker domestic currency might help offset.

Like Switzerland, Japan is facing the threat of deflation. Both countries are seeing exports demand shrink as world trade crumbles. In both cases, their export efforts are being hampered by relatively strong currencies.

Indeed, Japan's exports are falling at a record pace and the economy is already in its deepest recession since 1974.

But most importantly, Japan spent 35 trillion yen ($358 billion) in the 15 months to March 2004 to prevent a strong yen from snuffing out an economic recovery and worsening deflation.

The historical precedent makes Japan the most obvious candidate to follow the SNB, strategists at UBS said in a client note.

But despite that legacy, the Ministry of Finance, which decides on intervention, has resisted the urge to intervene so far during the crisis, despite strong temptations.

It declined to intervene in October when the Group of Seven industrial powers issued a rare inter-meeting statement singling out yen volatility, giving Japanese authorities the green light to stem its surge.

Even when the yen hit a 13 1/2-year high of 87.10 per dollar in January and exports demand collapsed, the BOJ held back.

Now, the yen has fallen back and stood near 97.95 yen on Friday, putting intervention further in doubt, analysts said.

DIPLOMACY

Switzerland's surprise move came just before the financial heads from the Group of 20 countries meet in England to prepare for a G20 summit in April. Avoiding trade protectionism is a main part of the agenda.

"Japan would not want to weaken the yen when the G20 countries are trying to hold protectionism at bay," Nagasaki said.

A significant factor behind Japan's heavy intervention in 2003 and 2004 was the state of the global economy.

At that time Japan was facing difficulties when other economies were in a much healthier state, said Toru Umemoto, chief FX strategist for Japan at Barclays Capital.

"Currently, almost all countries are suffering from the financial crisis and the global recession ... If Japan intervened in the market currently it would be severely criticised," Umemoto said.

That seems especially true given Japan's large presence in the global economy and role as a major exporter.

"A weaker currency is not necessarily a cure-all because it can fuel capital flight. Japan certainly doesn't want to take on that risk," Mizuho's Sato said. ($1=97.66 Yen) (Additional reporting by Charlotte Cooper and Shinichi Saoshiro; Editing by Neil Fullick)

title: Moody's issues annual sovereign credit report on Switzerland
text:
Switzerland's Aaa ratings are underpinned by very high levels of economic, institutional and financial strength, which contribute to low susceptibility to event risk, says Moody's Investors Service in its new annual sovereign credit report on Switzerland. The country's ratings have a stable outlook.

"Switzerland has high average incomes that are expected to be maintained over the long term, as well as an open, highly developed and diversified economy," says Alexander Kockerbeck, a Vice President-Senior Credit Officer in Moody's Sovereigns Group. "Furthermore, Switzerland has a long history of fiscal prudence, low inflation and a strong net external creditor position."

Moody's also notes that Switzerland's institutions are very robust and its governance system is highly transparent. This is supported by the country's political stability, although its referendum democracy can lend itself to a cumbersome reform and deregulation process. Furthermore, there is broad consensus on fiscal discipline and on the general goal to achieve balanced federal budgets.

"The small and very open Swiss economy will face recession - like many other European economies - due to the global financial and economic crisis," explains Mr. Kockerbeck. "The high losses among large Swiss banks and ongoing problems in the global financial markets have increased pressure on output and employment within Switzerland's important banking and insurance sector. However, the challenge should be manageable with no substantial macro imbalances or structural problems in the rest of the economy."

Although Switzerland's economic, financial and political characteristics have a track record of high solidity Moody's considers the country's susceptibility to event risk as "low" rather than "very low" due to the risks in the banking sector.

Moody's recognises that the Swiss government has recently extended support to its banking system during the ongoing financial crisis. Moody's considers the potential net impact on the government's balance sheet to be muted at this stage, since potential government capital injection into banks is counterbalanced by bank assets, and potential government guarantees for the banking sector represent (explicit) contingent liabilities.

Moody's also notes that the government takes calculated risks with the banking system, but still displays a strong crisis management capacity. The Swiss government's key strategy in combating the current financial crisis appears to be timely intervention and further crisis prevention.

Moody's believes that Switzerland's Aaa ratings are able to withstand a large-scale government support operation for the Swiss banking system due to: (i) the underlying economic and institutional strength and financial robustness of the Swiss government; (ii) the quality of any bank assets that it would acquire through these support operations; and (iii) the likelihood that such an interposition of the government's balance sheet would be a better alternative to the potential damage to Switzerland's economic vitality.

Moreover, the government has a variety of options in case of an emergency. Moody's recognises the Swiss government's ability to raise potentially larger amounts of debt through: (i) its access to a large pool of domestic savings, as Switzerland has a savings rate equivalent to nearly one-third of GDP; (ii) the Swiss franc's role as an international currency, supporting the country's excellent reputation; and (iii) for short-term liquidity pressures, the Swiss central bank's unlimited swap line with the US Federal Reserve, which provides very precious relief at times when dollar funding is scarce.

Finally, Moody's does not rule out international support cooperation to prevent shock waves across the global financial system that a massive negative shock from the large Swiss banks may trigger, given their very international nature as highly integrated heavyweights in the global financial infrastructure.

The last rating action with respect to the Government of Switzerland was in November 1998 when the Aaa rating was assigned to the Swiss local currency government bonds.

Other methodologies and factors that may have been considered in the process of rating this issuer can also be found in the Credit Policy & Methodologies directory on Moody's website.

title: SNB may  intervene  in markets to help economy-Jordan
text:
WEINFELDEN, Switzerland, Jan 15 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank will use means like market interventions if needed to help the economy weather the unavoidable recession as interest rates are practically at zero, SNB board member Thomas Jordan said on Thursday. The once-in-a-lifetime financial market crisis has triggered a massive global recession, hitting Switzerland's main growth driver exports, Jordan said in the text of a speech to be held at a business event in the Swiss town Weinfelden.

"Despite all uncertainties, it seems almost unavoidable from today's point of view that the Swiss economy will fall into a recession in 2009," Jordan said, repeating the SNB's December forecast of a 0.5 to 1.0 percent drop in gross domestic product.

(For abstracts of Jordan's speech click on [ID:nLF539965])

The SNB already reacted with four cuts of its target for the 3-month Swiss franc LIBOR by a total of 2.25 percentage points to just 0.5 percent.

"With the current de-facto zero-interest-rate policy the arsenal of monetary policy options has not been used up by any means," Jordan said. "The expansionary degree of monetary policy can be increased through a number of alternative instruments if necessary.

"Market interventions beyond the money market or the extension of the duration of our money market operations are for example conceivable," he said.

INFLATION

Jordan said the inflation outlook had improved significantly recently due to the fall in oil prices.

"All in all, the Swiss economy faces an extremely difficult year," he said. "Downward risks dominate as regards growth, while inflation risks tend to be balanced."

The SNB has already added a number of new tools such as currency swaps to its monetary policy kit to bring the three-month LIBOR down.

The rates in its Swiss franc funding offers are at 0.05 percent now and economists expect the central bank to use unorthodox measures to ease conditions with many betting on interventions to weaken the Swiss franc.

The currency has been rising again in recent days against the euro, the currency of Switzerland's main export markets, making Swiss products more expensive abroad and dealing exporters an additional blow, Jordan noted.

BANK LENDING

Jordan said that the Swiss economy was well placed to weather the crisis after the five-year boom as the government's and companies' finances were sound and the banking system fundamentally healthy.

In October, Switzerland had to bail out its largest bank UBS after some $50 billion in writedowns related to the crisis triggered by the collapse of the U.S. housing market.

Jordan said it was crucial banks resumed lending to each other and that the SNB would foster efforts to get excess liquidity from the state-controlled and regional banks to the big banks.

While the SNB had no indications for a credit crunch so far, risks remained, Jordan said. "The economic slowdown might still trigger a tightening of credit conditions," he said.

The slump in exports had already started an economic domino effect, Jordan said. The manufacturers were cutting production and investments and were to lay off workers. Consumers' mood had turned gloomy already and they would cut spending eventually.

title: DAVOS-INTERVIEW-IMF's Krueger-No need for  FX intervention  now.
text:
DAVOS, Switzerland, Jan 24 (Reuters) - A top policymaker at the International Monetary Fund said on Saturday that neither foreign exchange intervention nor interest rate cuts were warranted with the euro at current levels against the dollar.  

In an interview with Reuters, IMF first deputy managing director Anne Krueger said foreign exchange rates should be left to markets and financial policymakers should only consider action "in the most extreme circumstances".  

At current euro/dollar rates, she said "there is a strong presumption against" currency intervention.  

"I know of no evidence as yet that this is the most extreme of circumstances - or even close. I emphasise 'as yet'," Krueger told Reuters on the sidelines of the annual World Economic Forum meeting.  

The euro has shot up 11 percent against the dollar in the past four months and has hit record highs, raising concern currency strength will strangle the building euro zone recovery.  

European finance ministers are seeking support from their Group of Seven colleagues at an early February meeting in Florida for calming the rapid currency moves - whether through a G7 statement stressing currency stability is desirable or a commitment to intervene if needed.  

Krueger noted the euro/dollar real effective exchange rate is not far from its 30-year average. When asked whether a euro/dollar exchange rate of $1.30 would change her view, Krueger said: "No."  

"I know of no reason at this stage that we should be concerned or intervene in what seems appropriate in terms of the individual macroeconomic circumstances," Krueger said.  

Some analysts are speculating that the European Central Bank will be forced to cut interest rates to calm the euro's rise and ensure it does not undermine economic recovery.  

Krueger said the ECB should base its interest-rate decisions on what is best for the euro-zone economy and "not be constrained internationally," she said.

title: Swiss upturn prospects seen balancing soft dollar.
text:
ZURICH, Jan 13 (Reuters) - A euro zone recovery and the relative weakness of the Swiss franc against the single currency will boost Switzerland's economy and offset the impact of the soft dollar as it pulls out of a recession, the central bank said on Tuesday.   

However, whether the Swiss National Bank(SNB)would take part in any future concerted intervention to prop up the dollar remained uncertain, economists said, as the problem was seen as one of greenback weakness rather than franc strength.   

Top European bankers have expressed concern about the abrupt rise in the euro, while euro zone politicians called for ECB action to bring the euro-dollar rate back into line.   

The SNB also believes the weak dollar could harm the Swiss economy.   

"It puts an additional burden on economic development because we have companies which export largely to the dollar area," SNB spokesman Werner Abegg said.   

"But on the other hand we have seen quite a stable euro and a marked appreciation of the euro against the Swiss franc so at least there are counterbalancing elements there," Abegg said.   

Having fallen two percent since the start of the year, the dollar was last trading around 1.2270 francs on Tuesday.   

Bumping along at seven-year lows against the franc, the weak dollar makes life harder for firms with a high exposure to the U.S. and Asian nations whose currencies are tied to the dollar.   

Lombard Odier analysts warned that "as Swiss chemicals companies are all net exporters of goods, the competitive advantage they held for five entire years is seriously eroding."   

Switzerland's famous watchmaking industry has also been hit hard by the dollar's decline during a disappointing 2003, since around two-thirds of its exports go to the dollar area.   

Swiss Watch Industry Federation President Jean Daniel Pasche said the dollar weakness had made life tough for exporters. "But we are more confident for 2004 because we see a recovery in the U.S., Hong Kong and Japan," he said.   

SOFTENING SWISSIE   

Faced with a supercharged franc, the SNB slashed interest rates to near-zero levels on March 6 and took the wind out of the safe-haven currency's sails ahead of the war in Iraq.   

Some economists said at the time that the SNB had spent its ammunition too soon should the franc rise strongly again.   

However, the SNB's early move appears to have paid off with the franc falling steadily under what the export industry's pain barrier of 1.5000 level against the euro and helping stimulate a recovery driven by trade with major partners such as Germany.   

In a reverse of the watch industry's trade ratio, two-thirds of Swiss exports go to the euro zone while the remainder is destined for the United States or Asian nations.   

"An export-led recovery is picking up in Europe so the demand factor is compensating for any impediment from a weaker dollar," said Julius Baer Chief Economist Janwillem Acket.   

Acket added that since Switzerland had been able to keep the franc in check against the euro, it is not certain to join any future attempts to support the dollar through intervention.   

"It is really the Europeans in the corner and Switzerland has been able to decouple a little thanks to the fact that the franc is weaker against the euro," Acket said.   

While the SNB has repeatedly stressed it would intervene to stave off a unwanted rise in the franc against the euro, traders note that it last took part in intervention in 1995 in a concerted move to prop up the dollar.   

"They feel too small to do it," Huenerwadel said. "The SNB would be increasingly worried if the U.S. economy deteriorates going forward but so long as it is stampeding ahead they are not going to take decisive action."

title: UPDATE 1-Swiss cenbank says would  intervene  if franc jumps.
text:
FRIBOURG, Switzerland, June 26 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank would intervene on currency markets if the Swiss franc spikes higher and threatens to hamper a recovery in the Swiss economy, SNB Chairman Jean-Pierre Roth said on Thursday. 

 Speaking to Swiss watchmakers, who have been hit hard by recent franc strength which makes their goods dearer abroad, Roth reiterated the central bank considered its current expansive monetary policy stance appropriate as long as inflation was low. 

 "Deflation associated with a significant and lasting contraction in demand and production seems unlikely, as long as the Swiss franc does not rise strongly," he said in the text of a speech to the Swiss Federation of Watchmakers' annual meeting. 

 "In this case, we would take the necessary measures to reestablish the appropriate monetary conditions, including directly intervening on the currency market," he added. 

 The central bank has said that with interest rates already near zero, they would be ready to intervene alone in currency markets to quell any sharp rise in the Swiss franc. 

 When asked if he stood by those comments, Roth told reporters: "Indeed we are sticking to our policy. It is appropriate to our present situation." 

 Roth said Wednesday's 25 basis point cut in U.S. interest rates was good news. "Any effort made to strengthen the (United States) economy is good news for us," he said, but reiterated that the SNB saw zero growth in the Swiss economy in 2003. 

 While Roth signalled that the SNB was satisfied with the development of the franc against the euro, the weakness of the dollar was still a concern as a potential threat to any upturn in the battered Swiss economy. 

 "We are pleased to see the franc has weakened vis-a-vis the euro," Roth told reporters, but added in his speech: "The fall in the rate of the U.S. currency penalises firms which export to the dollar zone, particularly watch exports." 

 "The National Bank is well aware of the problems which the recent correction in the dollar poses for our economy." 

 Exports account for some 45 percent of Swiss gross domestic product and Switzerland is home to big export players such as the world's biggest watchmaker Swatch. 

 Data released on Thursday showed that while overall exports rose slightly in May as the Swiss franc eased, sales of luxury goods such as timepieces continued to fall and imports to the stagnating domestic economy dipped further. 

 "The watch business is suffering from the value of the franc against the U.S. dollar because we export a lot of products to the dollar zone," Jean-Daniel Pasche, president of the Federation, told journalists ahead of the annual meeting. 

 Pasche acknowledged that the SNB's hands were tied by near-zero interest rates, but warned that the watch industry faced a tough year after a six percent decline in sales in the first five months. 

 The SNB has reiterated that cutting rates to the current target band of 0.0-0.75 percent had created the right conditions for Switzerland to benefit from an upturn in the global economy. 

 "Monetary policy (in Switzerland) is currently expansive and it will remain so as long as price stability is not threatened," Roth said.

text:

 Roth reiterated the central bank would maintain its current expansionary monetary policy stance as long as inflation was low, adding that the SNB saw no risk of a protracted period of deflation for Switzerland. 

 "Deflation associated with a significant and lasting contraction in demand and production seems unlikely, as long as the Swiss franc does not rise strongly," he said in the text of a speech to the Swiss Federation of Watchmakers' annual meeting. 

 "In this case, we would take the necessary measures to reestablish the appropriate monetary conditions, including directly intervening on the currency market," he added. 

 The central bank has said that with interest rates already near zero, they would be ready to intervene alone in currency markets to quell any sharp rise in the Swiss franc. 

 Exports count for some 45 percent of Switzerland's gross domestic product and key industry groups, such as watchmakers, have railed against the safe-haven highs of the franc before the war in Iraq, which made their goods more expensive abroad. 

 Roth said that exchange rate developments were satisfactory overall. The franc has recently traded around 2-1/2 year lows against the euro, the currency of its main trading partners. 

 "The recent correction in the franc versus the euro has caused an additional - and welcome - easing of monetary conditions," he said. "The course of our policy is therefore well adapted to the currenct circumstances." 

 However, he added the SNB was aware of the problems which the recent weakness in the dollar caused for Swiss exporters. 

 "The fall in the rate of the U.S. currency penalises firms which export to the dollar zone, particularly watch exports," he said. "The National Bank is well aware of the problems which the recent correction in the dollar could pose for our economy." 

 However, Roth said the trend in the dollar was a correction which reflects the readjustment of international capital movements: "In this sense, it is a problem of the U.S. currency rather than an appreciation of the Swiss franc." 

 The SNB has reiterated that cutting rates to the current target band of 0.0-0.75 percent had created the right conditions for Switzerland to benefit from a long-awaited upturn in the global economy. 

 "Monetary policy (in Switzerland) is currently expansive and it will remain so as long as price stability is not threatened," Roth said.

title: SNB Rules Out Major  Intervention  To Weaken Franc/Dlr
text:
FRIBOURG, Switzerland -(Dow Jones)- Swiss National Bank President Jean-Pierre Roth Thursday said he doesn't expect the economy to grow in the second quarter of this year and ruled out substantial intervention to weaken the Swiss franc against the dollar. 

 "We knew that the dollar was overvalued when it was worth CHF1.80, it is certainly today nearer to a balanced exchange rate," Roth said in a speech to the Federation of the Swiss watch industry. 

 Roth ruled out any substantial intervention to weaken the Swiss franc against the dollar, as some exporters are asking. 

 However, Roth reiterated the SNB would intervene in the foreign exchange market if the Swiss franc weakened too much against the euro, the currency of Switzerland's main trading partners. 

 At 0916 GMT, the euro was trading at CHF1.5406, well above what is seen as the exporters' pain threshold at CHF1.52. The U.S. dollar was trading at CHF1.3424. 

 Roth said the SNB's expansive monetary policy is adequate for the current weak economic conditions and prevents the Swiss franc strengthening against the euro. 

 In the last two years the SNB has cut key interest rates by 3.25 percentage points. 

 The central bank's range for three-month Libor is 0.0%-0.75%, targeting 0.25%. 

 Roth said that before the Swiss economy starts to grow again exports have to increase, but that needed a global economic recovery. 

 Roth said that he considered deflation to be a minimal risk as long as the Swiss franc didn't appreciate considerably. However, Roth said consumer prices may fall in some months due to lower prices for imported goods. 

 The central bank predicts an average inflation rate of 0.6% for this year, slowing to 0.4% next year and then rising to 1.2% in 2005.

title: UPDATE 1-SNB's Roth - ready to  intervene  to stop franc gains.
text:
WARSAW, June 18 (Reuters) - Further appreciation by the Swiss franc could have dire consequences for Switzerland's economy and force the central bank to intervene to weaken the currency, Swiss National Bank Chairman Jean-Pierre Roth said. 

 "If again, as a result of global political uncertainty, the franc becomes a safe haven for investors, we will have no other choice but to intervene to weaken the currency," Roth told Poland's Rzeczpospolita daily in an interview on Wednesday. 

 Roth was in Warsaw on Monday. The interview was published in Polish and translated into English by Reuters. 

 "Things have gone far enough and further appreciation in the current situation could have very negative consequences for the economy," the daily quoted Roth as saying. 

 Roth said the SNB last intervened on the forex market in 1995 in a co-ordinated effort with other central banks to boost the value of the dollar. The SNB's last unilateral market intervention took place in the early 1980s. 

 The SNB, which keeps interest rates 150-200 basis points below those in the euro zone, last week vowed to push beyond the limits of traditional monetary policy to foster growth for the recession-hit, export-dependent Swiss economy. 

 Asked about the risk of deflation, Roth said: "With inflation at 0.4 percent there is a danger that some negative event would bring about a fall in consumer prices. But the real danger for us would be franc appreciation, which could be regarded as deflation of imported goods."

title: Swiss money mkt sees rate cut over franc strength.
text:
ZURICH, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Swiss money market is increasingly speculating on an imminent interest rate cut by the Swiss National Bank, with the talk fanned by SNB comments that it was concerned over the strength of the Swiss franc. 

 The central bank added fuel to the fire, they said, by providing ample money market liquidity on Wednesday, bidding to nudge market rates down so that it could also cite falling market rates as additional justification for a rate cut. 

 "If you look at the curve, then you can see that (the market) is expecting a cut," one dealer at a Swiss bank said. 

 Money market futures have been gaining in recent days, with June contracts  pointing to three-month market rates of 0.45 percent by the summer. That is a solid 30 basis points below the SNB's target rate. 

 The SNB offered overnight and two-week liquidity via repurchase agreements. It left the repo rate at 0.50 percent for now , below overnight and tomorrow/next rates in the market at 0.60 to 0.70 percent. 


With the franc trading below 1.36 to the dollar  and around 1.46 to the
euro          , the central bank said it was keeping a wary eye on
developments.



"We are concerned about the rise in the Swiss franc, which is under the
current economic circumstances especially unwelcome," SNB spokesman
Werner Abegg told Reuters.



He declined to comment on what the particular pain threshold for the
currency might be and would not be drawn on how the SNB might react to
the latest rise in the currency.



"We never talk about levels, it is the dynamics which are of concern,"
Abegg said. The central bank has said it aims to slow any rapid and
dramatic rise rather than stop it outright.



FRANC STRENGTH BLOCKS ECONOMIC RECOVERY



The franc's rise on the euro - the unit of Switzerland's main trading
partner, Germany - is making life hard for Swiss exporters already
suffering from weak domestic demand.



Market players see further room for a cut in Switzerland's already low
rates or forex market intervention to curb the franc, which could give
the economy a much-needed boost.



"To weaken the franc, they (SNB) won't do that first with a rate cut,
but rather intervene in the foreign exchange market," the dealer said.
"A rate cut will be the very last resort becuase they hardly have any
powder left."



Should the European Central Bank reduce rates, the SNB would only make
a move if the franc spiked higher versus the euro.



The SNB now targets the middle of a 0.25-1.25 percent range for the
three-month London Interbank Offered Rate - its benchmark - but the
repo rate already undercuts that midpoint.



Libor was fixed at 0.57667 percent  on Tuesday, also below the midpoint
of the target range of 0.75 percent.



Dealers say the SNB is likely to nudge down that goal to the repo rate
level. Alternatively, it might lower the repo rate and shift the target
to the lower end of the range.



WEAK DATA UPS PRESSURE



Earlier this week, Switzerland recorded its biggest trade deficit in 20
months as the flat global economy and strong franc strangled exports,
while figures showed that employment also fell in the last quarter of
2002.



Analysts will closely watch fourth-quarter GDP figures which are
expected to show growth of only between 0.4 to 0.7 percent
year-on-year, compared to 0.6 percent for the third quarter.



The numbers are due out on Thursday.



An upturn in the Swiss economy is not expected before the second half
of 2003, especially if a war in Iraq further dents the global economy
through rising oil prices.



The dollar was at 1.3573/78 francs after changing hands at 1.3546/51
francs late on Tuesday.



The euro was at 1.4606/11 francs, practically unchanged from the rate
late on Tuesday.

title: Swiss franc firms vs dollar after UN report.
text:
ZURICH, Jan 28 (Reuters) - The Swiss franc firmed slightly versus the dollar in early European trade on Tuesday after the UN weapons report on Iraq, but handed in gains made on Monday when the greenback hit multiyear lows versus European currencies. 

 The dollar  eased to 1.3554/59 Swiss francs from 1.3561/66 francs late on Monday. It had fallen to as far as 1.3460 during Monday's session ahead of the UN weapons report, seen as a possible trigger for a war in oil-rich Iraq. 

 The euro  also traded slightly softer at 1.4671/78 francs, compared with 1.4684/89 francs in late Monday trade. 

 "There are plenty of risks looming over the franc," UBS Warburg said in a note, adding that history showed the franc tended to strengthen versus other key currencies in times of geopolitical and financial markets uncertainty. 

 "In fact, the strong statements on the independence of the Swiss central bank as of late could motivate some investors into a franc engagement again," it added. 

 Outgoing SNB Vice President Bruno Gehrig said on Friday forexintervention was definitely an instrument of monetary policy in Switzerland. "But I'm not saying we will do it tomorrow," he added. 

 The SNB has to date been coy on what franc level would trigger action, leaving dealers with the impression that the central bank is basically powerless against the franc's rise. 

 While Gehrig's comments reinforce the SNB's stated intention to act, analysts say words from a departing directorate member were less likely to change the course of trading in a major way.

title: Swiss franc firms on dollar ahead of U.N. report.
text:
ZURICH, Jan 27 (Reuters) - The Swiss franc firmed further on the dollar in early European trade on Monday, touching levels not seen in just over four years, with players cautious on the outlook for the greenback ahead of a U.N. report on Iraq. 

 The dollar  eased to 1.3535/41 francs from 1.3565/70 late on Friday, hitting levels not seen since December 1998 as U.S. rhetoric on Iraqi disarmament war remained tough, even in the face of dissent of by Western partners. 

 The euro  eased slightly to 1.4661/63 francs from 1.4665/75. 

 U.N. arms inspectors, presenting a key report to the Security Council later on Monday, are expected to say Iraq has not been fully cooperative and that inspections need more time to be conclusive. 

 In the absence of a "smoking gun", London and Washington may have a tough job persuading Council members and Western partners that war on Iraq is justified. The U.S. meanwhile insists there is evidence that Iraq has weapons of mass destruction. 

 Analysts said that with such geopoltical issues unresolved, there was scope for further franc strengthening. 

 Meanwhile, they did not expect the Swiss National Bank to do more to brake the franc than talking it down. 

 Outgoing SNB Vice President Bruno Gehrig said on Friday forexintervention was definitely an instrument of monetary policy in Switzerland. "But I'm not saying we will do it tomorrow," he added. 

 The SNB has to date been coy on what franc level would trigger action, leaving dealers with the impression that the central bank is basically powerless against the franc's rise.

title: Swiss SNB May Cut Rates,  Intervene  If Franc Too Strong
text:
ST. GALLEN, Switzerland -(Dow Jones)- The Swiss National Bank said Friday it is prepared to cut rates further and to intervene in the foreign exchange market if the franc's strength were to pose a risk to growth. 

 "With money market rates below 0.75%, there isn't much room to maneuver, but there is still some," SNB Vice President Bruno Gehrig said in a speech to students at the university of St. Gallen, although he added that steering the franc reliably through interest rates was impossible. 

 The SNB, which targets the middle of a 0.25%-1.25% range for three-month Swiss franc Libor, or effectively 0.75%, has made six consecutive rate cuts in less than two years. 

 Libor has recently moved down to around 0.6% but the central bank allows for fluctuations within the band without taking rate action. 

 "In addition, if necessary, we would intervene in the foreign currency market to correct exchange-rate fluctuations (strengthening of the Swiss franc) and provide the economy with more liquidity," Gehrig also said. 

 The SNB has often lowered rates when the franc strengthened beyond what is considered a pain threshold of CHF1.45 against the euro. Exporters and unions put that ceiling at CHF1.50. 

 The euro zone takes almost two-thirds of Swiss exports. 

 On the economy, Gehrig said he expects growth barely above 1% this year and inflation between 0.5% and 1%. Deflation was unlikely, Gehrig added. 

 "A comeback to long-term trend economic growth of around 1.5% to 2% will take a couple of quarters," he said, because of slow recovery elsewhere in Europe, especially Germany. The SNB views 2% growth as sustainable and non-inflationary. 

 Gehrig said the main risks to its outlook were political and military events that could both lead to a strong appreciation of the franc - because of its safe-haven status - and endanger economic stability. 

 The franc, which has strengthened to CHF1.4667 against the euro recently because of increasing fears of a war in Iraq, was at a record CHF1.4441 versus the euro last July, when the bank last cut rates by a generous half point. 

 Gehrig, whose resignation from the SNB's board takes effect in mid-2003, is credited with being the driving force behind the SNB's bias toward loose monetary policy in the past few years. 

 -By Antonio Ligi, Dow Jones Newswires; +41 1 212 2181; antonio.ligi@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-Swiss cenbank says would  intervene  if need be on franc.
text:
ST GALLEN, Switzerland, Jan 24 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank said on Friday it would intervene if necessary if the Swiss franc rose too sharply on foreign exchange markets. 

 Outgoing SNB Vice President Bruno Gehrig said in a speech at the university of St. Gallen the biggest risk for the Swiss economy was a rise in the currency serious enough to endanger its stability. 

 "The national bank would decisively act against such a distortion," said Gehrig, who is due to leave the central bank's three-man policy-making committee in mid-2003 to join insurer Swiss Life. 

 The Swiss franc  on Friday hit a fresh four-year high against the dollar. The dollar has been under pressure for several weeks as investor concerns that a war in Iraq will prove costly for the U.S. economy, prompting the sale of U.S. assets and the flow of cash out of the greenback. 

 "Beyond this, we would if necessary intervene in the currency markets to correct an exchange rate distortion and provide the economy with additional liquidity," he added. 

 He told reporters after the speech that he had wanted to make the point that forex intervention was an instrument of monetary policy in Switzerland. 

 "But I'm not saying we will do it tomorrow," he added. 

 Gehrig also said that while room for maneuver on interest rates was no longer large, it was not yet exhausted. 

 He added that further moves by the central bank - whether a cut in its already low interest rates or market invention - would come if there were signs that Swiss franc strength could have a long-lasting negative impact on the economy. 

 "(The motivation) would be fresh upward pressure on the Swiss franc that would seriously endanger cyclical stability," he said. 

 The SNB has tried to rein in the strength of the franc with a near-zero interest rate policy. It targets the middle of a 0.25 percent to 0.75 percent range for the three-month London Interbank Offered Rate, after cuts of 2.75 percentage points since March 2001. 

 The SNB has made clear that it is concerned about the franc's strength and its effect on the nation's exports, but has restricted itself to trying to contain the upside verbally. 

 Chairman Jean-Pierre Roth said this week the SNB still had some room for maneuver on rates and the bank would become more active in the case of disturbances which drive the franc up on the dollar and euro, the unit of main trading partner Germany. 

 While Gehrig's comments reinforce the SNB's stated intention to act, analysts say words from a departing directorate member were less likely to change the course of trading in a major way. 

 Riding on the Christian Democrat (CVP) party ticket, former UBS (UBSZn.VX) chief economist Peter Buomberger has been widely tipped as the frontrunner to replace Gehrig. He is seen as a strong proponent of acting against franc strength. 

 The U.S. dollar last traded at around 1.3531/37 francs at 2220 GMT vs 1.3575/81 earlier on Friday, while the euro was at 1.4657/59 against 1.4641/47. (Reporting by Tom Armitage, edited by Gary Crosse; zurich.newsroom@reuters.com; Reuters Messaging: tom.armitage.reuters.com@reuters.net; +41 1 631 7506).
