title: POLL-Swiss  central bank  to cap further franc gains.
text:
LONDON, Oct 24 (Reuters) - The threat of central bank intervention will prevent the Swiss franc rising any higher against the dollar over the next year, even if war does break out in the Middle East, currency strategists said in a Reuters survey. 

 Against the euro, the Swiss franc will come under pressure as currency markets also focus on Switzerland's dismal growth prospects compared to the slightly better ones in the euro zone. 

 In the poll of 45 currency strategists taken October 7-10 the mid-range of forecasts put the euro at 1.4987 Swiss francs by the end of this year, at 1.48 by end-March 2003 and at 1.4924 by end-September from around 1.4675 on Thursday. 

 Until the end of next September one dollar is expected to buy about 1.48 Swiss francs, from around 1.5050 on Thursday. 

 "The Swiss franc is caught between two cross-currents," said John Normand at JP Morgan in London. "As long as there are fears of war...the risk aversion factor will be a positive. 

 "But the Swiss National Bank will resist further Swiss franc appreciation, either through interest rate cuts or through outright intervention." 

 Ever since equity markets started tumbling in 2000 the Swiss franc has been climbing as investors trying to dodge the carnage by parking their money in Switzerland. 

 After the September 11 attacks the currency was forced even higher as more money fled to the sanctuary of the Swiss franc on heightened geopolitical risks. 

 WHAT THE EXPERTS SAY 

 War rhetoric against Iraq by U.S. President George Bush has added to the uncertainty and currency strategists put the chances of war between the United States and Iraq within the next six months at 70 percent. The average length of any conflict is put at around six weeks. 

 Eight expect it to start by end-2002, 27 said January or February, one said first quarter 2003, one said March, one said June and one thought anytime between November and January. 

 In a Reuters survey of 22 defence and Middle East experts, 13 said a U.S. invasion of Iraq with United Nations backing was likely or very likely within the next six months. Most expected the conflict would start in January or February and last no more than three months. 

 The timing of any invasion tallies with when strategists expect the Swiss franc to peak briefly against the dollar at 1.45, a level last seen in July. 

 "The dollar will come under a bit of pressure in January when we think an invasion could start," said Ray Attrill at 4CAST in London. "We don't think it will take too long...but the Swiss franc will become a safe-haven again for a while." 

 Any Swiss franc gains against the euro are expected to stop short of the 1.44 "pain level" for the economy, specified by SNB board member Niklaus Blattner last February. 

 Some think the euro's decline against the franc is unlikely to exceed 1.4450 - a level last seen in September 2001 - where traders have orders to take profits. 

 The euro zone's modest growth advantage and euro interest rates at 3.25 percent versus the less then one percent for the Swiss franc should support the euro, strategists said. 

 STAGNATION 

 Forecasts for the euro by the end of March next year ranged between 1.2430 and 1.7444 francs. 

 Michael Lewis at Deutsche Bank in London said any euro advantages will be eroded by Switzerland's persistent current account surplus which in uncertain times is a big attraction. 

 "Despite explicit central bank rhetoric warning that the SNB will contemplate intervention...we would recommend selling euro/Swiss franc on any rallies," he added. 

Switzerland's central bank has in the past used intervention to suppress franc gains and in the 1970s introduced a tax on foreign deposits to stop capital inflows. 

 This time, so far, they have halved two-week money market interest rates from above one percent in May. 

 Dollar forecasts for end-March 2003 ranged between 1.33 and 1.59 Swiss francs. Advocates of a stronger dollar cite Switzerland's stagnating economy. 

 In the first and second quarters of this year gross domestic product contracted by 0.4 and 0.7 percent year-on-year. 

 "It's likely Switzerland will have zero growth this year," said Tony Norfield at ABN Amro in London. 

 "It's not a determining factor, but the franc is one of the few world currencies with interest rates lower than the dollar." 

 The U.S. Federal Reserve has cut benchmark interest rates to 40-year lows of 1.75 percent from 6.5 percent in January 2001. 

 Growth in the United States has slowed, but is nowhere near stagnation and the possibility of another cut in the funds rate is more likely to underpin the dollar then weigh on it. 

 Signs that equity markets are stabilising, perhaps even recovering, after the one of the longest bear runs in recent history are also a plus for the dollar. 

 The Swiss authorities may try to prevent another surge in the franc's exchange rate against the euro and the dollar, but some believe the market will win in the end. 

 "The good chance of action in Iraq over the next few months and Middle East tensions mean global risk aversion is still rising," said David Mann at Standard Chartered Bank in London. 

 (Additional reporting by Ruth Pitchford and Hament Bulsara).

title: Swiss  fx intervention  seen likely as tension rises.
text:
LONDON, Oct 4 (Reuters) - The threat of a U.S.-led war against Iraq is drawing money to the safety of the Swiss franc, increasing the likelihood the Swiss central bank will intervene to rein in its runaway currency, analysts said on Friday. 

 Switzerland's political and military neutrality and its large current account surplus make it an attractive place to put money at times of war. 

 But the country's own domestic picture is one of a stagnating economy, which needs a weaker franc in order to find buyers for its exports. 

 "Switzerland has been the slowest growing economy in the OECD since 1990, even slower than Japan - the motivation is not really economic for money going in there," said Steven Englander, currency economist at Citibank. 

 "The Swiss authorites would prefer to see the world return to a less risk-averse stance - they are going to talk a lot about the currency being too strong, and intervention is definitely a possibility." 

 The Swiss franc has closely followed the tensions between the United States and Iraq. 

 The currency weakened sharply last month when Iraq first agreed to let weapons inspectors into the country under existing U.N. conditions, easing fears of war. 

 But the franc strengthened as the United States made it clear it sought a new tougher U.N. resolution. 

 Credit Suisse First Boston said on Friday it revised its three-month forecast for the euro/Swiss franc rate down to 1.46 francs from 1.48 . 

 "War risk is limiting imminent Swiss franc weakness, despite weak fundamentals," analysts at CSFB said in a client note. 

 ECONOMICS - WHO CARES? 

 Data on Friday showed the number of Swiss jobless topped the psychologically key 100,000 level in September for the first time since April 1999. 

 This followed the release this week of the Swiss purchasing managers' index for September, which indicated a further contraction in Swiss manufacturing. 

 But analysts said poor domestic Swiss data was not playing a key part in currency trading decisions. 

 "Traders don't look at the Swiss data, they don't really care about Switzerland," said Jan Poser, analyst at Sarasin in Zurich. 

 The Swiss National Bank is aware of the problem. 

 SNB vice chairman Bruno Gehrig last week issued a rare warning of intervention to weaken the franc if a sharp rise in the currency threatened to hurt the economy. 

 "This is a measure of last resort, we have never used it in the recent past," he said. 

 Analysts said the central bank is likely to cut rates or even intervene if the franc returns to a record high around 1.44 per euro hit last September and approached once more in July. 

 The value of the franc against the euro is of the most concern, because the euro zone is Switzerland's main trading partner. 

 "Intervention is not in the SNB's tradition but I would not exclude it," said Poser. 

 "Every time we reach levels around 1.44 we see some sort of action - rumours about intervention, or rate cuts on two occasions." 

Switzerland last cut rates at the end of July, dropping its benchmark target range for three-month London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) to 0.25-1.25 percent. The SNB effectively targets the middle of that range, or 0.75 percent. 

 RACING AHEAD 

 Phil Roberts, technical analyst at Barclays Capital, said the charts pointed to a strong upmove for the franc, and he said the currency could revisit 1.44 by the end of the month. 

 The franc strengthened to a two-month high of 1.4540 per euro earlier this week. It is currently holding a little above a key chart level at 1.4640, Roberts said. 

 "The Swiss franc has been locked in a clearly defined appreciation trend against the euro, or the deutschemark, ever since 1993." 

 The worsening global growth outlook is also dulling investors' appetites for riskier markets, analysts said. 

 "Weak stock markets, weak growth, and all this talk of war - this is exactly the environment where a safe haven currency is well bid," said Michael Klawitter, senior currency strategist at WestLB. 

 But analysts remained doubtful that intervention could work, particularly when undertaken in isolation by a central bank, rather than as a concerted action. 

 "They could try intervention, but it's not clear whether it would be successful," said Englander.

title: UPDATE 1-Swiss won't exclude  intervention  to dampen franc.
text:
FEUSISBERG, Switzerland, Sept 26 (Reuters) - The Swiss National Bank will act quickly and decisively - perhaps even resorting to "extraordinary measures" such as currency intervention - should international jitters drive the Swiss franc higher, SNB Vice Chairman Bruno Gehrig said on Thursday. 

 "If some kind of shock causes a currency movement that would seriously damage our economy, then we would intervene," he told reporters after a speaking engagement. 

 The remarks from Gehrig, well respected by financial markets for his experience as a commercial banker, were the clearest sign yet that the central bank was ready to go to almost any lengths to prevent a too-strong franc from crushing growth in the still fragile export-dependent economy. 

 "This is a measure of last resort, we have never used it in the recent past, but it is certainly a possibility which we would never exclude in principle," Gehrig added. 

 Addressing a business audience earlier on Thursday, Gehrig acknowledged that many people - mainly exporters and their suppliers - worried about the franc's exchange rate, especially against the euro, the currency of Switzerland's main trading partners. 

 At times of increased uncertainty, money tends to flow into the currency of countries like Switzerland with large current account surpluses, he said. 

 "Unfortunately one cannot rule out the possibility that political/military events could trigger fresh fears and further strengthen upward pressure on the franc. But it is also possible that the development normalises," he said. 

 "If extraordinary shocks subject our stability to serious dangers, we will react decisively, if necessary with extraordinary measures as well," he said. 

 The National Bank rarely intervenes directly to buy or sell currencies on foreign exchange markets, and then normally only as part of concerted action by other central banks. 

 Three decades ago, Switzerland went so far as to introduce negative interest rates on foreigners' Swiss franc deposits as a way to choke off an unwanted influx of funds and relieve upward pressure on the franc. 

 But the sweeping changes on financial markets in the meantime make a repeat of such stringent capital controls unlikely in this day and age, SNB officials say. 

 AGGRESSIVE CUTS 

 Aggressive rate cuts by the central bank have dropped its benchmark target range for three-month interest rates by 2.25 percentage points over 2-1/2 years to just 0.75-1.75 percent. 

 Gehrig acknowledged that central banks are unable to steer a currency's exchange rate directly by raising or lowering interest rates, but noted easier monetary policy can help offset the restrictive impact of a rising currency. 

 The SNB has done that repeatedly over the past 18 months, he said, so even though the euro has moved in a rough range of around 1.45 to 1.48 francs since the September 11 attacks, the spread between Swiss and euro rates has widened to around 2.5 points from one point. 

 The SNB left rates steady a week ago at its quarterly policy review, but stressed its generous policy would continue until there was clear evidence that the sluggish economy was gaining momentum and pressure was easing on the safe-haven franc. 

 The economy expanded at a seasonally adjusted rate of just 0.4 percent in the second quarter versus the first and contracted 0.4 percent from the year-earlier period. 

 Gehrig said the SNB would not make the mistake of raising rates too early. 

 "Despite very low interest rates, no danger of inflation is perceptible for the foreseeable future. Even if the economic rebound turns out to be a positive surprise in the months and quarters ahead, there is enough time to make the necessary adjustments to interest rates," he said. 

 At the moment, however, "all indications now are that development in the second half of the year will remain weak. Overall growth this year should be just above zero percent," he said, and only a slow pickup was shaping up for 2003. 

 Gehrig told reporters later the Swiss economy could be growing at a rate of 1.5 to 2.0 percent toward the end of 2003. 

 Risks to the economy have shifted to the downside in recent months for the United States and even more so in Europe, he said, but he played down the prospects for Japanese-style deflation in Switzerland. 

 "Although inflation rates are low in Switzerland, we view deflation as very unlikely." Gehrig said, noting core inflation that strips out volatile items has been around one percent and domestic prices have been rising.

title: BIS- FX intervention  may not be a strong option now.
text:
BASEL, Switzerland, June 5 (Reuters) - The Bank for International Settlements in its annual report on Monday sidestepped any judgement on whether intervention should be used to address perceived problems with currencies. 

 But in remarks in its annual report released on Monday, it suggested this is not a strong option now, although this might perhaps change at some unspecified time in the future. 

 It said the situation in currency markets could raise the question of what central banks might do "aside from moving policy rates" to address perceived discrepancies. 

 "The current answer appears to be, not much. However, circumstances could conceivably change," it said. 

 It acknowledged that a strong yen and weak euro were "somewhat inconsistent" with domestic economic aims in Japan and euro zone countries. 

 The BIS, a forum for the world's central banks which itself does not intervene in currency markets, declined to make any direct remarks on when intervention would be appropriate. 

 It noted unilateral intervention by Japan has only limited impact, and bilateral intervention with Europe "has also been eschewed to date, even though, prima facie (at first glance), it would seem potentially useful in the right market conditions". 

 "One reason (intervention has not been used) might be concerns in Europe that intervention would be misread as signalling a dilution of the committment of the newly created central bank to price stability," it said. 

 As for multilateral intervention which would involve the U.S., "concerns have been expressed that this might be interpreted as the harbinger of a managed global exchange rate system, for which there currently seems to be little official enthusiasm," it said. title: DAVOS-Mundell urges ECB  intervention  to aid euro.
text:
DAVOS, Switzerland, Jan 28 (Reuters) - Nobel price-winning economist Robert Mundell on Friday urged the European Central Bank (ECB) to intervene in the forex market to stop the euro's slide. 

 "I think it's a good time for the ECB to act. The ECB should intervene in the exchange market both spot and forward," Mundell said on the fringes of the World Economic Forum's annual meeting here. 

 On Friday afternoon the euro EUR=) fell to a record low against the dollar, piercing key support at 97.79 cents and trading down to 97.39 cents. 

 Mundell said the ECB could even act on its own without consulting the Federal Reserve or the Bank of Japan. However, in the long run these countries have to agree, he stressed. 

 He said that despite the euro's continuous slide over the past year, the single European currency was credible. 

 "The euro has been credible so far," he said. This was reflected in higher forward than spot rates of the euro throughout 1999, he said, explaining this reflected the market's expectation of a higher rate in the future. 

 A factor that should push the euro higher was the increasing demand of central banks for the euro as a reserve currency. "By 2010 central banks would want to hold the same amounts of euros and dollars in reserves," he said. 

 The ECB should intervene because a further decline of the euro exchange rate would result in higher import prices and consequently increased wage demands, pushing inflation in the euro zone up. 

 "That would force a tighter monetary policy," he said. 

 He said the ECB should not ignore the euro. "If the ECB neglects the forex rate it would neglect one of the most important early indicators of inflation." 

 Turning to the overall volatility between the euro and dollar, Mundell said: "I don't believe the dollar euro rate would fluctuate like the mark/dollar rate did in the past."

title: Swiss franc slips on dlr as downtrend lasts.
text:
1600 GMT - The Swiss franc slipped against the dollar on Friday, continuing its week-long downtrend, dealers said. 


The dollar	  rose to 1.5840/50 francs from an early 1.5755/60, having broken above the 1.5743 level last seen four months ago. The U.S. currency had started the week at 1.5533/40.

 Dealers said the ECB apparently lacked the appetite to support the euro through market intervention. 

 Although Switzerland is outside the European Union     , the bloc is a key market for the Swiss and its economic fate is closely linked to that of the EU.

title: DAVOS-Japan against excessively strong yen-Sakakibara.
text:
DAVOS, Switzerland, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Japan is prepared to intervene to stop the yen from becoming too strong, the country's top financial diplomat, Eisuke Sakakibara, said on Friday. 

 He told the Davos World Economic Forum: "I didn't say a strengthening of the yen was alright. An excessively strong yen is not desirable, as well as an excessively weak yen. So when we see the currency going into the area of excessive strength, we do intervene." 

 Sakakibara, a senior Ministry of Finance official, said it was unrealistic to expect the emergence of an Asian currency bloc centred on the yen. 

 "The Asian area is a dollar-denominated area and it will continue to be a dollar-denominated area for some time to come. 

 "We are internationalising the yen... but it will probably take five to 10 years for the Japanese currency to be accepted as an international currency. So we would be patient in internationlasing the yen," he said.

title: SNB's Roth sees stable euro/Swiss franc rate.
text:
ZURICH, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Swiss National Bank Vice-Chairman Jean-Pierre Roth said the Swiss franc would probably be stable against the euro as financial markets came to realise that the two were really "sister currencies". 

 In the text of a speech to be delivered at a financial seminar in Vienna, Roth said the European Central Bank's priority to maintain price stability dovetailed perfectly with the SNB's monetary stance. 

 Also, experience has shown that converging fundamentals and similar policy objectives provide a good chance that exchange rates between the euro and the franc will remain within an acceptable fluctuation band, he said without elaborating. 

 He noted that the franc had firmed against the mark at a low annual rate of 0.5 percent from 1983 to 1998 and had fluctuated within a band of plus or minus five percent even without the SNB's having intervened on foreign exchange markets. 

 "The more Switzerland behaves like a European country, the greater the chance of currency stability between the Swiss franc and the euro," he said. 

 "We are thus confident that that the absence of major tensions observable over the last two years will be an enduring phenomenon and that the market will gradually come to recognise that the Swiss franc and the euro are two currencies belonging to the same European family." 

 He said the euro would probably be used frequently by Swiss companies, which would make the franc less widely used to pay for foreign trade transactions. Travellers will also find it easier to use euros. 

 "Given the very close relations between Switzerland and Euroland, the exchange rate sensitivity of the Swiss economy is expected to increase, which will require not only an efficient clearing system but also tight management of exchange rate risks at all levels," Roth added. 

 He reiterated that the SNB had no intention of setting a fixed parity for the franc against the euro because markets would not take it as an irrevocable decision. 

 "As long as Switzerland is not a member of the European Union, it will be difficult to convince the market that any parity of the Swiss franc will never be adjusted," he said. 

 "Any attempt to set a parity would thus stimulate speculation instead of calming it down. It is therefore in our interest to maintain a flexible relation between the Swiss franc and the euro." 

 A strong link between the franc and the euro could also endanger Switzerland's traditional advantage of having lower interest rates than elsewhere in Europe, he added. 

 Roth repeated that the SNB would not rule out intervention on foreign exchange or money markets to combat exchange rate fluctuations that it considered out of line with economic fundamentals. 

 "A relaxation of monetary policy in reaction to pressures on the Swiss franc is a clear option," he said, repeating the SNB's standard line. 

 He noted that the SNB had been able to keep the franc's fluctuations against the mark within acceptable margins over the past two years without trying to stabilise the exchange rate. 

 "Our intention is to maintain such a flexible approach when the Monetary Union starts on January 1, 1999," he said.

title: Swiss Franc Maintains Upward Edge Vs DM, Rate Cut Talk
text:
ZURICH (Dow Jones)--Upward pressure on the Swiss franc (CHF) against the Deutsche mark (DM) continues early afternoon Tuesday despite renewed money-market intervention by the Swiss National Bank. 

 For the third trading day running, the SNB Tuesday added generous liquidity to the money market, at a rate said by traders to be below the central bank's 1.0% discount rate. 

 The move led to brief mark gains to above CHF0.8050, but by 1120 GMT mark-franc cross trading was back to CHF0.8045. Late Tuesday, the mark was at CHF0.8034. 

 Meanwhile, dollar franc trading remains tightly range bound. One dollar currently buys CHF1.4618, down from CHF1.4643 late Monday. 

 'The SNB was in the money market again this morning,' said a trader at a bank in Liechtenstein. 'But (these liquidity injections) are only fighting the symptoms.' 

 Root cause of the Swiss currency's unwelcome strength are its 'safe haven' image on the back of worries about European economic and monetary union, the stand-off in the Gulf and the Asian financial crisis. 

 In the interests of reviving the country's moribund economy, the SNB has fought since 1996 to bring the Swiss franc's strength down. The nearer the mark slips to CHF0.8000 the more speculation rises that the central bank will have to cut its key discount rate. 

 'I expect we'll get to test CHF0.8000 again this week,' said another trader in Switzerland. Should this barrier be breached, direct foreign exchange intervention or a discount rate cut could be on the cards, he said. 

 While the mark has strengthened against the franc in comparison to Monday, traders noted persistent selling of the German currency above CHF0.8050. 

 Support is currently pegged at CHF0.8025-0.8030, with traders eying Friday's franc-high of CHF0.8012 as a vital marker beyond that. 

 Whether Thursday's meeting of the SNB directorate will bring a rate cut is far from certain. Some traders said the SNB may be happy to continue its money-market operations for some time yet before reaching for more drastic tools.

title: Official  forex  reserves surge in 1995 - BIS.
text:
BASLE, Switzerland, June 10 (Reuter) - Central bank intervention to brake and reverse the dollar's decline against the yen and mark in 1995 boosted official foreign exchange reserves at the fastest pace since 1987, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said. 

 In its annual report, BIS also said the dollar's share in global official reserves had remained stable in the 1990s at about two-thirds, surprising many observers. 

 Dollar reserve growth in 1995 of $121 billion accounted for more than two-thirds of the growth in exchange-rate adjusted reserves of $168 billion. 

 The amounts of official foreign exchange reserves outstanding at end-1995 amounted to $1.36 trillion with dollar reserves amounting to $881 billion. 

 "The similarity to 1987 extends to the reliance of the United States on official sources of funds to finance the bulk of its $153 billion current account deficit," BIS said. 

 Net of the $6.0 billion build-up in reserves by U.S. authorities, financing by central banks and other official holders totalled about $115 billion. 

 "Thus, central banks and governments financed more than two-thirds of the U.S. current account deficit, much the same proportion as in 1987," BIS added. 

 BIS said the dollar's share in global official reserves had remained stable in the 1990s, surprising many observers in light of the long list of countries that are thought to have diversified their reserves away from the dollar. 

 But the apparent contradiction is resolved by looking at the country composition of reserve growth, BIS said. 

 "Developing countries with currencies closely aligned with the dollar, and with reserves weighted more towards the dollar that the global average, have been gaining reserves at a higher-than-average rate," BIS said. 

 BIS added that the willingness of investors to buy into the money and equity markets of developing countries suggests that these countries' reserves will continue to grow.

title: Switzerland /Lusser -2: Not Obligated To  Intervene
text:
ZURICH (AP-Dow Jones)--Outgoing Swiss National Bank President Markus Lusser said Tuesday that the Deutsche mark-Swiss franc cross rate is 'decidedly stable.' 

 Lusser, in a speech set for delivery in Freiburg, Germany, noted that Switzerland isn't a member of the European Monetary System. 'The Swiss National Bank explicitly follows no currency rate target,' he told a business audience. The central bank 'is therefore also not obligated to intervene if the currency rate reaches a certain level. 

 'Despite this, the currency rate of the Swiss franc to the German mark, which has an especially important meaning to the Swiss economy, is decidedly stable,' Lusser said. 

 He traced this stability to the monetary policies of Germany and Switzerland that aim to keep inflation at bay. Lusser said both central banks are the only ones in the world that follow monetarist policies so strictly. 

 It came as no surprise, he said, that the more problematic currencies were the weak European ones and the dollar. 'The countries with these currencies don't follow a consistent monetarist strategy in the way the Deutsche Bundesbank and the Swiss National Bank do,' he said. 

 He also said that Switzerland's medium-term monetary policy allows it to react flexibly in the short-term to shifts in money demand. 

 The resolute fight against inflation pursued by the German and Swiss central banks, he said, makes both countries 'safe havens' and gives them the advantage of low interest rates. 

 'Foreign investors are prepared to invest their assets with us, with relatively low yields,' he said. 'They assume that our currencies, in the case of a crisis, won't lose value.' 

 But he noted that the Swiss franc can be subjected to more severe overshooting phases than the Deutsche mark faces. 'This represents a greater problem for our country,' he said.

title: Swiss central banker questions value of  intervention .
text:
ZURICH, June 2 (Reuter) - The head of Switzerland's central bank challenged the value of intervention in foreign-exchange markets on Friday, saying experience showed it was costly. 

 Swiss National Bank President Markus Lusser said his bank and most other central banks had grown "increasingly sceptical about the benefits of short-term exchange rate management." 

 His comments in a speech prepared for delivery in Los Angeles came just two days after his own bank joined the U.S. Federal Reserve and 10 other central banks to buy dollars in a coordinated intervention that caught markets by surprise. 

 SNB officials have often said privately they doubt the value of trying to manipulate the currency market. They say the bank generally only takes part in coordinated intervention to show solidarity with other central banks. 

 Lusser said the SNB had come under pressure again recently from trade unions, industrialists and people in the Swiss tourism sector to curb the Swiss franc's strength because of what they saw as its adverse impact on the economy. 

 But he noted the SNB's attempts in 1978 and 1987 to intervene to halt a soaring franc had been unhappy experiences. 

 Heavy intervention in late 1978 to try to keep the German mark above 80 Swiss centimes had caused the money supply to jump. After a delay, inflation rose sharply too and the economy did not get back to normal till 1983, he added. 

 Lusser said the situation in 1987 was similar. The franc had been appreciating for two years when the SNB loosened monetary policy to try to make the economy competitive again. The result was that "in 1989, with the usual time lag of two years, inflation began to rise sharply." 

 He went on: "With benefit of hindsight, we realise that even brief interventions have turned out to be more costly than originally anticipated." 

 The long-term costs of inflation by far outweighed the benefits of a short-term depreciation, he added.

title: Intervention  May Provide Some Short-Term Aid For Dollar
text:
LONDON (AP-DJ)--Wednesday's coordinated intervention exercise may provide some short-term support for the dollar against the Deutsche mark and the yen, unlike previous attempts to help the U.S. currency this year. 

 But, market analysts warned, the impact on the market has been largely psychological and the dollar will only be able to extract longer-term benefits if the operation is backed by policy. 

 'The key question is whether this is a prelude to interest rate changes,' said Michael Burke, currency analyst at Citibank in London. If not, he suggested, the dollar will end up right where it started. 

 The exercise, the first intervention by the major central banks since April 5, certainly came as a surprise. 

 Central banks outside the U.S. had previously made it plain they didn't see the dollar's decline as their problem. Although as many as 19 had participated at one stage last year, their presence in later intervention exercises had become conspicuously token. 

 This time round, however, market sources reported a two rounds sharp round of intervention led by the U.S. Federal Reserve and backed by the other countries in the Group of Ten major industrialized nations (G-10). 

 The Central Bank of Ireland confirmed that smaller countries such as itself weren't asked to participate. The group actually consists of eleven countries: the U.S., Japan, Germany, France, Canada, Italy, Britain, the Netherlands, Sweden, Belgium and Switzerland. 

 The total amount of intervention was hard to gauge with estimates for the exercise ranging up to $5 billion. Julian Jessop, an economist at Midland Global Markets, described it as 'very aggressive.'
